title: Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months
abstract: Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue. The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP , a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js , the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled. Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin , as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

title: All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t
abstract: Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results. For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang. Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees. Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company. Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer. Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him. An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang. So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back. China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China. But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025. Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact. So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up. China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money. The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China. Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals ?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans. Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come , has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

title: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
abstract: OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public. At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.” The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients. The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing. The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure. “OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.” The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court. It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed. In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.” In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” Updated 12:23 p.m. PT: Added OpenAI statement.

title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
abstract: U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy. “He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims. The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report. Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang. “A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.”

title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
abstract: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement. Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom. Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information. “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.” OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips. Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up. “Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.” Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure. “I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
abstract: The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry. In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks. Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up. In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.” The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease. Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people. The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers. The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers. A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim. Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials. “Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen. A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers. After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks. It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online , which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea. Updated with response from Barracuda.

title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the ‘Wolf of Wall Street’
abstract: Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York. I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense , but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him. It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”) You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July , noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year. But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.) Now he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”). Belfort says the platform, called Tone , is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice. It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer). But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard. Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. What have you built? It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically. Is this effectively trained on you? It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made. How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together? Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own. Who are your customers, and how do they use it? We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale. How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script? It never says, “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that. Have you generated any revenue from Tone yet? Have you raised funding for it? Revenue, probably about a million bucks — $700,000, maybe. We’ve raised friends and family and seed, about $10 million. I want to address the elephant in the room. You have a fraud conviction. Pishevar has faced misconduct allegations that he denies . Why should a bank or a hospital or a consumer brand trust this product coming from the two of you? All I can say for myself is that I did make mistakes. It was a very, very long time ago, and I’ve spent the last 20-plus years teaching people all over the world. I’ve been hired by companies all over the world to teach sales and persuasion. If some companies don’t want to work with us, that’s their decision. But I think there would be more than enough that would see the value of what we created. What close rate does Tone have versus a typical sales force? I still don’t think it’s quite as good as a top producer. A top producer in the field would outdo it call for call. I think that will change in the next six months to a year. To make a model respond this quickly, you’re not using frontier models. We’re using our own very small, very light models, so they don’t have quite as much intelligence. I think it will significantly outperform a mediocre closer. Where is it used most effectively? Low-dollar sales opportunities? I’d think the more money someone is spending, the more human contact they’d demand. I don’t think it’s about replacing humans. What I see most with customers is that they simply don’t have the human capital available. They could get a lot more leads than they have people to call, or they need coverage at different times of day or in different languages. I think there’s always going to be a need for great human salespeople. I really believe that. You’re competing with ElevenLabs and Cartesia and a lot of other voice AI companies. Tone is your edge? I don’t think sounding human is really what this is about. They’ll all sound human in six months or a year.

title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
abstract: OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing. OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI. The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat. The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user. Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions. Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers. With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI. Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release. At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits. Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations. Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work. Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged. In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.” In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.” The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable. Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route follow-up through OpenAI. That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside independent AI safety research group Redwood. Buck Shlegeris, CEO of Redwood, said in a post on Monday that the agreements announced don’t meet the bar of granting third parties “employee-like access,” saying it’s “disappointing but not surprising.” OpenAI said that they'd have embedded evaluations with employee-like access; the agreements announced today obviously don't meet that bar. This is disappointing but not surprising. Maybe future agreements will be better. https://t.co/kmDbg1Dqav — Buck Shlegeris (@bshlgrs) November 16, 2026 The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.” That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators.

title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
abstract: OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement. The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM. OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images. What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently. OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children , the Lucy Faithfull Foundation , and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages. The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI. OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children . The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint , updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content , retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content , and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens .

title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks
abstract: Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The company on Monday launched a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample. The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says. The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews. The feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let users engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets. Audible’s new feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews. But such a feature could limit users’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.) Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata. The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books. The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company said. “Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.

title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
abstract: The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. Under the interim rule , the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries. The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others. The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries. “This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.” The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions. Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S. The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group. The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S. Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect. Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media. The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies. “By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”

title: Google Maps can now build trip itineraries with real-time details about each stop
abstract: Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users. The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day. Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions. Image Credits: Google For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop. When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop. Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses. Image Credits: Google The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf. Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
abstract: Dreamteam , a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge. The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation. Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring. Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said. That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks. At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers. Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers. The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.” Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them. Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software. “We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms. Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products. Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code. Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

title: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
abstract: Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people. The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months. The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys. Image Credits: Apple Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues. Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours. Image Credits: Apple “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week .

title: Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
abstract: Tech AI News Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. by Emma Roth Nov 16, 2026, 11:17 PM UTC Photo by Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Part Of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. What happens next? see all updates Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO. At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; s ubsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia , including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg . David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times ’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN , which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor ’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying : “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.” Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said , “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.” SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole. More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter , calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
abstract: AI News Policy California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims. OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims. by Emma Roth Nov 16, 2026, 8:46 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday , Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters . The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing. After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website , a German wiki site , and the software package manager RubyGems . OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.” OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge . “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
abstract: AI News Tech Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’ Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’ Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 16, 2026, 8:41 PM UTC Part Of RAM price hikes: the latest on the global memory shortage see all updates Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.” The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday. Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast , Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month , saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.” AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles . Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.” Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying: “The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.” Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated. title: Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
abstract: Science AI Policy Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers They may have a point.﻿ They may have a point.﻿ by Ellen Thomas Nov 16, 2026, 8:29 PM UTC Constellation’s Clinton Clean Energy Center’s single nuclear reactor power plant, July 25, 2025 in Clinton, Illinois. Meta signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation for the output from the plant. Image: Getty Images Part Of Fall 2026 earnings watch see all Ellen Thomas is an independent reporter focused on business investigations, analysis and news. She previously covered the AI data center boom for Business Insider. Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave. “I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said. Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors. Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate. Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”) Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said. Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale. Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation. “The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.” Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about. In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle. In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat. The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life. Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “ mixed ,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills. Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for. On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.” “The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.” Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have welcomed them with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures. Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power.

title: US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
abstract: AI Science Climate US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create. The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create. by Justine Calma Nov 16, 2026, 8:27 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Part Of All the latest updates on AI data centers see all updates Justine Calma is a senior science reporter covering energy and the environment with more than a decade of experience. She is also the host of Hell or High Water: When Disaster Hits Home , a podcast from Vox Media and Audible Originals. Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions. The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels. “We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.” “The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.” Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025. Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative. Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal. Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.” Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year. The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes. Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge. Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use. “Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.
