title: Apple is testing daily usage limits for more complex Siri AI interactions
abstract: Tech AI News Apple is testing daily usage limits for more complex Siri AI interactions Frequent users of some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features will require an iCloud Plus subscription to avoid limits.﻿ Frequent users of some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features will require an iCloud Plus subscription to avoid limits.﻿ by Andrew Liszewski Nov 16, 2026, 7:24 PM UTC Image: Apple Andrew Liszewski is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid. Apple released betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 today, and the company is using the update to test new per device daily usage limits for some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features, according to MacRumors . Basic Siri commands and requests will remain free and unlimited, but more advanced features that rely on cloud-based processing like generating, cleaning up, or extending images in Photos will be subjected to the daily limits. There are four categories of limited usage, MacRumors reports, including using Siri AI for “multi-step, personal context requests,” image generation and editing tools, automations in Shortcuts that “rely on Apple Foundation Cloud and Cloud Pro Models,” and third-party apps that use those same cloud models. Apple hasn’t specified exactly how many times those features and tools can be used each day before limits are reached, but they’ll vary based on the task. The company reportedly plans to provide notifications when users are approaching their limit and have finally reached it. Instead of having to wait until midnight each day for your usage to reset, most of Apple’s existing iCloud Plus plans (excluding the 50GB option) will include higher daily limits at their same price. The $2.99/month 200GB subscription includes 2x the usage, the $9.99/month 2TB plan includes 5x the usage, while the $29.99/month 6TB and $59.99 12TB/month options bump the usage limit to 10x and 20x, respectively. Family members sharing an iCloud Plus subscription will have a shared usage pool that’s used on a first come, first served basis. Last week Apple updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for that app’s intelligent assistant through $49.99 Intelligence Usage Packs that are expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers. title: OpenAI wants to stop deepfakes from overwhelming child abuse tiplines
abstract: Policy AI Report OpenAI wants to stop deepfakes from overwhelming child abuse tiplines The classifier flagged fewer false positives for humans to review, while getting better at identifying abusive content. The classifier flagged fewer false positives for humans to review, while getting better at identifying abusive content. by Lauren Feiner Nov 16, 2026, 7:23 PM UTC Image: The Verge Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform. OpenAI is announcing a tool that it says will help child sexual abuse investigators cut through the noise to find harmful material they can act on quickly. At a Monday press briefing in Washington, DC, OpenAI announced a classifier it says can better detect abusive imagery of kids, including whether it’s AI-generated. It’s also offering free access to vetted organizations, giving developers more guidance on how to detect this type of content, and helping to train law enforcement on how AI can aid their investigations. The news comes as policymakers and others are pushing for more safety restrictions on AI tools, accusing OpenAI and other companies of facilitating harm to children. In recent years, AI-generated sexual images of children have threatened to overwhelm systems like the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) CyberTipline, which collects and triages reports of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The CyberTipline received 400,000 generative AI-related reports in 2025, an exponential increase from the 67,000 it received in 2024, and researchers have warned that the influx could make NCMEC’s workload “unmanageable.” The US government has stated that both AI-generated and non-AI-generated CSAM is illegal, and 48 states have laws to address sexually explicit AI deepfakes. But the tools to make them are widely available , and researchers say that a flood of fake images can make it harder to tell when a child is actively experiencing harm. The influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive” North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who cochairs the AG Alliance’s AI Task Force , said at OpenAI’s event that the influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive” — and if they keep going that way, “it is going to mean that we fail in our mission.” Tech companies are facing a range of policy proposals that could require them to take more action against CSAM and other potentially harmful content for kids. The Take It Down Act now requires social media platforms to remove real or AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours, and the newly elected Congress could seek to take stronger action against AI companies like SpaceXSI, whose Grok chatbot went on an undressing spree earlier this year. Last month eight states sued OpenAI for a separate set of alleged harms to children, citing lawsuits alleging ChatGPT encouraged illegal substance use and suicide. OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images, while the images it did identify were twice as likely to contain abusive material. It’s designed to catch abusive AI-generated images produced by a variety of tools, including open-source models and nudifying apps. It’s also the first broadly available CSAM classifier with a specific flag for AI-generated material, said OpenAI’s head of child safety public policy, John Buckley, at the briefing. “It’s important for industry to be able to understand what images may contain a fictional child versus a real child,” Buckley added. “That triage is critical in law enforcement reporting flows.” He also emphasized, however, that laws should recognize the harm of AI-generated CSAM: “It potentially erodes social norms in offending against children, and it’s often found colocated with child sexual abuse imagery of real children,” Buckley said. OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images OpenAI’s own ChatGPT image generator is designed to deny user requests for CSAM. Now, users who attempt to produce it will be shown a new warning developed with expert guidance to try to encourage them to seek help. A first offense will trigger a 24-hour pause in accessing ChatGPT and warn the user their account could be permanently closed, while offering support resources to combat the behavior. OpenAI says it reports “all instances of CSAM” to NCMEC. In a statement, Buckley explained that the 24-hour pause is based on expert advice for best practices “and international evidence on what works to prevent and respond to CSAM seeking vs CSAM generation.” The point is “to interrupt harmful behavior and direct people toward specialist help to stop it.” Jackson said that North Carolina and many other states now have laws that cover synthetic CSAM, but that partnering with a tech company like OpenAI to help deter its creation is a fairly novel approach to an emerging issue. “Most of what AGs do is accountability work,” he told reporters at the briefing. “Most of our jurisdiction kicks in after the fact to hold people accountable for harm. But with this, we wanted to see if it was possible to develop a model of working together to prevent that harm. And I would say it’s still basically an experiment.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back
abstract: Tech AI News Nvidia’s board is reportedly ‘not considering’ hiring Jensen Huang back Nvidia’s board of directors is still focused on an investigation into Huang, CNBC reports. Nvidia’s board of directors is still focused on an investigation into Huang, CNBC reports. by Emma Roth Nov 16, 2026, 6:43 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC . A source tells the outlet the board “is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back.” Since Huang’s resignation last week , tech executives, along with current and former Nvidia employees, have called for his reinstatement. An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures , including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad. President Donald Trump said on Monday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues. Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct . title: Audible is trying to make it easier to find audiobooks you’ll actually like
abstract: Tech AI News Audible is trying to make it easier to find audiobooks you’ll actually like Audible’s new audio discovery feature will read you an AI overview of your next audiobook.﻿ Audible’s new audio discovery feature will read you an AI overview of your next audiobook.﻿ by Jess Weatherbed Nov 16, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Here’s what the new audio discovery feature looks like in the Audible app. Image: Audible Jess Weatherbed is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews. Audible is introducing an AI-assisted synopsis feature that’s designed to help users determine whether they’ll enjoy an audiobook before they jump in and start listening to it. The new audio discovery feature combines audiobook samples, AI overviews, and author commentary to give users more information before choosing their next story, in addition to recommended audiobook collections that are personalized to individual listening tastes. Audio discovery provides a soundbite synopsis, with the aim of preventing Audible users from having to research titles on other platforms. The feature plays users a snippet of the audiobook and a brief AI-generated overview including its themes and listener reactions, drawing from reviews and other publicly available data. It can also include commentary from an author or Audible editor, which is pulled directly from past Audible interviews. “Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend. With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you, from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author,” Audible chief product and analytics officer Andy Tsao said in the announcement. “Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily.” Audio discovery is rolling out on select English-language titles in the US, with plans to eventually expand to other regions. Audible is also using AI to personalize audiobook collections around users’ listening tastes, in an effort to make titles that don’t appear on best-selling lists easier to discover. Like audio discovery, these personalized collections are rolling out to customers in the US, and also include commentary from Audible’s editors. Audible users in the US will also start seeing AI-curated recommendation categories based on what they usually listen to. Image: Audible These are the latest AI-powered features that Audible is introducing in an effort to attract new users and fend off growing competition from rival platforms like Spotify . As part of this update, Audible is also expanding two beta features: Ask a Question , which allows users to ask AI about characters, plot points, references, and more; and Recaps, which provides spoiler-free audio summaries of what the user has already listened to. These are now available for a “select set” of additional English-language titles in the US, according to Audible, with a broader rollout planned to start in December. title: Google Maps can now create trip itineraries for you
abstract: Tech AI News Google Maps can now create trip itineraries for you The AI-powered Ask Maps feature can suggest stops for your next trip, while providing real-time details about each location. The AI-powered Ask Maps feature can suggest stops for your next trip, while providing real-time details about each location. by Emma Roth Nov 16, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Image: The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Google is launching a new AI trip-planning feature for Maps that allows the app to create custom itineraries for you and provide real-time details about each stop. The update, which is rolling out to the Gemini-powered Ask Maps chatbot inside the app, lets you plan a one-day outing or a trip spanning several days. As an example, Google says you can use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping, or have it create a schedule for a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. From there, Ask Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with a list of stops, while also showing your route and numbered pins for each location on the map. You can share the itinerary with friends or family members, as well as export it to Google Docs on desktop. You can ask Maps to show your trip schedule before you leave, or select the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. Along with directions, Google Maps will display real-time information about traffic, a location’s hours, and more. You can also view “know before you go” details about parking, car charging, weather conditions, potential delays, and tolls during your trip. In addition to trip planning, you can now use Ask Maps to find specific beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, and have it call the locations for you. You can also use Ask Maps to find saved places on your list by asking something like, “Which spots on saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” Google is expanding Ask Maps to over 30 countries in Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK. Trip-planning and saved list search is rolling out to the more than 200 countries where Ask Maps is available, while “know before you go” tips and appointment-finding are launching in the US to start. abstract: New Ask Maps features to help with holiday travel and prep Nov 16, 2026 | Build custom road trip itineraries, get route tips, find local appointments, and search your saved lists with new Ask Maps features. Maz Khorasani Product Director, Google Maps Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. These tools provide real-time route details, check business availability, and manage your schedule to simplify your seasonal travel and errands. Our new agentic capabilities allow you to book beauty, pet care, and home repair appointments easily. You can search your saved lists to find local spots with immediate availability for your guests. We are launching new Ask Maps features to help you manage your holiday plans. These tools provide real-time updates on traffic, business hours, and parking to keep your trips moving. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer The holidays are a busy time between shopping for gifts, planning travel, and celebrating with loved ones. To help you stay one step ahead this season, we’re launching new Ask Maps features that make it easy to create itineraries, find available appointments, and search your lists in a snap so you can enjoy stress-free festivities. Get on-the-go help with your holiday road trips Now you can build step-by-step trip itineraries and get helpful, real-time details about your route right when you pull up directions. Use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping or something more complex — like a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. You'll get a day-by-day schedule with insider tips and numbered map pins for each stop, making it easy to visualize the plan. Once you're happy with the itinerary, share it with friends and family, or export it to Google Docs on desktop. When you’re about to head out, use Ask Maps to pull up your itinerary or look for the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll see real-time details like live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and even what the vibe is at your next stop. You can also adjust your schedule on the fly. Just use Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or lunch spot along the way. Then, tap to get directions to your next stop right from your itinerary. Whether you're taking a multi-day road trip or running errands around town, Maps keeps you a step ahead. Pull up directions to see helpful “Know before you go” tips about your route, including where to park or charge your car, and real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls. Check off your holiday prep and let Maps find appointments for you Holiday prep comes with a long list of to-dos. Now, with new agentic capabilities, you can choose to have Ask Maps find beauty, pet care, auto and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. Just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses so it’s easy to decide what to book. Show your guests the best spots on your lists If you have friends visiting and want to show them around, now you can use Ask Maps to find saved places on your lists in seconds. Just ask, “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability so you can pick a place and go. These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS just in time for the holidays. As part of today’s news, Ask Maps starts expanding to 30 countries across Europe — including Spain, Germany, and the U.K. — bringing Ask Maps to more than 200 countries and territories globally. title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
abstract:
Back to Articles Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run Published November 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 35 +29 Célina Hanouti celinah Follow Victor Mustar victor Follow Bertrand Chevrier kramp Follow Lucain Pouget Wauplin Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Eliott Coyac coyotte508 Follow Julien Chaumond julien-c Follow Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Routing powered by OpenRouter OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability
zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput
zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price
zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video and audio generation Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . See where your requests go On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Breaking change: custom provider keys Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. What's next This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face. More tasks routed through OpenRouter. Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

title: Meet Meta’s JiTTests: LLM-Generated Tests Designed to Fail Before Risky Code Lands
abstract: Meta has moved Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) from research prototype into its production infrastructure . Meta JiTTests is an LLM-based system that writes executable tests designed to fail on a risky code change. A failing test is concrete evidence that a diff changed behavior. Meta team reports that JiTTests caught 74 privacy SEVs at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. The method is described in the FSE 2026 research paper ‘Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ‘. Catching JiTTests are LLM-generated tests that should fail when a diff introduces a bug. Traditional hardening tests pass when written and guard against future regressions. Catching tests target the change under review, before it lands. Meta formalized the details in its 2025 paper ‘Harden and Catch’ . Most AI bug tools act like faster human reviewers. They read the diff and leave comments. JiTTests instead execute code and show a concrete behavioral difference. Meta team concedes this takes more computational steps. It argues the approach catches bug classes that LLM or agent review can miss. The production pipeline has 5 stages: The dodgy diff workflow assumes every diff is buggy. It treats the diff as a mutant of its parent and generates tests that tell them apart. The intent-aware workflow first infers what the diff should do from its code, title and summary. It lists risks, builds a mutant for each, and writes tests to kill them. Tests that then fail on the real diff become ‘weak catches.’ The research team analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Diff-aware methods produced 4x more candidate catches than hardening tests. They produced 20x more than tests that failed by coincidence. The intent-aware workflow produced weak catches in 6.4% of its tests and on 7.9% of diffs. Dodgy diff scored 2.5% and 4.0%. Meta’s earlier ACH mutation-guided hardening scored 0.8% and 1.6%. The rule-based and LLM assessors cut human review load by 70%. *Figures from Table 1 of the JiTTests paper (self-reported, Meta codebase). TestGen-LLM row uses the “need not add coverage” setting. A weak catch is a candidate failure, not a confirmed bug. The initial deployment was modest. Meta reported 41 candidate catches to engineers. 8 were confirmed true positives, a 19.5% rate. 4 of those would have caused serious failures in production. The October 2026 engineering post reports much stronger production numbers: Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews every output. Human-on-the-loop means engineers set criteria and monitor results in aggregate. They intervene at the policy level, not on each test. Meta team rarely need to read test code. They only confirm whether an observed behavior change was intended. The answer is No. JiTTests is internal Meta infrastructure. Meta has not released code, models or an API. Teams can still copy the pattern: diff-aware mutation-guided test generation, an LLM judge ensemble, deterministic filters and aggregate human oversight. Check out the engineering post , the FSE 2026 paper and Meta’s announcement on X . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . title: Alibaba Releases Qwen4-Max: 2.4T MoE, 71B Active, 1M Context
abstract: Alibaba’s Qwen team has released Qwen4-Max , the first model of its Qwen4 generation. Qwen4-Max is a proprietary sparse MoE model with a 2.4T-parameter backbone and 71B parameters active per token. It accepts text, images and video, and supports a 1M-token context window . Alibaba also cut API prices and reports a 62% drop in average cost per task. Qwen4-Max is a multimodal MoE language model from Alibaba, built for long-horizon professional work. A Token Plan-only preview opened this month only . Qwen4 upgrades the sparse MoE design in 3 places: attention, residual connections and embeddings. Alibaba reports no loss spikes across the 2.4T-scale pre-training run. On in-house tests, Qwen4-Max-Base shows 5 to 13% lower bits per byte than Qwen3.8-Max-Base. It does this while activating 25% fewer parameters. Alibaba’s comparison chart covers 16 benchmarks. Rivals are Qwen3.8-Max-0902, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Kimi K3.1. Several scores are cited from third-party leaderboards. None were independently reproduced at launch. Qwen4-Max ranks first on 4 of 16 benchmarks: Claude Opus 5.5 leads 7 of the 16 charts. Qwen4-Max trails most clearly on coding and vision: On Alibaba’s own Work360 benchmark, Qwen4-Max scores 52.69, up from 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Work360 spans 26 top-level domains and 721 specialized fields. Two things stack: fewer tokens and lower prices. On Work360, token use drops about 24% at Xhigh effort and 35% at High effort. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, the drops are about 48% and 49%. Average Work360 cost per task falls from $4.43 to $1.67, a 62% cut. List prices fell too. Input is $1.50 per million tokens , down from $2 for Qwen3.8-Max . Output is $4.50, down from $6. Implicit cache reads drop 70%, from $0.25 to $0.075. *Scores from Alibaba’s Qwen4-Max chart . Qwen3.8 column is Qwen3.8-Max-0902. The chart labels Kimi as “Kimi K3.1”. Moonshot’s own card reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 of 65.7 for Kimi K3.1 Pro and 66.4 for Opus 5.5. The model ID is qwen4-max on QwenCloud . The API works with OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible clients. Supported features include function calling, structured outputs, context caching, batch processing, web search and fine-tuning. The default rate limit is 5,000,000 tokens per minute. Thinking mode is toggled with enable_thinking . Subscription access runs through the Token Plan . Check out the official Qwen4-Max blog , the QwenCloud model page and the Token Plan pricing page . title: Hark Releases Handoff², a 2x Faster Computer-Use Agent for Hark Pro
abstract: Hark has released Handoff² , the second version of the computer-use agent inside its Hark Pro app. The Hark Handoff 2 computer-use agent finishes web tasks about 2x faster than the original, on average. Hark states that the gains come from reinforcement learning (RL) that penalized wasted turns and latency. For teams building browser agents, it is a case study in training for speed, not only accuracy. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Handoff² is a computer-use agent from Hark that operates websites the way a person does. It clicks, types and scrolls on live pages instead of calling APIs. Hark previewed Handoff in August and shipped it in Hark Pro in October. Since then, Hark says it has logged over 5.6M browsing sessions and handled over $20M in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications. Hark co-evolved 2 things: the agent harness and the RL training recipe. The new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn. Training then penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency. Each request runs on a dedicated virtual computer with its own browser, file system and terminal. The model outputs cursor and keyboard actions aimed at screen coordinates. Because savings stack per turn, gains grow on longer, browsing-heavy tasks. Hark reports these speedups over v1 : Hark reports 2 internal benchmarks: Hark ran Claude Opus 5.5 (max) in the same harness as Handoff². Handoff² lands within 5 points of it. Note that v1 was measured in its original harness, not the new one. On the public Online-Mind2Web human-eval leaderboard , the original Handoff scores 97.67%. Yutori’s Navigator n1.5 sits at 97.3%. Hark has not posted an Online-Mind2Web result for Handoff² yet. Handoff² ships inside Hark Pro on the web, iOS and Android . Hark has not announced a public API or weights. Per the pricing page , Hark Pro is free. Pro² costs $20 a month for 2x usage. Pro³ costs $100 a month for 10x usage. All features are offered on all plans. Check out the Hark’s Handoff² announcement , the original Handoff research preview , and the Online-Mind2Web leaderboard . Try Hark Pro . title: 5 Things That Break When AI Agents Start Acting on Their Own
abstract: 5 Things That Break When AI Agents Start Acting on Their Own Five governance problems emerge when AI agents begin taking real-world actions, from unmanaged access and identity sprawl to approval bottlenecks and manual oversight. By KDnuggets on November 16, 2026 in Partners Sponsored Content An agent is asked to investigate a data quality issue. It traces the pipeline and finds the root cause. Then it exports 1,800 sensitive customer records to a shared workspace “so the team can verify.” Nobody asked it to, and by its own measure it succeeded. That scenario is illustrative, but agents do write to production systems now. Five problems follow. 1. The Models Are Good Enough. Rollouts Are Stuck. Task completion on the OSWorld benchmark went from about 12% in 2024 to 66% in 2026. Yet no more than 10% of enterprises are scaling agents in any single function. Most teams can’t say what their agents are allowed to touch. 2. Most of the Damage Starts Inside. 80% of organizations report risky agent behavior such as improper data exposure. Few of those cases involve an attacker. A sales team clones a quoting agent and edits the prompt. The copy keeps applying discount rules legal retired a quarter ago. 3. Your Agent Inventory Is Wrong. There are about 45 nonhuman identities for every human. Fewer than half of CISOs know where their agents are or what they can access. 1 A developer wires an agent into the CRM over a weekend and quits in March. The agent keeps running on their credentials. Every agent needs its own identity and an owner who still works there. 4. Per-Agent Approval Is a Dead End. If your process ends with a committee signing off on each new agent, drop it. That works at ten agents. It collapses at a hundred, now that agents ship inside software you already pay for. Machine-readable agent contracts hold up better: one baseline every agent inherits, plus narrower rules by risk and domain. 5. Manual Review Is Already Eating Your Team. A Harris Poll surveyed 306 US data, privacy and AI decision makers. 87% said their teams spend hours re-verifying the context their agents rely on. Guardian agents check each action against its contract while it runs, then flag, redirect, or block it. People see only what crossed a line. Everything else just runs. Where to Go Next Download the playbook for the Scan, Set, Supervise framework and a 10-step action plan. Take the AI Trust Score assessment to see which problem to fix first. Request a demo of Collibra AI Command Center. 1 Source: Global CISO Insights 2026: Identity security in the age of AI , Okta. <= Previous post

title: How to Give Claude Code Up-to-Date Documentation With Context7
abstract: How to Give Claude Code Up-to-Date Documentation With Context7 Stop wasting tokens debugging outdated code. Give Claude Code up-to-date docs with Context7. By Kanwal Mehreen , KDnuggets Technical Editor & Content Specialist on November 16, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence If you do vibe coding, have you ever run into this issue? You ask Claude Code to build an AI application, and it generates the code using a library version that is incompatible with your project. For example, you have LangChain 1.x installed, but Claude Code generates code from an older tutorial that uses LLMChain : from langchain.chains import LLMChain You run the application and get an import error because this older API is not available in your installed setup. Now Claude Code has to investigate the version mismatch, look for the updated API, rewrite the code, and try again. Depending on the issue, it might take several attempts before everything works. There is no doubt that Claude Code can generate entire applications for you. The problem is that the frameworks and libraries it relies on keep changing, and Claude's built-in knowledge does not always reflect these changes. These failed runs are not just frustrating. They also cost time and tokens. One way to address this is Context7 , an open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) server developed by Upstash that lets AI coding agents retrieve version-specific library documentation and code examples while working on a project. So, instead of manually searching documentation and pasting examples into Claude Code, you can connect Context7 and let the agent retrieve relevant information while working on your project. In this tutorial, we will explore how Context7 works, connect it to Claude Code, configure automatic documentation retrieval, and test it with some examples. So, let's get started. What Is Context7 and How Does It Work? Context7 is a documentation retrieval service that integrates with AI coding assistants through two main MCP tools: resolve-library-id , which identifies the correct library, and query-docs , which retrieves documentation related to a specific question. Whatever it returns acts as additional context before Claude writes the implementation. Context7 also has several benefits, including: Current documentation: Retrieve relevant framework and library references instead of relying entirely on the model's built-in knowledge Version-specific examples: Find documentation for supported library versions Fewer outdated APIs: Reduce the chances of generating code using deprecated functions MCP integration: Connect documentation retrieval directly to Claude Code and other compatible coding assistants Less manual work: Avoid repeatedly searching documentation websites and copying examples into your prompts Now, let us set it up with Claude Code. Step 1: Installing Context7 for Claude Code Before getting started, make sure you have Claude Code installed and working. You can check your Claude Code installation by opening a terminal and running: claude --version For the recommended Context7 command-line interface (CLI) installation, you also need Node.js 22.13 or newer. You can check your versions with: node --version npm --version If both commands return version information and Node.js meets the minimum requirement, you are ready. Now install and configure Context7 using a single command: npx ctx7 setup --claude This command launches an interactive setup that allows you to configure Context7 specifically for Claude Code. You will be asked to authenticate with Context7 and select an integration mode. There are two options: MCP server: Connects Claude Code to Context7 through MCP tools CLI + Skills: Installs a skill that teaches Claude Code to retrieve documentation using Context7 CLI commands For this tutorial, select the MCP option because it allows us to examine how Claude Code interacts with Context7's documentation tools. The setup process authenticates your account, creates an API key, and configures the necessary integration. It also installs instructions that help Claude Code recognize when documentation retrieval is needed. When everything is set up, you will see something like this at the end: Press Enter to open the browser, or Ctrl-C to quit... ✔ Authenticated with API key ✔ Context7 setup complete Claude Code + MCP server configured with API Key + Rule installed + Skill installed Step 2: Verifying the Context7 Connection After completing the setup, open Claude Code: claude Inside Claude Code, enter: /mcp This opens the MCP management interface, where you can inspect the available servers and their connection status. Look for Context7 and check that it is connected. Output: Context7 MCP Server Status: ✔ connected Auth: ✔ authenticated URL: https://mcp.context7.com/mcp Capabilities: tools You can also inspect configured MCP servers directly from your terminal using this command: claude mcp list If the MCP connection is working, Claude Code should be able to access the two Context7 tools: resolve-library-id and query-docs . If Context7 is missing or disconnected, restart Claude Code, check your authentication, and repeat the setup if necessary. Step 3: Testing Context7 With a Coding Task Now we can test whether Claude Code can retrieve documentation before generating code. For this example, we will use Next.js 16. Start Claude Code inside an existing Next.js project, or create a new project and open Claude Code there. Enter the following prompt: Use Context7 to retrieve the Next.js 16 documentation for the proxy convention. Show me how to protect a dashboard route by checking an authentication cookie and redirecting unauthenticated users to `/login`. Explain which Next.js APIs are required, and implement the solution using the current documentation. Here is what happens: Claude Code recognizes that your request requires Next.js documentation Context7 resolves the correct Next.js library, if necessary The agent retrieves relevant documentation about the proxy convention Claude Code uses the retrieved examples to generate or modify the project's code Here is what Claude Code returned in our run. In the terminal, you can see that it called Context7 four times and named the documentation version it used: Called context7 4 times Sources: the Next.js docs on Context7 (/vercel/next.js/v16.2.9), specifically the proxy file convention, the Proxy getting-started guide, the authentication guide, the redirecting guide and the v16 upgrade guide. It then summarized what changed in Next.js 16: middleware.ts is now proxy.ts . The old file name and the middleware named export are deprecated. Export a function called proxy instead (a default export also works). File location. Put proxy.ts in the project root, or in src/ , at the same level as app/ or pages/ . Runtime. Proxy always runs on Node.js and can't use the edge runtime. If you need edge, the docs say to keep using middleware . Migrating. npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy . renames the file and the function for you. It also listed the APIs required for the solution: API From Purpose proxy(request) export proxy.ts Runs on the server before a matched request completes NextRequest (type) next/server The incoming request; request.cookies.get(name) reads a cookie and request.nextUrl.pathname gives the path NextResponse.redirect(url) next/server Sends the redirect; the URL must be absolute, so use new URL('/login', request.url) NextResponse.next() next/server Lets the request continue export const config = { matcher } proxy.ts Limits which paths proxy runs on. Without it, proxy runs on every request, including static files and images Finally, it added the code. The important part of this experiment is not just the generated code. It is whether Claude Code actually used the documentation tools and selected APIs appropriate for your project. You can ask Claude to explain which documentation it retrieved and why it selected a particular implementation.

title: Agentic System Design: A Self-Study Roadmap
abstract: Agentic System Design: A Self-Study Roadmap Learn agentic system design with this 7-step roadmap covering tools, memory, control loops, multi-agent coordination, evaluation, and deployment. By Bala Priya C , KDnuggets Contributing Editor & Technical Content Specialist on November 16, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Introduction If you're learning to build agents , start by learning how they fail. An agent is a language model with a few tools and a goal. It chooses its own path through the task, and that freedom is what makes it useful. It also means the agent will sometimes repeat a call, invent an argument, or lose a detail the task depended on. These failures are ordinary, and you can plan for them. Agentic system design is the practice of planning for them. You give the agent a control loop to work inside, tool contracts it can be held to, and a response to each kind of failure, all decided before the first run. This roadmap teaches that practice through one project, built in seven steps. The project is an incident investigator, an agent that finds the root cause of a production alert. Each step adds one piece, so every idea lands on code you've already written. You'll learn how to: Decide which steps your code controls and which steps the model controls Trace the reasoning-action loop through a full multi-turn tool interaction Design tools, memory, and multi-agent coordination that hold up under real use Evaluate and deploy an agent so it makes the jump from demo to daily use We'll try to wrap up each step with a few resources and one addition to the project. The Project: An Incident Investigator You'll build an incident investigator. It receives an alert, gathers evidence from logs, metrics, deploy history, and runbooks, and returns a root-cause report with cited evidence and a proposed fix. A human approves any action. Note : Every step works with any agent orchestration framework . You'll build the loop by hand in Step 2 to see the mechanics. Then you can carry the same design into LangGraph , CrewAI , Google's Agent Development Kit , or whichever framework you already use. Step You add to the project Shape Ten synthetic incidents and a fixed triage pipeline Loop A tool-calling loop that investigates one incident Tools Six well-specified tools behind a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server Memory A scratchpad, output compaction, and a history of solved incidents Team An orchestrator with three parallel workers Evals A thirty-incident replay suite with graders Deployment Budgets, read-only access, an approval gate, and tracing Step 1: Choosing Between a Workflow and an Agent Every agentic system starts with one decision about control: who picks the next step? In a workflow, your code fixes the sequence of steps and the model fills in the content at each step. In an agent, the model chooses its next action from a set of tools, based on what it has seen so far. Autonomy is a spectrum, and each move along it adds cost, latency, and variability. So start with the simplest shape that meets the goal, and move up when a measured failure calls for more flexibility. The table lists the common shapes in order of increasing autonomy: Shape How it works Fits tasks that Single prompt One model call with clear instructions and examples Have one input and one output Prompt chain A fixed sequence of calls, each using the previous output Split into stable steps, such as draft then translate Routing A classifier call sends the input to a specialized handler Fall into distinct categories Parallelization Independent calls run at once and the results merge Contain independent subtasks Orchestrator-workers A lead model splits the work and delegates it at runtime Have subtasks that emerge while the work proceeds Evaluator-optimizer One call generates, another critiques, and the pair repeats Have clear quality criteria and gain from revision Agent The model picks tools in a loop until it finishes Have open-ended paths shaped by what each step reveals Task decomposition is the design skill behind this choice. Write the task as numbered steps a person would follow, then mark each step as fixed or open-ended. Fixed steps stay in code, and open-ended steps go to the model. Resources Building Effective AI Agents | Anthropic Choose a design pattern for your agentic AI system | Cloud Architecture Center Agentic AI | Coursera Adding to Your Project Set up the foundation. Ask a large language model (LLM) to generate ten synthetic incidents, each with an alert, an application log, a metrics CSV, a deploy list, and a hidden root cause. Build a fixed pipeline that classifies severity, loads the files, and writes a summary with one LLM call. Run it on all ten and list the incidents it misjudges, because those blind spots justify the agent in Step 2. Step 2: Building the Reasoning-Action Loop The loop sits at the center of every agent: reason, act, observe, repeat . The model emits a structured tool request, your code executes it, and the result returns as the next message. The loop ends when the model gives a final answer or a step cap triggers. Let's trace one example. A support agent that's asked "Where is my order?" runs like this: The model reasons that it needs the order record and calls order_lookup The result shows the order shipped Tuesday with a tracking number The model calls carrier_tracking with that number The result shows a delay at a regional hub and a new estimate for Friday The model answers with the status and the new estimate That's two tool calls and three rounds of reasoning, and the second call depends on the result of the first. Build this loop by hand once before you switch to a framework. It teaches you what every framework automates: the message list, the tool registry, the dispatcher, and the stop conditions. You'll also run into these failure modes: Failure mode Symptom First fix Malformed arguments The tool call fails schema validation Tighten the schema and return an error the model can act on Repeated identical calls The agent circles one tool Keep call history in context and cap identical calls Early final answer The agent answers before gathering evidence Require the answer to cite tool results Runaway loop The run continues past its useful life Set a step cap and a time budget Resources Tool use with Claude AI Agents in LangGraph | DeepLearning.AI Building Your First LLM Agent Application | NVIDIA Technical Blog Adding to Your Project Replace the fixed gathering stage with a loop. Start with two tools, deploys_list and logs_get , cap the loop at 12 steps, and save every message to a trace file. Compare the agent's summaries with the Step 1 pipeline on the incidents in your blind-spot list. Step 3: Designing Tools the Model Can Use A tool definition is a contract, and the model follows what the schema and description say. Most agent quality problems trace back to ambiguous descriptions, mismatched parameter names, and tools that try to do multiple jobs at once. Write each description to include what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns: Design choice Suggestion Example Scope Give each tool one purpose search_customer_by_email with one required parameter Naming Namespace by domain logs_search , metrics_query Output Return compact, useful context and mark truncation A [312 more lines] marker Errors State the fix in the message " start must be an ISO 8601 timestamp" Selection Present a focused set of tools per agent Give a billing agent the billing tools The MCP standardizes how agents discover and call tools, so one tool server can serve many agents and applications. Test each description by handing the schema alone to a model and checking the call it makes. If the call is wrong, the description needs work. Resources Writing effective tools for AI agents — using AI agents | Anthropic MCP: Build Rich-Context AI Apps with Anthropic | DeepLearning.AI What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

title: Updating our coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy timelines
abstract: 01 Responding to AI-enabled vulnerability discovery Over the last several months, frontier models have become much better at discovering vulnerabilities . We remain optimistic that this will help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities faster than ever before. However, the speed at which AI is improving has changed how we think about our own disclosure practices. We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027. In-progress reports as of that date will keep their existing deadlines. In addition to shortening the disclosure window, we are making two related changes. First, we will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to our initial vulnerability report. Second, we will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of our policy remains the same. Finally, there are high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we reported over 90 days ago and that now exceed the deadline in our current CVD policy that have not yet been disclosed publicly. We are now notifying the maintainers of these projects that we are providing them an additional 30 days, after which time we will publish these reports on our dashboard in line with our updated policy starting January 1, 2027. Responding to AI-enabled vulnerability discovery Many coordinated disclosure norms, including those found in our own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities. These policies assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. Neither assumption holds today. Models can now help develop fixes, and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another. We are seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders. Some vulnerabilities still can’t be fixed quickly. Flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC can’t always be resolved in 30 or 45 days. In these cases, we will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Our seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation remains unchanged. This new policy update will not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by OSS Scanner . We recognize that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers. To reduce that burden, we will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible, to best enable the maintainer to confirm a finding and fix the vulnerability. We will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project. We offer programs to help maintainers and defenders work at this new pace. Maintainers of critical open-source projects can apply to OSS Scanner , a no-cost service that periodically scans their code with our strongest models and sends them findings directly. Eligible maintainers and contributors can apply to the Claude for Open Source Program for six months of Claude Ultra at no cost. And security professionals, including open-source maintainers, can apply to our Cyber Verification Program , which tailors Claude’s safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work.

title: Accelerate Molecular Dynamics Simulations with Accurate, Flexible Primitives Using NVIDIA cuPotential
abstract:
Molecular dynamics (MD) is an indispensable tool across physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science. Owing to its arithmetic structure, particularly the parallel evaluation of many atom-pair interactions, MD codes were among the first to be ported to run on GPUs. However, as GPUs evolve, optimizing kernels and ensuring compatibility across heterogeneous hardware have become more difficult than ever for many MD engine developers. Specifically, in simulations run with classical forcefields, the evaluation of long-range interactions under periodic boundary conditions, such as electrostatics and dispersion, remains the major computational and engineering bottleneck. NVIDIA cuPotential , a focused library designed for molecular dynamics, addresses these challenges. By offering modular primitives with a C API, cuPotential empowers developers and users to select specific components from multiple layers of the stack to accelerate workloads (Figure 1). cuPotential provides direct space and reciprocal space utilities such as cutoff-based interaction evaluators and charge spreading functions. This release also provides a plugin specifically for OpenMM given its popularity in the developer ecosystem as an example. The goal is seamless drop-in replacements with minimal changes to the user’s code. This post explains how to integrate the plugin into OpenMM, evaluate accuracy against high-accuracy references, and measure simulation throughput. It also introduces two examples for developers who need control over parameter representation and updates. Finally, it briefly discusses the science and error analysis behind the new splitting and spreading methods. This rigorous attention to accuracy and energy drift in simulation allows developers to integrate and benefit from the acceleration provided by cuPotential kernels without affecting simulation results. Figure 1. cuPotential library stacks can be integrated into MD engines such as OpenMM through a C API Building the cuPotential runtime and plugin for OpenMM cuPotential is composed of two parts: a core methods library and a plugin for OpenMM that consumes the primitives that can be built directly in a conda environment on Linux. The following tutorial walks through building the runtime and plugin, installing the Python wheel, and running the supplied molecular dynamics sample. Prerequisites Linux x86-64 with a supported NVIDIA GPU An installed NVIDIA driver compatible with CUDA 13.1 Conda or Micromamba installed and initialized for your shell A clone of the cuPotential repository from the NVIDIA/cuPotential GitHub repo The environment supplies the CUDA toolkit and compilers; a separate system-wide CUDA toolkit installation is not required. The GPU driver must already be installed on the host. Step 1: Create and activate the environment Using Conda, create and activate the environment: conda create -y -n cupotential-build -c conda-forge \ python=3.12 openmm=8.4.0 \ cuda-version=13.1 cuda-toolkit=13.1 \ cmake make gcc_linux-64=13 gxx_linux-64=13 \ swig pip setuptools wheel numpy conda activate cupotential-build Alternatively, you can use Micromamba: micromamba create -y -n cupotential-build -c conda-forge \ python=3.12 openmm=8.4.0 \ cuda-version=13.1 cuda-toolkit=13.1 \ cmake make gcc_linux-64=13 gxx_linux-64=13 \ swig pip setuptools wheel numpy micromamba activate cupotential-build Next, install the Python build dependencies: python -m pip install "pybind11>=2.12" nvidia-mathdx The cuda-toolkit package supplies the CUDA compiler and development tools. Setting cuda-version alone does not install those tools. Step 2: Point the build helper to the active environment In plugins/openmm/run_build , replace: OPENMM=/opt/openmm with: OPENMM="${CONDA_PREFIX:?Activate the conda environment first}" Both Conda and Micromamba set CONDA_PREFIX when an environment is activated. Step 3: Build and install Use the cuPotential repository root, with the environment active: export CUDACXX="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/nvcc"
export CUDAHOSTCXX="$CXX" ./plugins/openmm/run_build
python -m pip wheel \ --no-deps --no-build-isolation \ --wheel-dir plugins/openmm/dist \ ./plugins/openmm
python -m pip install plugins/openmm/dist/*.whl The build helper compiles the cuPotential runtime if it’s not already present, then builds the OpenMM plugin. The final installation command also installs the wheel’s declared pip CUDA dependencies. Step 4: Verify the installation Run the supplied sample directly: cd plugins/openmm/samples
./solvated_systems/run The sample evaluates DHFR (Dihydrofolate reductase), BACE (Beta-secretase 1), and ApoA1 (Apolipoprotein A1), under both NVT and NPT conditions. The DHFR and ApoA1 systems are from the OpenMM benchmark suite , while BACE is from the OpenFE benchmark set . A successful run ends with: PASS The samples use AMBER14/TIP3P force field, a 0.9 nm nonbonded interaction cutoff length, a 5 x 10⁻⁴ electrostatic accuracy target, and mixed precision. Its 4 fs timestep is paired with constrained hydrogen bonds, rigid water, and hydrogen mass repartitioning to 1.5 amu. These runs measure accuracy and performance separately. For electrostatics, it compares both implementations with a double-precision reference, using twice the cutoff length for the short range part and twice the mesh resolution in each dimension for the long range part, with the Ewald splitting parameter held fixed. For truncated Lennard-Jones interactions, it uses a double-precision reference at the same cutoff, preserving the interaction model being tested. For throughput, each implementation runs 500 warm-up steps followed by 3,000 timed steps. The cuPotential arm uses its own force and integrator, plus its barostat for NPT. The reported speedup therefore describes that integrated configuration. Using cuPotential with OpenMM The cuPotential OpenMM plugin provides replacements for the OpenMM nonbonded force, Langevin integrator, and Monte Carlo barostat. In your production MD simulations, the key steps to integrate cuPotential into OpenMM are: Replace the system’s OpenMM nonbonded force before creating the simulation context Use integrator and optionally barostat from cuPotential import openmm as mm
import openmm.unit as unit
import nv_openmm_plugin as nv temperature = 300 * unit.kelvin # Temperature, 300 K
timestep = 0.004 * unit.picoseconds # Timestep, 4 fs
friction_coeff = 1.0 / unit.picoseconds # Friction coefficient in Langevin thermostat
pressure = 1.0 * unit.bar # Pressure if using barostat for NPT # Prepare the system using OpenMM. Replace with your system.
pdb = app.PDBFile("solvated.pdb")
forcefield = app.ForceField("amber14-all.xml", "amber14/tip3p.xml") system = forcefield.createSystem( pdb.topology, nonbondedMethod=app.PME, nonbondedCutoff=0.9 * unit.nanometers, ewaldErrorTolerance=5e-4, constraints=app.HBonds, rigidWater=True, hydrogenMass=1.5 * unit.amu,
) # replace OpenMM NonbondedForce instance with the plugin's NonbondedForce
for index, force in enumerate(system.getForces()): if isinstance(force, mm.NonbondedForce): system.addForce(nv.NonbondedForce(force)) system.removeForce(index) break # The cuPotential integrator handles center-of-mass motion removal.
for index, force in enumerate(system.getForces()): if isinstance(force, mm.CMMotionRemover): system.removeForce(index) break integrator = nv.LangevinMiddleIntegrator( temperature, friction_coeff, timestep,
)
# Optionally, add cuPotential barostat for NPT simulations
system.addForce(nv.MonteCarloBarostat( pressure, # Pressure temperature, # Match the integrator temperature. frequency=25, # Attempt a volume change every 25 steps.
)) # Create the simulation after configuring all forces.
simulation = app.Simulation( pdb.topology, system, integrator, mm.Platform.getPlatformByName("CUDA"), {"Precision": "mixed"},
)
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)
simulation.minimizeEnergy() # OpenMM 8.4 only
simulation.context.setVelocitiesToTemperature(temperature) simulation.

title: Post-Training NVIDIA Nemotron to Increase Accuracy in Your Scientific Domain
abstract: Agentic AI is reshaping scientific research and innovation. Researchers communicate complex scientific hypotheses in natural language and let autonomous agents independently plan tasks, execute simulations, evaluate results, and self-correct across multiple iterations. Scientific agents are taking on longer, more complex, and increasingly visual workflows. Accuracy and inference efficiency matter at every step. Without verification, errors compound across the workflow, while latency and compute costs multiply with continued operation. NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, a collection of models, datasets, tools, and recipes for accelerating agentic scientific workloads, addresses these hurdles. It includes Nemotron 3.5 Super VL —an open, customizable, multimodal mode l for these specialized workflows—and the NVIDIA Nemotron Litmus-Bench V2.0 , an open source chemistry-reasoning dataset and benchmark that was designed to train and evaluate LLMs and agentic AI models on molecular properties. Out of the box, Nemotron delivers frontier level accuracy for scientific benchmarks (see Figure 1 below), along with the fastest time to solution for scientific coding. Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL accuracy results across several scientific benchmarks (higher is better) An important benefit of Nemotron models is NVIDIA post-training support. You can customize models for your specific research domain to increase accuracy. This blog provides a practical recipe for post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for scientific use cases. Starting from a raw experimental dataset, you’ll walk through how to build a custom reinforcement learning (RL) environment using NVIDIA NeMo Gym , apply RL, and measure improvement using molecular similarity scoring. NeMo Gym supplies the environment infrastructure, and NVIDIA NeMo RL supplies the post-training framework. This guide uses drug-metabolism prediction as a practical example. Given a parent compound, the starting molecule, and its transforming enzyme, the model predicts the resulting metabolite. The examples below use records from MetxBioDB, which is a comprehensive database of experimentally confirmed biotransformation reactions. The blog first describes direct RL, then an optional distillation step that can be used before RL when a teacher model provides useful examples. Build the reinforcement learning environment from experimental data The starting point is a CSV file of existing experimental records such as sequences, Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) strings, reaction conditions, and any other metadata paired with measured properties or outcomes. In this example, molecular structures are represented as SMILES strings, a text notation for describing a molecule’s atoms and bonds. These input-output pairs are reformatted as question-answer or user/assistant prompt pairs, with the experimental ground truth serving as a verifier to score the model’s responses. This setup constitutes a basic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment and requires no human preference labelling: The reward signal comes directly from the data. The fidelity of that reward signal can be tuned to the task. A simple sequence-similarity function works as a lightweight verifier, while more sophisticated tools like cheminformatics libraries, molecular simulators, or even a live autonomous lab can be a tool call and can all be wired in as the environment’s scoring layer. The richer the tool, the more precisely the model is steered toward chemically or biologically meaningful outputs. For the metabolism example, the model receives the parent molecule and enzyme, then submits a predicted metabolite. The verifier compares the predicted and reference molecular fingerprints—numerical representations of structural features—using Tanimoto similarity. Tanimoto similarity is a metric used to measure the overlap between two sets or binary vectors and is calculated by dividing the size of their intersection by the size of their union. For the bit fingerprints used here, the score ranges from 0 to 1; higher scores indicate more similar fingerprints. Figure 2. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL post-training workflow Direct RL post-training on the custom environment With the environment in place, fine-tune the model using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with low rank adapters (LoRA). The environment presents the model with an experimental input and asks it to reason through the problem step-by-step before submitting a predicted answer via a tool call. Each submission is scored automatically by the verifier, giving a dense reward signal that requires no further annotation. The training loop, reward server, harness, and rollout workers are fully self-contained, so the same pipeline generalizes to any domain that can return a scalar reward. At a 16,384-token output budget on the drug-metabolism RLVR environment, supervised fine tuning (SFT) improved the accuracy of Nemotron for Science by 12% and RL post-trained lifted it a further 17%. It demonstrates that even a highly capable instruction-tuned model continues to improve meaningfully when given targeted RL feedback on a domain-specific task. Figure 3. This chart shows mean molecular similarity before and after post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. Distillation from stronger models as a “warm-start” for RL If the base model needs a capability boost before RL training or if RL convergence is slow, a distillation step can provide significant lift. A stronger teacher model (e.g. a larger frontier model or a specialist) is run against the same environment to generate high-quality reasoning traces. A reasoning trace is high quality if the teacher model’s step-by-step logic for identifying the enzyme, predicting the reaction site, and deriving the metabolite structure leads to a SMILES that matches the ground truth metabolite. It is a low-quality reasoning trace even if the reasoning looks fluent and plausible but has some flawed logic that resulted in the wrong prediction. The high-quality reasoning traces are used to fine-tune the student model via SFT or direct on-policy distillation, giving it a much better starting point before the RL loop begins. This is known as a “warm-start” and it typically accelerates convergence and raises the performance floor, making the subsequent RL training more efficient and more likely to find a strong policy. Data distillation for SFT The distillation pipeline runs Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 across the training set, scores each rollout by Tanimoto similarity (tool call) to the ground truth metabolite, and keeps only the (question, reasoning trace) pairs where the model got it right. Those become the SFT corpus for the smaller model. In this environment 1,123 high-quality reasoning traces were filtered from 1,934 training prompts at Tanimoto threshold ≥ 0.7. Here is a distilled reasoning trace for a question-answer pair from Claude Sonnet 5.5. Note that a fixed system prompt is included with every request, which can be varied across environments. LLM requests are formatted as chat messages containing both the question and the system prompt. MetxBioDB environment (CYP1A2 N-demethylation) Question: Parent compound SMILES: Cc1nn(C)c(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C Metabolising enzyme: CYP1A2 Reason through this biotransformation step by step, then call submit_metabolite with the predicted SMILES of the primary metabolite. Ground truth: Cc1[nH]nc(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C — Tanimoto similarity = 1.0 (exact match) System prompt: You are an expert computational chemist specializing in drug metabolism. Your task is to predict the SMILES string of the metabolite produced when a given parent compound is biotransformed by a specified enzyme or enzyme family. Response format: 1. Provide step-by-step scientific reasoning: a. Identify the functional groups in the parent compound relevant to the enzyme. b.

title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Leads Agentic Inference Performance on MLPerf Endpoints v1.0
abstract: Agentic workloads are demanding more from inference systems. AI agents carry growing conversation histories across turns and generate a mix of reasoning, tool calls, and responses. Inference systems must support users at scale while remaining responsive. MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 evaluates this balance between serving capacity and responsiveness using coding and enterprise workflows through API endpoints. During performance runs, generated tool calls and workflow intent are checked against reference values. Separate SWE-bench Verified evaluations assess end-to-end task-solving capability. These checks evaluate whether faster serving preserves model quality. In MLPerf Endpoints v1.0, provisional NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 results show over 10x the throughput per kilowatt of provisioned power of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user. 1 This post presents the benchmark results and outlines the hardware and software optimizations used in the submissions. 1 MLPerf® Endpoints v1.0, Kimi K3, Standardized division, Available category, published November 9, 2026. Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores , and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions. Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. Efficient serving must preserve reusable state, distribute requests across workers, and accommodate the different execution requirements of prompt processing and token generation. Prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing help reduce redundant computation and balance serving load, while disaggregated serving supports independent optimization of prefill and decode. title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Achieves up to 2x Blackwell Ultra Performance in MLPerf Training v6.1
abstract: As AI agents tackle increasingly complex workflows, reducing time-to-train is critical for rapidly iterating on both models and the agents they power. MLPerf Training v6.1 marks the debut of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture, and these early results demonstrate that its CUDA software stack is already highly mature. In its first appearance, the Vera Rubin NVL72 platform delivered the fastest time to train on six of the seven benchmarks, achieving up to 2x more performance than a highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 baseline. For the seventh benchmark, DeepSeek-V3 671B, NVIDIA captured the absolute fastest time of the round by demonstrating massive scale on a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster. This dual-platform approach deliberately showcases the strengths of both systems. While the GB300 results highlight the massive, reliable cluster scale NVIDIA is deploying today, Vera Rubin demonstrated its own exceptional scaling architecture by maintaining above 97% overall efficiency when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs. Together, NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every benchmark in v6.1. NVIDIA platforms were also the only ones to submit results across all seven benchmarks, with Vera Rubin successfully completing the entire suite in its inaugural run. For developers, this breadth matters as much as any single top-line number. It proves that the performance gains inherited on day one span the entire modeling pipeline, comprehensively supporting everything from large-scale pretraining to the reinforcement learning post-training required for modern AI agents. Comprehensive AI performance across all MLPerf training benchmarks The simplest way to read this round is per benchmark: How much more performance does the new platform deliver per GPU on the same model? Model type Benchmark GPU Count Vera Rubin NVL72 vs. optimized GB300 NVL72 Submission ID (Vera Rubin / GB300) Mixture-of-Experts DeepSeek-V3 671B 1,024 2x 6.1-0116 / 6.1-0030 Mixture-of-Experts Qwen3.5 397B GRPO (RL) 64 1.4x 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0020 Mixture-of-Experts gpt-oss 20B 64 1.6x 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0049 Dense Llama 2 70B LoRA 72 1.5x 6.1-0123 / 6.1-0138 Dense Llama 3.1 8B 72 1.6x 6.1-0073 / 6.1-0138 Diffusion FLUX.1 72 1.5x 6.1-0124 / 6.1-0138 Recommender DLRMv4 128 1.4x 6.1-0129 / 6.1-0038 Table 1. Performance per GPU of Vera Rubin NVL72 relative to GB300 NVL72, MLPerf Training v6.1, closed division MLPerfTraining v6.1 results retrieved from www.mlcommons.org on Nov 16, 2026, from the following entries: 6.1-0116 , 6.1-0030, 6.1-0135, 6.1-0020, 6.1-0049, 6.1-0123, 6.1-0138, 6.1-0073, 6.1-0124, 6.1-0129 and 6.1-0038. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. Figure 1. Vera Rubin NVL72 performance relative to GB300 NVL72 at the same GPU count on all seven MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmarks MLPerfTraining v6.1 results retrieved from www.mlcommons.org on Nov 16, 2026, from the following entries: 6.1-0116 , 6.1-0030, 6.1-0135, 6.1-0020, 6.1-0049, 6.1-0123, 6.1-0138, 6.1-0073, 6.1-0124, 6.1-0129 and 6.1-0038. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. The pattern is clear. The largest gain lands on the largest, most communication-heavy model. While the platform is consistently 1.4x to 1.6x faster across the rest of the suite, the generational advantage widens even further for the massive DeepSeek-V3 benchmark. The suite covers natural language, image generation, recommendation, and reinforcement learning, so the gains hold across multiple modalities as well as across different model shapes and architectures. DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload DeepSeek-V3 671B is a 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and the most demanding workload in the suite. Expert parallelism turns every iteration into a burst of all-to-all communication, so fabric efficiency shows up directly in time to train. Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks. GB300 NVL72 ran the identical 1,024-GPU configuration in 8.03 minutes, close to 2x per GPU, and the largest generational improvement in this round. Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality. At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack. Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark , Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding.
