The continuous cycle of generating rollouts, scoring them, and updating weights pushes system architectures to their limits by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines. Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved the fastest time for this new benchmark with a time of 10.44 minutes at 1,024 GPUs (6.1-0117), compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 (6.1-0031) at the same scale. The Vera Rubin platform also proved its flexibility by submitting on two different inference backends: NVIDIA NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM at 10.44 minutes and with vLLM at 10.94 minutes (6.1-0118). Shipping two viable inference backends on a benchmark this new says as much about software maturity as it does about silicon. Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act requires running each rollout in a simulated environment and executing tool calls, code, or API validations. Because driving these simulations is intensely CPU-bound, the NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture , sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack. While the GPUs handle massive token generation and rapid weight updates, the Vera CPUs work in lockstep to simulate the environments, ensuring the accelerators are continuously fed with the rich feedback required to perfect agentic workflows. NVLink, Quantum-X and Spectrum-X: Co-designed networking for high-efficiency AI scaling Every result above is also a networking result. Modern AI training requires thousands of processors to act as one, a challenge NVIDIA solves by co-designing the internal rack domain and the external cluster fabric. Inside the rack, Vera Rubin NVL72 connects 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs through a copper NVLink 6 spine. Delivering 3.6 TB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s per rack, this all-to-all domain keeps MoE expert dispatch off the critical path. Beyond the rack, the platform scales out via ConnectX-9 SuperNICs over Quantum-X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet. To manage bursty MoE traffic, both fabrics use adaptive routing and congestion control to keep all-to-all communications hidden behind the compute layer. This cohesive design translates directly to efficiency. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved above 97% scaling efficiency as it scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs (4 to 16 racks). GB300 NVL72 showcased the platform’s large-scale capabilities , extending to 10,240 GPUs to capture the fastest absolute result of the round. Because the NVL72 architecture provides a consistent 72-GPU domain, developers see predictable performance jumps every generation without altering their operating model. Each cycle simply delivers more compute and bandwidth across the same consistent fabric. Figure 2.

title: Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
abstract: Users of a knowledge-grounded application expect it to remember them, not only to search well. They ask follow-up questions that make sense only in the context of the previous turn. They expect an answer about a policy or a procedure to reflect what they told the application about themselves last month. And they still expect every answer to be grounded in the documents they are allowed to read, with citations. Whether the application is a customer support assistant, a document chat inside a SaaS product, or an internal assistant over company policies, the expectation is the same. Meeting that expectation is hard, because the context that would sharpen a search lives outside the knowledge base. A user’s location, role, or product tier was often mentioned in an unrelated conversation weeks ago. To use it, the application has to store every conversation, extract durable facts from it, decide which facts matter for the current question, and inject them into the request. When many users share the application, every one of those steps also has to be isolated per user, and so does every document. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , now take over these steps: storing each conversation, extracting facts from it, and bringing the relevant facts into the search. You turn this on by adding a memoryConfiguration to the AgenticRetrieveStream request, which makes AgentCore memory a retrieval source alongside your knowledge base. Within the same call, the service restores the conversation, and the planner decides on its own when a fact about the user would help. It retrieves that fact from long-term memory and uses it to compose the sub-queries it sends to the knowledge base. After generating the answer, the service saves the turn back to memory. The same request carries a userContext , so the knowledge base returns only the documents that the user’s access control lists (ACLs) allow. The integration is opt-in and backward compatible. Your application keeps only what is genuinely yours: authenticating the user and passing who they are. This post shows how to build such an assistant for many users who share one knowledge base and one memory resource. Each user sees only the documents they may read, and each user’s memory stays private. The running example is an internal employee assistant for AnyCompany, a fictional company. Employees sign in with Amazon Cognito and ask questions over HR policies, IT guides, engineering runbooks, and sales plans. We show how to read the user’s identity from the Cognito ID token, how to pass it to AgenticRetrieveStream for document ACLs and for memory, how to design memory namespaces for many users, and how to read the trace to see when the planner used memory. Finally, we make AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforce per-user memory isolation even when application code gets it wrong. If you deployed the application from Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , this post replaces its “persist conversation history yourself” step. AnyCompany keeps its documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). One managed knowledge base syncs them through an ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data source. A global ACL file in the same bucket says which employees may read each folder: everyone reads HR and IT, only engineers read the engineering runbooks, and only salespeople read the commission plan. One AgentCore memory resource is shared by every employee. Amazon Cognito authenticates employees, and its ID token supplies two claims: the sub (user ID) identifies the user’s memory, and the verified email identifies the user to the knowledge base’s ACL filter. Three test users sign in: two engineers, Maya and Liam, and one salesperson, Sofia. The trace excerpts in this post are taken from a run of the sample application in the GitHub repository . Figure 1: Architecture of the memory-aware employee assistant. The application authenticates the user and constructs the request (steps 1–4). Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base restores the session, retrieves information, returns an answer, and saves the exchange to AgentCore memory (steps 5–8). Short-term events and long-term records belong to the same memory resource. Figure 2: One AgenticRetrieveStream turn with userContext and memoryConfiguration . Everything between the first and last arrow is the service’s work. Managed Knowledge Base owns ingestion, ACL filtering, indexing, ranking, planning, retrieval, and generation. With memoryConfiguration , it also owns session restore, memory search, and persistence. AgentCore memory owns storage, retention, encryption, and extraction. Your application owns authentication, the UI, and reading the user’s identity from the token. There is no conversation table: when the UI lists or reopens a conversation, it reads the same memory resource. Every value is derived by the application from the verified ID token. None comes from the request body. Two different claims do two different jobs. The knowledge base identifies users by email, because that is what the connected data source records in its ACLs. Memory needs an actorId that never changes and is never reused. The Cognito sub is both. An email address can be changed, or reassigned to a new employee after someone leaves, and that person would then inherit the old memory. You can use another stable user ID from your own user store as the actorId . What matters is that it never moves to a different person. The following steps create the knowledge base and its data source, set up the memory resource and Amazon Cognito, build the request, and read the trace to confirm the result. A managed knowledge base needs no vector store: Configure the service role for your setup by following Create a service role for managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , and pass its ARN in roleArn . For model access requirements, also review the prerequisites for managed and custom models . Documents live in the bucket under docs/<folder>/ . Amazon S3 has no permission system of its own to crawl, so you supply the ACLs in a global ACL file in the same bucket. Each entry maps an S3 prefix to the emails that may read it: The sample’s file also gives everyone docs/it/ . Then create the data source. For a managed knowledge base, every connector has the type MANAGED_KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTOR , and connectorParameters.type picks the source: aclEnabled cannot be changed after the data source is created. CreateDataSource is asynchronous, so wait for the status AVAILABLE . Then call StartIngestionJob and wait for COMPLETE . The sync reads the documents and the ACL file and indexes each document with its ACL. In the sample, all 11 documents were scanned and indexed with 0 failures. A document that no ACL entry covers is not ingested, and a user whose email matches no entry receives no results from this data source. The same model applies to connectors that crawl permissions from the source system, such as Microsoft SharePoint, Google Drive, and Atlassian Confluence. There, the permissions come from the source, groups are resolved from the source, and the knowledge base also checks each result against the source in real time. Your application code does not change: it still passes the user’s email in userContext . For the full list, see Access Control Lists awareness enablement . One memory resource serves every user. Per-user separation comes from {actorId} in the namespace templates, which AgentCore memory resolves from each event at extraction time. Two choices matter. Strategies . The two strategies extract different things. The summary strategy summarizes each conversation, so it captures facts that a user mentions in passing, such as “I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.” Those facts are what personalize a later answer about, say, PTO.

title: How Duco transforms financial data automation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Financial institutions face a critical challenge: processing massive volumes of data with speed, accuracy, and compliance while operating under some of the world’s strictest regulatory frameworks. Duco is the agentic Operations platform for financial services, serving tier-one banks and other financial institutions. It processes 20 billion transactions monthly for 200+ clients, including 7 of the top 20 banks and 10 of the top 20 asset managers. To keep pace as data processing demands grew, Duco evolved from traditional machine learning models to the agentic AI capabilities of Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. In this post, we share how Duco rebuilt its agentic AI stack on these services, cutting deployment time and onboarding costs while keeping each bank’s data isolated. Duco’s platform empowers teams to automate mission-critical data processes using AI and no-code models, handling everything from data extraction to downstream publication. It already used traditional machine learning models for predictive labeling and pattern recognition, helping banks consolidate and automate over 20,000 processes. However, these classical machine learning approaches had inherent limitations. They required extensive historical data for training, struggled with novel scenarios, and demanded significant customization for each new use case. Most critically, they couldn’t adapt quickly to the diverse, constantly evolving data formats and business rules that characterize modern financial operations. “The classical prediction models worked to an extent, but they weren’t agile or flexible enough. Traditional machine learning models can only amplify what they’ve already learned — they can’t help with the next step or find new problems.” — Rob Gates, Chief Architect and Innovation Officer, Duco Duco made a strategic decision to adopt Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to run agents at scale. This was more than a technology upgrade. It was a fundamental shift in how its system could understand, reason about, and act on financial data. About Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with a broad set of capabilities to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI. Learn more about Amazon Bedrock . Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale. Build with any open source framework and any model. Connect agents to your tools and data with authentication and access controls built in. Monitor and improve agents in production with tracing and evaluation. AgentCore handles the infrastructure so you focus on agent logic, not backend plumbing, and you get enterprise security and reliability without giving up open source flexibility. Learn more on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page. Several factors made Amazon Bedrock the ideal choice for Duco’s regulated financial services industry (FSI) environment: Duco’s existing agent infrastructure was built on LangChain and LangGraph, both of which were already in production. When evaluating runtime options for its agentic workloads, AgentCore emerged as the clear choice for three key reasons: Duco’s platform operates as a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) offering with strict tenant isolation (figure 1). This is a non-negotiable requirement for regulated institutions. The architecture reflects this at every layer, from the underlying cloud infrastructure right up to the AI agent runtime. Figure 1: Multi-tenant architecture Isolation is enforced through identity as well as infrastructure, with every hop between the user and their data authenticated (figure 2): The isolation principle extends fully into the agent architecture: The architecture helps maintain a model where each agent only has access to one bank’s data, context, and reasoning, facilitating real isolation of context across banks. Figure 2: High-level architecture Rather than committing to a single foundation model, Duco uses the right model for each job, assigning each role in its agent design to the model best suited to it. This approach delivers both quality and cost efficiency by matching the right model capability to each specific workload: This multi-model approach is architecturally designed to allow model swapping without disrupting the stack, which is critical in a landscape where model capabilities evolve rapidly. One of Duco’s most significant technical innovations addresses a challenge familiar to anyone building production agent systems: context window management. With 300–400 tools exposed per tenant through AgentCore Gateway (which fronts a separate MCP server for each underlying Duco service), approximately 200,000 tokens of tool descriptions were loaded into context before work began. This caused context overloading : response quality degraded as conversations lengthened, and the model lost the thread of earlier reasoning. The team emphasized that a feeling an agent is becoming less capable isn’t enough evidence on its own. Evaluations must be run before engineering decisions are made. Duco created a skills architecture using MCP resource types to move tool descriptions out of the static context and load them only when needed: Three new meta-tools, implemented in Duco’s agent harness, replaced the bloated tool description payload: Figure 3: Context loading and MCP connectivity A key architectural decision was implementing MCP tool discovery at boot time. When a new service is deployed, its MCP server is registered as a target on the tenant’s AgentCore Gateway as part of the deployment. When an agent boots, the harness builds a registry of every tool the Gateway exposes and shares just the tool names. The agent then uses find_tool and invoke_tool to discover the details and invoke tools on demand. As a result, the agent automatically gains that capability with no redeployment or agent reconfiguration required. Access control is enforced by the underlying services themselves: because the user’s identity is passed through the Gateway, each tool call succeeds only if that user is permitted to perform the action. This provides operational agility: the platform team can ship new capabilities to agents by deploying a new microservice, without touching the agent configuration or requiring downtime. For a platform that serves 200+ clients with diverse and evolving operational needs, this dynamic capability model is a significant competitive advantage. Duco implemented Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore to power two critical workflows that previously required extensive manual effort: Previously, onboarding new reconciliation processes was a manual, time-intensive exercise requiring significant professional services resources. Banks would take years to migrate thousands of processes, moving at a pace of roughly one per week. With Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore, Duco can now: One global bank experienced a 70% decrease in onboarding costs for new reconciliations and achieved an increase of over 20% in straight-through processing through better match rates and allocation rules. Financial institutions run thousands of quality gates between systems, generating countless exceptions daily. Traditionally, armies of analysts manually investigate each break to determine if it’s worth worrying about, already being investigated, or represents a new risk. Duco’s agents now handle the “first mile” of investigation: This agentic approach excels because financial workflows involve highly variable paths through information, exactly the kind of complex, context-heavy reasoning that foundation models handle well. Deploying AI agents in financial services requires more than technical capability. It demands rigorous compliance, auditability, and risk management.

title: Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing
abstract: Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model. Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, and many teams taking it on haven’t yet built distributed systems instincts. The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production . Stanford HAI demonstrated that two models can perform worse collaborating than either alone when coordination overhead exceeds the benefit. The pattern is clear: teams are adding complexity faster than they build understanding. Ten steps that are each 95 percent reliable deliver only 59.9 percent end-to-end reliability, and 20 steps deliver 35.8 percent. This illustrative model assumes a strictly sequential chain with no retries, but the direction holds: each dependent handoff multiplies risk. In this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early. You also see how takt time, safety boundaries, edge data, and shift cycles shape the architecture. Coordination patterns fall into two tiers, based on who controls the flow. In Tier 1, you define the path. In Tier 2, the model chooses the path at runtime. That flexibility handles work whose steps you can’t define in advance, at a higher cost in tokens, latency, and debugging. The practical default is to start with Tier 1 and move a task to Tier 2 only when its subtasks emerge during the work. 1.1 Sequential Pipeline: Orchestration patterns that implement linear execution where each node’s output feeds into the next node (A -> B -> C) supporting ordered processing with predictable execution timing In the following diagram, input flows to agent A (extract), then agent B (transform), then agent C (validate), and then output. The user defines that order at build time, and nothing is decided at runtime. As a result, the pipeline is straightforward to debug and test, and its cost is predictable. Typical fits include document processing, extract, transform, and load (ETL) chains, and warranty-claim triage. Figure 1: Sequential pipeline where each agent’s output feeds the next, from extract to transform to validate 1.2 Conditional Workflow: Logic-based edges select the next node by condition, so the workflow can branch and send each case down a different path. In the following diagram, a user request goes to agent A (write code) and then to agent B (test code). A pass/fail check sends passing work to agent D (deploy). Failing work loops back to agent A for a retry, up to a maximum of N times, and then escalates to a human. The orchestration layer enforces that cap, for example through an AWS Step Functions iteration limit, which keeps the loop from becoming the unbounded iteration anti-pattern described later in this post. Figure 2: Conditional workflow that retries failures up to N times before escalating to a human A classification step examines the input and directs it to the appropriate processing path. Only one path is executed per request. Best for intent-driven dispatch, quality-gate decisions, customer inquiry routing, and anomaly triage. The following diagram shows a plant supervisor’s request being read by a classifier and sent to exactly one specialist. Questions about whether parts meet spec go to the Quality Agent, overdue equipment services go to the Maintenance Agent, and shift changes go to the Scheduling Agent. This decision is made at the entry point. Figure 3: Conditional router that runs one path per request, with bounded retries before human escalation 1.4 Parallel Workflow: A task splits into independent subtasks that run simultaneously across handlers, each on its own data. A fan-in step combines the results when all handlers complete, and a failure in one path retries only that path. Best for multi-source analysis, batch processing, and work that decomposes into independent pieces. In the following diagram, a research orchestrator decomposes the task and dispatches it to three specialist agents that run concurrently: a financial data agent, a geopolitical agent, and a logistics agent, each analyzing its own source. A combined step waits for all three, then synthesizes the results, resolves conflicts, and ranks the findings. Latency equals the slowest single agent rather than the sum of all three. Figure 4: Parallel fan-out to specialist agents followed by a fan-in step that synthesizes and ranks the results In autonomous patterns, control flow is determined at runtime by the AI model itself, not predefined by developers. Agents read task state, reason about what’s needed and coordinate through shared context rather than fixed paths spanning a spectrum from structured orchestration to fully emergent behavior. In plan-based orchestration, a single orchestrator agent acts as a project manager. The orchestrator maintains an explicit task plan with assignments and dependencies, sees all context while each worker receives only its slice, distributes work dynamically against the current plan, and monitors progress centrally. Key design choice is that the workers are stateless and independent. If one fails, it doesn’t contaminate others. The orchestrator retries only the failed worker, not the entire workflow. The following diagram shows how a planner agent decomposes a task into an explicit plan and dispatches each step to a worker’s agent. Each step goes to a dedicated worker (a research agent, an analysis agent, and a report agent) that sees only its assigned slice. Figure 5: Plan-based orchestration with a planner agent assigning each step to a stateless worker agent Agents operate with limited, local knowledge and coordinate through peer-to-peer delegation. Each makes local decisions about when and to whom to transfer control, based on the task and the agents it knows. Control passes with state: each transfer carries validated task state, the evidence behind it, and any unresolved questions, so the receiving agent continues rather than reinterpreting a summary. A handoff that moves only through the conversation is not a handoff. In the following diagram, a customer service agent transfers control, together with its context, to either a technical support agent or a billing agent, and technical support can hand off further to a senior engineer. Each agent knows only the small set of peers it can transfer to. Figure 6: Handoff pattern passing validated state between peer agents through local delegation In conversation-driven patterns (also known as group chat patterns), all agents participate in a shared conversation where orchestration emerges through turn-taking rather than explicit plans or structured handoffs. This mirrors human team collaboration where everyone can see the discussion and contribute when appropriate. In the following diagram, an agent-selection mechanism decides whose turn it is, and agents A, B, and C each add to one shared conversation, where every turn is a message plus a tool call. The selection mechanism sets the turn-taking, and state lives implicitly in the conversation history. Figure 7: Conversation-driven pattern where turn-taking selects the next agent and state lives in the conversation Multiple agents independently evaluate the same input, and their conclusions are reconciled by majority, by a judge agent, or by escalation when they disagree. Unlike a conversation-driven pattern, the agents do not see each other’s reasoning before committing to a position, which is what makes disagreement informative rather than socially convergent. Use it sparingly. Debate is the most expensive pattern here, and on perceptual tasks it buys latency rather than accuracy (see the quality-inspection case in anti-pattern 3 that follows). Reserve it for high-stakes, low-volume decisions where being wrong costs more than deliberating.

title: How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage. A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy. First they open the analytics dashboard to see what worked last time, then the content library to find the right tone, and then the campaign builder to build the campaign itself. Repeat that across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp, and much of a marketing team’s week goes to navigating tools instead of making decisions. The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library. This capability points to a broader shift in software platforms. Beyond a user interface for business users and an API for engineering teams, a third layer is emerging, where a user describes an outcome in plain language and an agent carries out the steps across the platform. For a customer engagement platform, that means a capability already exposed as an API can become a tool an agent calls, and a campaign that once moved across several tools can move through one conversation instead. MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use across channels including push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services (RCS), set out to build this layer. MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that work with live platform data. Marketing and product teams can now draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation, while agents decide what to send each customer. One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result. MoEngage treated this as an architecture problem. The question was how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage solved it with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. The post covers the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant’s data isolated. It closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse. Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents. All four share the same foundation: foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock . Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents at the exact point in the workflow where marketing and product teams do that piece of work: Conversational agents work across campaigns, analytics, segments, and flows. A user can ask a question in plain language and the agent calls the right tools to answer it or act on it. The Campaign Insights Agent, embedded on the analytics page, delegates to specialized sub-agents. One sub-agent runs analysis across several metrics at once. A second diagnoses why a metric is underperforming, and a third compares performance across time periods or segments. A final step formats the findings into a clear answer. Custom agents let lifecycle and customer relationship management (CRM) teams design agents that run continuously on MoEngage data and tools, inside rules the product and marketing team defines. Every agent shows its work through an activity log of the data it pulled, the decisions it made, the channels it touched, and the content it sent. Teams can run an agent with full autonomy or require human review before anything executes. Decisioning agents act for each individual customer. Each agent decides what to say, when, how often, and on which channel, and it learns from every outcome. Product and marketing teams set the content, goals, and guardrails, and the agents handle the rest, with visibility into every decision. Offer Decisioning selects the best offer on web and app surfaces. Campaign Decisioning delivers 1:1 decisions across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp. Together with workflow agents, this puts both halves of agentic marketing in one system. The architecture has four layers. Each layer has a single responsibility and can change without affecting the others. In a typical request, a user signs in to MoEngage and asks a question. The client sends the request with the user’s existing JSON Web Token (JWT). AgentCore runtime validates the token and starts an isolated session for that user. The agent asks a model in Amazon Bedrock which tools to call. The MCP server calls the MoEngage APIs with the user’s tenant context and returns the results. The agent then composes the answer. The following diagram shows how these components connect. Figure 1: MoEngage Merlin AI architecture on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore runtime. MoEngage opens its platform to agents through an MCP server and agent-callable APIs. Its platform APIs for campaigns, analytics, segments, content, and flows were already OpenAPI 3.0-compatible, so MoEngage used the FastMCP framework to generate MCP tools from those specifications. Each operation becomes a tool with a structured schema, a description, and parameter validation. The following simplified example shows the pattern: The tools fall into five groups: The tools come from the specifications, so they stay in sync with the APIs. When a team updates a specification, the tool definitions update with it. A multi-tenant system cannot let a model decide whose data it is reading. MoEngage made three design choices to help prevent that. First, the MCP server reuses the existing authentication model, accepting the same JWT-based authentication that MoEngage APIs already use, and AgentCore runtime validates each token before a request reaches the server. Second, workspace and user context travel in request headers that AgentCore runtime forwards to the server rather than as tool arguments, so the model does not see these values and cannot change them. Third, AgentCore runtime runs each user session in its own isolated environment, so one user’s conversation cannot read another’s session state. On top of this, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content safety and personally identifiable information (PII) filters to agent responses. A backend-for-frontend layer then validates the structure of generated content before the MoEngage interface renders it. Give users control over agents. Users set guardrails on what each agent can do, review every action in its activity log, and choose between autonomous and human-reviewed execution. AgentCore runtime provides the production capabilities that a multi-tenant MCP server needs, and each one addresses a specific requirement of MoEngage’s workload. AgentCore runtime scales sessions as demand changes, so MoEngage does not plan capacity for traffic bursts across its customer workspaces. Each session runs in its own isolated environment by default, which keeps one brand’s conversation and data separate from another’s. The built-in JWT authorizer validates tokens against MoEngage’s existing identity provider, so the MCP server uses the same authentication model as the APIs. Hosting on AgentCore runtime is also framework-agnostic. MoEngage can change models or agent frameworks without touching the MCP server, which matters as the agent layer evolves. Built-in metrics, logs, and traces through Amazon CloudWatch give MoEngage engineers visibility into every session.

title: Modernizing mainframe Assembler to Java using Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform
abstract: Imagine a batch job that has run every night for decades without failing, and the only person who understands its code is about to retire. We have seen this situation again and again while working with banking, insurance, and airline customers. Their Assembler programs still run critical business operations, but fewer people can read them each year. Rewriting them by hand takes years, risks breaking business rules nobody remembers writing, and still depends on the same experts who are leaving. Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform change that equation. This post shows you a multi-stage transformation methodology using Amazon Bedrock , Kiro IDE (an AI-powered integrated development environment), and AWS Transform that can help reduce modernization time compared to manual approaches while maintaining business logic integrity through validation checkpoints. You will learn how to systematically extract business rules from Assembler code, convert them through an intermediate COBOL stage, and deploy modernized applications as Java Spring Boot services on AWS. Before starting the modernization process, make sure you have: You can transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications tightly bounded with COBOL into Java Spring Boot applications built for the AWS cloud through a systematic five-phase approach. This multi-stage methodology, converting Assembler to COBOL as an intermediate step before Java transformation, reduces risk and preserves business logic with greater reliability than direct Assembler-to-Java conversion. The intermediate COBOL stage provides a structured, human-readable format that subject matter experts (SMEs) can validate before final transformation. This makes sure that business rules remain intact throughout the modernization journey. The following sections describe both the current mainframe architecture and the target cloud-focused state. Your current architecture represents a traditional mainframe environment where Assembler programs execute batch processes, connected with COBOL, interact with databases, and process files. At its core, JCL (Job Control Language) jobs trigger Assembler program execution at scheduled intervals. These programs read input from VSAM (Virtual Storage Access Method) and sequential files and perform operations against IBM Db2 for z/OS. Your business logic executes using low-level register operations (direct CPU register manipulation) and memory management. Output is written back to files or database tables, and job completion status is reported through JCL return codes. All of this runs on IBM z/OS mainframe infrastructure. Figure 1: Mainframe Assembler architecture The modernization solution helps you transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications into Java applications built for the AWS cloud through a multi-phase, AI-powered workflow. The architecture uses Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE for AI-assisted code analysis and business rule extraction, and AWS Transform for automated COBOL-to-Java conversion. If COBOL source code is already available, you follow the conventional approach and provide it directly to AWS Transform for conversion to Java Spring Boot applications. With this solution, you can achieve: Figure 2: End-to-end Assembler-to-Java transformation architecture on AWS, showing five main phases: business rules extraction, spec-driven data flow, Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, validation, and COBOL-to-Java transformation You begin the transformation workflow by analyzing Assembler code to generate Business Rules Extraction (BRE) documentation. You then create detailed functional specifications with human-in-the-loop refinement. The validated specifications guide the Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, generating intermediate COBOL code that bridges the gap between low-level hardware instructions and business-oriented constructs. This COBOL code undergoes functional equivalence testing before AWS Transform converts it to Java, with validation checkpoints at each phase to reduce risk and verify business continuity. The quality of your Business Rules Extraction (BRE) directly impacts transformation accuracy, so focus carefully on this phase. Use Amazon Bedrock, through Kiro IDE or the Amazon Bedrock console, along with AWS Transform for mainframe to extract and document business rules from your Assembler source code. You can use the prompts in this post directly in Amazon Bedrock through the Chat Playground , or within Kiro IDE using its built-in AI chat and Spec panel . Replace the placeholder values with your actual Assembler code and context before running. Amazon Bedrock is the inference platform behind the first four phases: business rules extraction, specification creation, Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, and validation. Choose a foundation model with strong code reasoning and a large context window, because Assembler programs are long and dense. Set the temperature to 0 so you get consistent output across runs. To process many programs, call the same prompts through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and store each output in your Amazon S3 bucket so it can feed the next phase. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use your prompts or model outputs to train AWS models or share them with third parties. For details, see Data protection in Amazon Bedrock . Use sanitized test data instead of production data or personally identifiable information (PII). The more context you provide to the AI, the better it understands the business intent behind the code. Include relevant documentation, data dictionaries, and available business context alongside the Assembler code when prompting. Note: Save the output of each prompt as you go. You will need them as inputs in the next phase. Example prompt for context-aware analysis: You can customize this prompt by adding domain-specific terminology from your business context. When you run this prompt, you will see structured JSON output that you can use for automated validation and direct integration with downstream transformation tools. Data mapping accuracy directly affects conversion quality. Incomplete mappings can lead to lost or corrupted business logic. Treat AI-generated BRE documents as drafts, not final outputs. Have subject matter experts review and validate the extracted rules before moving forward. Document discrepancies in a validation log and update the BRE based on SME feedback before proceeding to specification creation. To help SMEs validate the rules, supplement textual BRE documents with visual aids like flowcharts and data flow diagrams. Maintain a validation checklist covering business rule accuracy, data mapping correctness, edge case handling, and error condition completeness. After you validate business rules with SMEs, translate them into detailed functional specifications that will guide code conversion. This spec-driven approach confirms that business requirements are clearly documented and agreed upon before code transformation begins, reducing costly rework later. Use the extracted BRE documents to create complete functional specifications that guide COBOL code generation. These specifications should include program overview, COBOL data structures, process flow design, and business rules coverage mapping. Example prompt for functional specification generation: You can adjust the data structure specifications based on your COBOL standards. When you run this prompt, you will receive a complete functional specification with full traceability from business rules to COBOL structures, ready for SME review and direct integration with Kiro for code generation. With validated functional specifications in hand, the next phase uses these structured outputs to guide the Assembler-to-COBOL conversion. The intermediate COBOL step helps you bridge the gap between low-level hardware instructions and business-oriented constructs, which helps you verify that business logic is preserved before the final Java transformation.

title: Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Novo Nordisk (Novo) is one of the world’s leading global pharmaceutical companies, manufacturing medicines for chronic diseases such as diabetes and obesity, and delivering them to patients across many countries. Behind every product lies a manufacturing network that adheres to strict quality requirements. Every quality-relevant process step must be described, controlled, and validated through formal documentation. Keeping this documentation current and accurate is a core responsibility of the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area, a responsibility that spans a large and diverse portfolio of controlled documents, including standard operating procedures, work instructions, forms, and training materials, across the global organization. Managing this portfolio presents significant challenges. Document updates are frequent, driven by regulatory changes, process improvements, equipment modifications, and audit findings. Each update demands careful review, structured approval workflows, and timely communication to all affected stakeholders. With thousands of active documents spread across multiple divisions, departments, and product programs, tracking which documents are due for revision, pending approval, or require immediate attention becomes increasingly complex. Much of this oversight currently relies on manual processes and fragmented tracking methods such as spreadsheets or disconnected systems. These methods are time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale. The result is a risk of outdated documentation remaining in circulation, delayed updates, and critical gaps in compliance visibility. Beyond document management, there is a deeper knowledge challenge. Valuable manufacturing knowledge is distributed across many controlled documents, versions, sites, and product programs. Finding the right answer at the right time often depends on experienced individuals knowing where to look. This dependency on tribal knowledge creates bottlenecks that slow down decision-making and, ultimately, impact how quickly life-saving medicines reach patients. To address these challenges, the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area has embarked on developing an intelligent support system powered by agentic AI, deployed on AWS. The goal is to reduce lead times, improve documentation visibility, and make critical manufacturing knowledge more accessible, ultimately helping the organization move faster and serve more patients around the world. This post dives deep into the architecture and the key design decisions made to meet the high standards of accuracy and traceability required in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The solution helped subject-matter experts (SMEs) complete work that used to take hours or days in minutes. We also describe an AI process-intelligence assistant that can answer complex process questions with grounded, cited responses. The solution is built around a GraphRAG architecture, combining a knowledge graph with hybrid search to retrieve the most relevant and contextually accurate information. AI agents, built on a managed agent framework, coordinate the retrieval and response process end-to-end. A guided mode helps clarify ambiguous questions before a search is initiated, helping make responses more precise and defensible. Teams supporting manufacturing repeatedly answer variations of the same question: what does the process require, for this site, this product, and this equipment? Answering well requires four things at once: Conventional keyword search returns documents, not answers, with no concept of scope, version, or relationship. A plain vector-based Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system improves recall on natural-language questions but still struggles with exact identifiers (document numbers, equipment codes), with multi-hop relationship questions, and (most importantly for a regulated domain) with identifying when relevant content is not available. The team needed a system that treats structure and relationships as first-class, stays grounded in approved sources, and clarifies instead of guessing. The assistant is built on a GraphRAG architecture: a knowledge graph in Amazon Neptune captures structure and relationships, and a hybrid search index in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless provides semantic and exact-match recall over document contents. The two stores are deliberately kept separate and bridged at query time rather than combined into a single engine. This is a common production GraphRAG pattern. The reasoning layer runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore was chosen for its managed agent runtime with built-in session isolation, native tool orchestration, and integrated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and observability. This removes undifferentiated infrastructure work so the team could focus on the domain logic. The agent runtimes are built with the Strands Agents SDK and powered by Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock . Documents are processed through an ingestion pipeline that uses Amazon Bedrock Data Automation for multimodal parsing, orchestrated with AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda . The stack is defined as infrastructure as code with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) . At a high level, a question flows through the system like this: Figure 1: End-to-end architecture where a query agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore uses Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, embeddings, and reranking, with hybrid retrieval across Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and Amazon Neptune linked by shared document numbers. An event-driven, serverless ingestion pipeline populates both stores, while memory, observability, and evaluations support personalization, monitoring, and quality assessment The graph is organized around two complementary layers, which is what lets the assistant take into account where a document sits and what it is about. High-level taxonomy: The process tree. The organization’s official process framework is modeled as a hierarchy of process nodes (roughly three levels, parent to child). Each controlled document is attached to the lowest applicable process level, so each onboarded document has a known place. This lets the assistant scope a question to a process area before retrieving anything, and automatically categorize newly ingested documents. Low-level taxonomy: Domain entities. SMEs define the entities that make an answer correct or incorrect in manufacturing: sites, product generations, equipment, process steps, and similar attributes. These are modeled as first-class graph nodes linked to the documents that describe them, using a small set of unified relationship types rather than an ever-growing list of edge names. Modeling both layers is what distinguishes a genuine GraphRAG system from two databases side by side . The document number on an OpenSearch passage is also a node in the graph, so a search hit is an immediate entry point into the graph’s structure with no fuzzy re-matching required. This chunk-to-graph bridge is a key design choice in the retrieval path. Early GraphRAG work favored open-ended extraction, letting a language model discover entities with no fixed schema. This approach is powerful for open-ended sensemaking over sprawling text, but it is noisy, hard to maintain, and difficult to audit. Over the past couple of years, the consensus has shifted toward ontology-guided extraction using a predefined, domain-specific schema to guide the model, which improves accuracy and reliability for specialized corpora. For regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing this is not a compromise, but the right default. The domain already has a real ontology, curated by experts, and a fixed schema with a human-in-the-loop promotion process for new entities supports the auditability the team needed in a regulated pharmaceutical environment.

title: Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
abstract: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so you can get answers from tables through agentic retrieval. When a question needs data from CSV, XLSX, or XLS files, tabular search looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row in one or more tables or sheets. It then combines the results with facts from related documents to answer analytical questions that take several steps. A finance team closing the quarter needs to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer. It depends on the variance policy’s threshold, the quarter-close memo’s budget revisions, and math over every department in the profit and loss (P&L) workbook. Like this finance team, most teams keep their narratives and data in the same place. For example, a Microsoft SharePoint site holds workbooks next to policies, and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket holds CSV exports next to PDFs. Tabular search answers questions across these files through the same AgenticRetrieveStream request you already use for documents. It runs code over the original file in an isolated sandbox, so the answer uses the whole table instead of only the rows that retrieval returns. For the finance team, one request returns the departments that must write commentary. The answer cites the policy and the memo, and the trace names the workbook the code read. In this post, you learn how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also build a knowledge base with sample finance files and use the trace to see which file the code read. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) returns a fixed number of passages that best match a question, which works well for prose. Tables lose information when they’re split into passages, in ways that depend on the table’s shape: Retrieval also has to match a question to the right table. Questions use business terms, such as “controllable spend,” but tables hold cost center codes, account names, and numbers. A draft and a final workbook look almost the same to search. The rule that gives the numbers meaning is often in a separate document, such as a policy. Tabular search therefore splits the work. Retrieval only has to return one passage from the right table file, and code then reads the whole table. Because retrieval still has to find that file first, naming the file in your question helps. Table 1 shows how plain retrieval and tabular search each handle the finance team’s question, “Which departments must write variance commentary?” Table 1: The same question with plain retrieval and with tabular search. In agentic retrieval , an agent uses retrieval to decide which documents matter and then writes the answer. Tabular search is part of that flow, so there’s nothing to turn on. When a question needs the data in a table, the request moves through these stages: Tabular search starts when retrieved passages come from a CSV, XLSX, or XLS file and the question needs a calculation across rows or a lookup of specific values. An AgenticRetrieveStream request can search one knowledge base or several. The Retrieve API keeps returning passages and doesn’t run code. Tabular search works the same way whichever connector brings the files into the knowledge base, including Amazon S3, Microsoft SharePoint, Atlassian Confluence, and others. Tabular search is built for questions that need calculations or lookups over the table files it retrieves. Running code adds at least one more agent turn, so answers that use table data take longer than text-only answers. Governed metrics, recurring dashboards, warehouse-scale joins, and reporting controls still belong in your business intelligence (BI) tools. Tabular search works on table files stored next to your documents, and you don’t define a schema. In this solution, an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base stores your CSV and Excel files together with related documents, such as PDF and Word files. Your application sends every question through agentic retrieval. When a question needs table data, the answer combines calculations over your tables with facts from your documents. It cites the passages it used, and the trace names the table files the code read. In Figure 1, an Amazon S3 data source syncs these files into the knowledge base, which keeps embeddings, text, metadata, and the original files. When your application sends a question with AgenticRetrieveStream , agentic retrieval plans the work and retrieves passages from the knowledge base. If the question needs data from a table file, it sends the files to read to an isolated sandbox with no network access. There, model-written code runs over the original file and returns printed results. The answer, with citations and trace events, streams back to your application. Figure 1: Table files and documents in an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, with tabular search inside agentic retrieval. The worked example uses fictitious AnyCompany Retail finance files: These files are in the tabular-search folder of the sample-managed-knowledge-base-patterns GitHub repository. The folder also has an AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app that deploys the resources in this post, and Python scripts that ask these questions. The calling identity needs this policy, from the agentic retrieval documentation: For costs, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . Put the table files and related documents under one prefix. The knowledge base needs an IAM role that Amazon Bedrock can assume. This trust policy allows only the bedrock.amazonaws.com service principal, and only for knowledge bases in your account. Next, set up the remaining resources: The inline policy for step 2 allows reads on this bucket only: This script runs steps 3 to 5 and prints the IDs: Tabular search can start only if the knowledge base assigns the right file type, so check the file type after the first sync. The first script runs steps 1 to 3: The second script runs steps 4 and 5 so you can check the table file type before asking the question with agentic retrieval. With your own files, ask a question that pairs a rule in one of your documents with a calculation over your tables, and name both. Send the same question through AgenticRetrieveStream . The script prints the answer, each CodeExecution status, and the files the code read. For these files, the answer combines two workbook tables with two documents: Trace events arrive in this order: In this example, the Planning event names only the final workbook, because the policy and the business review arrive as retrieved passages. On longer calls, the stream repeats the IN_PROGRESS event every 10 seconds, so a read timeout doesn’t fire. A code step that can’t finish reports FAILED , and the agent usually retries or falls back. Tabular search runs as part of response generation, which is on by default, so the script leaves generateResponse unset. If you set generateResponse to false, the agent returns retrieval results without running code. For details, see agentic retrieval . Each of the following questions also pairs a document with the workbook. This question needs a budget that exists only after the memo’s revisions: The answer uses the revisions from the memo and the Q3 actuals and original budget from the workbook. Spending came in 49,572.40 US dollars under the revised budget, so the answer is yes, even though the same spending is over the original budget. Plain Retrieve returns memo and workbook passages, but none of them contains these figures. Here is the full version of the finance team’s question from the introduction. It needs the policy’s threshold, the memo’s revisions, and the workbook: The policy requires commentary when the variance exceeds 5 percent of the approved budget, which includes approved revisions, and the memo approves a Marketing increase and an Engineering cut. The answer is Sales (-6.50 percent), Engineering (+5.

title: Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
abstract: With Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails , you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword. That same mechanism can also match more than you intend. A topic named Finance, meant to keep an assistant out of investment advice, also blocks “When does my direct deposit clear?”. Inputs close in meaning to the topic can get caught, not only the requests you intended. When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns: The rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns. It presents eight best practices for describing a topic precisely enough that the guardrail blocks what you mean and passes what you don’t. To ground the following practices in something concrete, we use one running example throughout this post: a fictional bank we call AnyCompany Bank. AnyCompany Bank is two weeks from launching its first customer-facing AI assistant, and its first pass at the Denied Topics policy is blocking the wrong things. Application: AnyCompany Bank’s chatbot is embedded in the AnyCompany Bank mobile and web app. It answers questions about accounts, statements, transfers, cards, and mortgages. It hands off to a human for account changes, dispute filings, and questions outside its scope. Must-block list (from legal and compliance): Must-pass list (the things the assistant exists to do): Against that target, AnyCompany Bank’s team first drafted four topics, all of them currently blocking legitimate queries: Every one of these topics names a subject domain the assistant works in, rather than the intention the bank needs to refuse. Fixing this is what the rest of the post is about. The next eight sections work through the practices, most of them closing with a “Back at AnyCompany Bank” subsection that shows the fix applied to this scenario. The post then closes with the one limitation to plan for regardless of how well you follow the practices: results are not fully deterministic. Note: Denied Topic structure in Standard tier. A topic has three parts, a name, a definition, and up to five examples, and the guardrail evaluates all three together as a single unit, not the definition alone. The name can be up to 100 characters. The definition can be up to 1,000 characters, with 100–300 as the practical sweet spot. Each example can be up to 100 characters, and a guardrail can hold up to 30 topics. This practice sets the general frame. Best practices 2 through 4 apply it to each part of a topic in turn: the name, the definition, and the examples. A frequent reason a topic blocks legitimate queries is that the topic describes a subject domain rather than what the user wants from the exchange. Two queries in the same domain can carry different intentions. “When does my direct deposit clear?” and “How much does an L5 engineer earn?” both concern pay, but only the second is a salary comparison. A domain-framed topic collapses those distinctions and can block queries semantically near the domain. A topic framed around the user’s intention matches only queries where that intention is present. Intention is the framing lens. To make it operational, name the topic after the specific action or content type that expresses the intention on the surface, such as a request, a claim, or a piece of generated content. Intention tells you what to catch, and action gives you a concrete shape the guardrail can evaluate. The guardrail evaluates both the topic name and its definition together. When either component names a domain, the topic matches too broadly. When both name an action that expresses a specific intention, the topic is precise. The next few best practices apply this idea to AnyCompany Bank’s own topics, with concrete examples. Best practice 2 renames them, and Best practice 3 tightens their definitions to match. The topic name has a meaningful effect on what is matched, often greater than expected. A broad category name (Finance, Security, Legal) can lead the guardrail to associate the topic with vocabulary in that category, even when the definition attempts to narrow the scope. A specific action name (Investment Recommendations, Hacking Instructions, Suing for Damages) helps narrow the scope before the definition is read. One of AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topics was named Legal: This is why “Can you help me modify my mortgage?” got blocked. Mortgages are legal instruments, so queries about them live in the semantic neighborhood of legal. Renaming solves half the problem before we even touch the definition: The new name uses a verb-derived noun (litigation), names a second specific behavior (non-servicing legal advice), and makes clear by contrast that servicing questions, such as modifications, forbearance, and escrow, are outside the topic. The name itself now carries some of the work the definition would otherwise do alone. AnyCompany Bank applied the same logic to the Fraud topic, renaming it to Fraud Investigation Requests. The assistant should still let customers report fraud, which gets routed to a human, but must not attempt to investigate fraud claims itself. After these three renames, AnyCompany Bank’s topic list is: The definition should describe the user’s action on a specific object, rather than the general subject of that action. We recommend the following structure: [Action or content-type opener] for [specific objects] by [qualifying constraint or purpose]. Includes [one or two sub-cases]. AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topic was named Finance, with a definition to match: This is exactly why “Where can I find my payoff quote?” was blocked. Payoff is a financial term, quote concerns money, and the input is “related to” the finance domain, even though the customer’s intention, retrieving a servicing figure, has nothing to do with what AnyCompany Bank wanted to refuse. Following Best practice 1, the team renamed the topic to Investment Recommendations and adjusted the definition’s vocabulary to match, without yet making it action-scoped: This was still domain-framed even though the name had improved. General education (“Explain what a mutual fund is”), historical financial news (“Why did rates rise last quarter?”), and portfolio review (“Show me my holdings”) all matched. The assistant should answer all of them. The team applied the structural template, with an action opener, specific objects, a qualifying constraint, and one or two sub-cases: Every piece of the template serves a specific purpose. “Asking for a personalized recommendation to…” is the action opener. “Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs, or cryptocurrencies” are the specific objects. “For the user’s own investment returns” is the qualifying constraint that excludes educational and third-party discussion. The “Includes…” clause names two sub-cases: a specific-security question and an allocation-percentage question. AnyCompany Bank applied the same template to the Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests topics: The team now had three named topics with action-scoped definitions. Examples teach the guardrail where the boundaries of your topic are. Not every example does this equally well. Five paraphrases of the same idea teach the guardrail nothing new, while five carefully chosen examples can draw the outline of the topic with much less definition text. The examples that carry the most weight are the ones sitting near the topic’s edge, close enough to a plausible non-match that they show the guardrail where to draw the line. We call these boundary examples. A good boundary example has three properties. First, it’s inside the topic’s scope. Second, it’s close to a plausible non-match, using vocabulary or structure that resembles inputs the topic should not match. Third, it differs from your other examples in sub-case, sentence shape, and vocabulary.

title: Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
abstract: With retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you can customize answers per tenant. The same product and policy documents often serve several audiences, such as customers in different regions or internal teams, and each audience needs its own answer. You set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy that agentic retrieval applies to each request. Before this feature, you couldn’t set the answer style, so agentic retrieval could use a different style from one request to the next. For a fixed voice or structured output, you had to turn off response generation, call a model yourself, and maintain the prompt in every application. Now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it. When you change an instruction, you can pin a version so that each application switches to the new version when you’re ready. Take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious company that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions. Its customer assistant serves all three regions, and its support, field sales, and legal teams use internal assistants that they built on the same documents. AnyCompany defines each region and internal team as a tenant here, and each needs a different answer. A customer in Sales Region Central needs Spanish with day/month/year dates, and a support agent needs a short ticket note. To keep the example compact, every tenant queries one knowledge base. However, agentic retrieval can search up to five knowledge bases in a single request, and the tenant’s instruction applies to all of them. Retrieval instructions change how the assistant answers, but they aren’t an authorization or data-isolation boundary. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to control what each tenant can retrieve. In this post, we show how to give each tenant its own answers from shared knowledge bases while keeping each tenant’s data separate. By the end, you can roll out a change to one tenant’s instruction and confirm which version answered each request. Tenants that share documents still differ in language, date and money conventions, voice, and which policy values they can quote. A retrieval instruction has four fields for these differences: The persona , answerFormat , and answerPolicy fields apply only when generateResponse is true , which is the default, and retrievalGuidance applies either way. For details, see Create and manage retrieval instructions . Table 1 shows how the answer to the same return question changes when the request includes the Sales Region Central instruction and names the customer’s region. Table 1: The same return question with and without the Sales Region Central instruction These patterns come up across industries. An enterprise software provider can run one assistant for many of its own customers. Each customer uploads its policies, standard operating procedures, and company values, and persona and answerPolicy give each one its own voice and rules. A regulated enterprise can put a fixed disclaimer in answerPolicy and a set citation form in answerFormat , so every answer includes both. A team that sends answers to downstream code can get strict JSON from an answerFormat , without a separate generation step. In each case, the documents are shared, and the voice, format, and policy change from caller to caller. An instruction belongs to your AWS account and AWS Region, not to a knowledge base, and goes through these stages: Instructions set voice, format, conventions, and policy wording. They don’t limit which documents the agent can retrieve, and they don’t choose the tenant’s own values, which come from naming the tenant in the request. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to limit what each tenant can retrieve. Each tenant gets its own instruction and metadata filter. The instruction sets the voice, format, and policy of the answer, and the filter limits which documents the agent retrieves. Your backend chooses both from the authenticated tenant, so one shared knowledge base can serve every tenant. In Figure 1, your backend maps the authenticated tenant to an instruction version and a metadata filter, and adds a short tenant line to the message. Then it calls AgenticRetrieveStream on one shared managed knowledge base. Figure 1: One managed knowledge base with per-tenant instructions and filters The same pattern works with a separate knowledge base for each tenant. A request can query a shared global knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base together, each with its own filter. The example uses 32 short, fictitious AnyCompany Smart Home policy and product documents for the AnySmartProduct-5 home controller and AnySmartProduct-6 room sensors. They’re stored in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, and each has region , audience_team , and sensitivity metadata. Each of the six tenants, three regions and three teams, has its own instruction pinned to version 1. Two restricted engineering notes belong to no tenant, so no tenant’s filter should return them. The code is in the GitHub repo , in Python and TypeScript, and runs in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) by default. To use another AWS Region, set AWS_REGION . For the latest Region support, see Supported AWS Regions . Examples use Python with these two clients. Later snippets leave out the client setup and import lines. The Sales Region Central instruction sets the language, date and money formats, and policy wording: To create and pin each tenant’s instruction: This code runs steps 3 and 6. The repo version adds the polling for steps 4 and 5. An update replaces the whole instruction, including the description, so resend every field you want to keep. To encrypt an instruction with your own key, set customerEncryptionKeyArn when you create it. You can’t add or change the key later. Your key policy also needs the statement in Encryption of retrieval instructions . An instruction doesn’t limit which documents the agent retrieves. On a shared knowledge base, a Sales Region North customer’s question can return the Sales Region Central and South addenda, and even notes that no tenant should see. To keep each tenant to its own documents, add a metadata filter built from the authenticated tenant, or give the tenant its own knowledge base. A request can still query the tenant’s knowledge base alongside shared ones. Figure 2 compares the three approaches. Figure 2: Where tenant isolation comes from A metadata filter keeps one knowledge base to sync and maintain, but every document needs accurate metadata, and your backend must build the filter correctly on every request. A separate knowledge base per tenant isolates tenant data by design, but each tenant adds a knowledge base and data source to create, sync, and pay for. You can combine them: one request can query a shared knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base, each with its own filter. With a tenant filter or a separate knowledge base, the agent retrieves only documents the tenant is entitled to, so answers don’t quote other regions’ values. An answer policy that limits the assistant to one region helps, but without a filter an answer can still quote another region’s value. Build the filter on your server from the authenticated tenant, because Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends: This filter uses the equals , andAll , and orAll operators on document metadata. It isn’t per-user access filtering through userContext . Answer policies are best effort. A line such as “Never share restricted engineering notes” can keep values out of the answer. If the notes are retrieved, though, an answer can still name the mechanism or record ID. To keep restricted content out of answers, exclude it with a metadata filter. For each request, your backend sends the tenant’s instruction ID and version, the tenant filter, and a tenant line.

title: Use prompt caching with open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Many generative AI applications send the same long context with every request, and prompt caching avoids processing it again each time. That context can be a system prompt, reference documents, tool definitions, or the conversation so far. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock can reuse it across requests, which helps reduce input costs and response latency. Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix, so repeated context is read from cache instead of being processed again. Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Depending on the model, you can use implicit caching, which works automatically, explicit caching, where you mark the reusable prefix, or both. The more context you reuse, and the more often you reuse it, the more you can save. As with other models on Amazon Bedrock, your prompts and outputs aren’t shared with the model provider or used to train models. For more information, see Data protection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching. In this post, we use both modes with an open-weight model through the Chat Completions API and show how to read cache usage from each response. We then apply implicit caching to an OpenCode coding agent session on the same API and close with best practices. When a request starts with the same content as an earlier one, Amazon Bedrock reads that prefix from cache and processes only the rest. Cache reads are billed at a lower rate than standard input, so the savings can grow each time a prefix is reused. Depending on the model, cache writes can be billed at a higher rate than standard input. See Amazon Bedrock pricing for the rates of each model. Supported modes depend on the model and the API. For each model’s caching modes, minimum prefix length, and how long entries stay cached, see Models at a glance . The two modes compare as follows: Implicit caching : Amazon Bedrock reuses eligible prefixes automatically, on a best-effort basis. In a conversation, each request resends the full context, so the previous request becomes the cached prefix of the next one (Figure 1). As the prompt caching guide recommends, put static content first and dynamic content last. Keeping the start of the prompt stable lets every later request reuse it. If an early part changes, as in turn 4 of Figure 1, the cache is rebuilt from that point. Figure 1: Implicit prompt caching across the turns of a conversation Explicit caching : You mark the end of each reusable prefix with a cache breakpoint. You can add several breakpoints, up to the maximum that the model supports, to cache layers that change at different rates, as Figure 2 shows. Content up to each breakpoint is written to cache once and then read on later requests, and content after the last breakpoint is processed on each request. Check the model card for the minimum token count before a breakpoint, the maximum number of breakpoints, and the time to live (TTL), which resets with each cache hit. Figure 2: Explicit prompt caching with a breakpoint after the shared prefix With implicit caching, Amazon Bedrock can also write content to cache that later requests never reuse, such as a question that’s different each time. When the content after a shared prefix changes on every request, use explicit caching to limit cache writes to the shared prefix. Content after the last breakpoint is billed at the standard input rate. On models that charge more for cache writes, you don’t pay the higher write rate for content that’s never read back. The following diagram shows how both examples in this post reach Amazon Bedrock through the same Chat Completions API endpoint. Figure 3: How the two examples in this post reach Amazon Bedrock To run the samples, you need the following: Before you use a model, review its license and service terms, linked from its model card . Your use of the model is also subject to the AWS Responsible AI Policy . The example is a support assistant for a fictional water filter, the AnyCompany AquaPure 500. The system prompt holds a one-line instruction and the owner’s manual, which is the reusable prefix. Each request asks a different customer question. The samples use the OpenAI Python SDK with the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions endpoint. For authentication, the provide_token() function from the aws-bedrock-token-generator package turns your AWS credentials into a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key , valid for up to 12 hours. You don’t need to create or store a long-term key. 1. Create a virtual environment and install the packages: 2. Create the manual. Ours is about 4,000 tokens of Markdown.
