title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
authors: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
abstract: AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation. Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction. The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower. TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know. The post TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient appeared first on Microsoft Research .

title: Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them: The road to Together Compiler
abstract: Introduction AI inference is becoming increasingly heterogeneous. New model architectures are released every week, inference traffic shifts across different batch sizes and sequence lengths, and hardware platforms continue to proliferate. Achieving peak performance across all these regimes demands optimization frameworks that can keep up. Last year, we helped release some of the first AI megakernels , where we executed an entire model forward pass within a single, highly fused GPU kernel. They reached record breaking speeds, but it was difficult to put them in production. After months of effort, we had a grand total of one model, one batch size, and one customer. This year, we examined what we could simplify and discovered something surprising. With just CUDA Graphs and PDL on top of default Torch Inductor kernels, we could recover 98% of megakernel performance without writing a single kernel. And with “multi-kernels” and agent loops, we could further beat our old megakernels by up to 1.7x, achieving over 1100 TPS for Llama 1B on H100. For the past two years, we've been investigating what a next-generation system for inference optimization should look like. After building a series of GPU programming and optimization systems, we arrived at Together Compiler, our framework for continual AI inference optimization. In this blog, we'll revisit the assumptions behind today's compilers, share the experiments that challenged our thinking, and explain the lessons that shaped Together Compiler. Our journey spans three parts: In Part 1, we show that Torch Compile’s heuristics and benchmarking leave performance on the table, providing motivation to build something radically different. In Part 2, we revisit the megakernels we built to close that gap, explain why they are not always the right optimization target, and decompose their performance gains into simpler primitives. In Part 3, we share our “bitter lessons” from crafting agent-driven optimization infrastructure and the final production system we ended up with. Together Compiler’s journey, coming to a theater near you! Part 1: Torch Compile For over a decade, PyTorch has been the foundation of AI development, providing modular, easy-to-use abstractions ( nn.Module ) that have enabled rapid experimentation. But this modularity comes at a performance cost: executing models as sequences of individual operations can introduce substantial launch overhead, limit opportunities to overlap computation and memory movement, and leave GPU resources underutilized. To address these inefficiencies, PyTorch introduced Torch Compile (“PyTorch 2.0,” powered by Inductor) to optimize and fuse operations, while NVIDIA developed CUDA Graphs to reduce kernel launch overhead. These systems have made enormous progress, but substantial performance gaps remain, often motivating Together’s researchers to invent specialized implementations such as FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, and Megakernels. We start with a brief overview of how Torch Compile works, then present our findings from investigating Inductor’s internals on Llama 1B. How Torch Compile Works At a high level, Torch Compile uses a just-in-time compilation pipeline to capture PyTorch operations into a computation graph, optimize that graph, and generate executable GPU kernels. The key components are: Graph capture. TorchDynamo traces Python execution to capture tensor operations in an intermediate representation called an FX graph. During tracing, it uses fake tensors , which carry metadata such as shapes, data types, and strides without allocating or computing the underlying tensor data. This allows the compiler to reason about the computation without actually executing it on the GPU. The resulting FX graph can be transformed and optimized before code generation. Operations and kernels. Inductor lowers the captured graph into its own intermediate representation, where operations are organized into categories such as pointwise (e.g., activations), reductions (e.g., summations and softmax), scans (e.g., cumulative sums), and templates (e.g., GEMMs and other specialized compute kernels). Some operations instead invoke existing implementations from libraries such as cuBLAS or custom PyTorch operators. Inductor represents these as external kernels ( ExternKernel ), whose implementations are generally opaque to its fusion machinery. Fusion and optimization. Inductor uses a greedy, pairwise algorithm to decide which operations to fuse into the same kernel. Its can_fuse() function checks whether a candidate fusion is legal, while score_fusion() ranks opportunities using heuristics such as estimated memory traffic savings. The algorithm repeatedly applies profitable fusions, potentially combining many operations into a single kernel. However, these decisions are based on local heuristics rather than a global search over all possible kernel partitions and execution strategies. For example, Inductor may avoid fusing operations that share no memory accesses, even when executing their work together could improve GPU utilization. On our target Llama 1B workload, Inductor delivers 669 TPS. As we’ll show in Part 2, these generated kernels are sometimes enough, and with small modifications, they can reach similar levels of performance to megakernels. However, on different architectures and newer hardware, Inductor’s heuristics can’t keep up. We investigated where Inductor struggles most and present three findings. Finding #1: Compiler heuristics cannot reliably select the best implementation across workloads. Inductor exposes a number of compiler tuning flags that can boost performance. We discovered that even these seemingly simple configurations exposed a surprisingly large and complex search space. The best optimization depends on the workload. Inductor exposes a freezing flag that tells the compiler that model weights will not change during inference. Knowing this, the compiler can transform the weights ahead of time to make subsequent computations faster. One such transformation converts weights to FP32 to perform certain optimizations, before converting them back to their original, lower-precision format. We found that enabling freezing improved throughput by 10–26% at larger batch sizes, where the GPU performs matrix-matrix multiplications. However, at batch size 1, where inference primarily uses matrix-vector multiplications, enabling the same flag caused a 49% slowdown . Upon inspection, we discovered that the FP32 conversion was not reversed for matrix-vector operations, leaving the GPU to process larger, 32-bit weights instead of the original lower-precision weights. In other words, the exact same compiler optimization could improve performance for one batch size while dramatically degrading it for another. Inductor config flags by quarter, 2022-2026 ‍ Optimizations interact in unpredictable ways. As of Q3 2026, Inductor exposes 607 tuning flags, 198 of which were added in the past year. These flags control everything from kernel fusion to memory access patterns and scheduling. Their effects are not independent: enabling the aggressive_fusion flag alone reduced Llama 1B throughput by 6 TPS, but enabling it alongside the combo_kernels , benchmark_fusion , and triton.coalesce_tiling_analysis flags improved throughput by 3 TPS. Even small configuration changes could produce measurable microsecond-level differences in execution time. Takeaway: the space of possible optimizations and configurations is large, and we should be searching it systematically instead of guessing the right flags to set. Finding #2: The fastest kernel in isolation isn't necessarily the fastest during inference. Inductor makes optimization decisions based on its benchmarking harness. We identify two distinct ways that this benchmarking misleads its decision, hurting overall performance as a result. First, it ignores that kernel performance depends on caching behavior.

title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
abstract: Summary Coding agents send the whole conversation again on every turn. Prefix caching keeps the inference engine from redoing that work, but only if the harness leaves the start of the prompt alone and the engine sends each turn back to the GPU that already has it cached. Together AI and Ollama work on opposite sides of that handoff, so we wrote down what each, the client side and the inference engine side, needs to do to successfully build agentic apps. Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more. This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. The problem is that if you’re not careful it's also very easy to break the prefix cache. We come at this problem from opposite ends. Ollama works on harness integrations which means deciding what goes into each request. Together AI works on the inference engine which means deciding what happens when that request arrives. We kept finding that much of our work on each side is about protecting the cache from things the other side can do to it, so we wanted to write it all down in one place to help agent and infra builders alike! What an agent turn looks like to a GPU Every request goes through two phases. The first is prefill: the engine reads the whole prompt in one big parallel pass and produces the first token. GPUs are good at this because it's a lot of math done all at once which maximizes arithmetic intensity. Prefill determines how long you wait before any new tokens appear. The second is decode: the model writes the rest of the answer one token at a time, and each new token requires reading back and attending through everything before it. Decode is limited by memory bandwidth more than by compute, and it determines how fast the text streams out. A normal chat response spends time in both phases while an agent turn is mostly prefill, because the input is the whole session and the output is usually a short tool call. Reasoning models add thinking tokens on top of that, sometimes a lot of them, but as a session grows into the tens of thousands of tokens the input still dominates. Each turn the input gets longer, and the output stays roughly the same size — a few tool calls. So for agents, "how fast is this model?" mostly means "how fast can it get through a long historical account of pervious turns?" The way to process a task with lots of previous turns quickly is to just cache it and read it back in rather then recomputing. Cache is king The easiest way to picture the KV cache(or even the prefix cache, for that matter) is reading. Imagine that to read each new word on a page, you had to start again from the top. The further down the page you got, the slower you'd go, because you'd keep having to reread everything you'd already read. That's a model with no cache. The cache solves this within a single request: the engine keeps the work it did on earlier tokens(stored as intermediate key, value pairs) and computes only the new one. Prefix caching does the same thing across requests. Turn 7 of an agent session is turn 6 plus a bit more, so if the engine still holds turn 6's work, it only has to process the new part. The arithmetic is simple. If each turn adds the same amount, ten turns without caching process 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 units of prompt. With caching, they process 10. At a hundred turns, which isn't unusual for a coding task, it's 5,050 versus 100. Real turns vary in size, so treat these as idealized numbers. A cached session isn't completely free either, since every new token still has to attend to the cached ones. But the pattern holds: without caching, the work you redo grows with the square of the session length. The catch is that a prefix cache matches from the beginning of the prompt up to the first token that's different, and stops there. Everything after that first difference has to be processed again. Adding to the end of the prompt costs nothing extra. Changing anything earlier, even a single character, means re-processing everything after it. If the change is near the top, you've effectively thrown away the whole session and now must rebuilt the cache. Almost everything else in this post follows from that one rule. The harness decides where that first change lands. The engine decides whether the cache is still there when the next request shows up. We'll start with the harness. The harnesses and APIs On the Ollama side, we shipped the ability to connect your favorite harness through the ollama launch command. So you can connect harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, Pi (and more) with open models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3 and maintain your existing workflows. Connecting a harness to an API might seem easy, but there are many layers of translation and varying expectations between a harness and a model. This often is the cause of cache breakages (incurring time and monetary costs), unexplainable agent behavior, and the harness outright erroring. Loading tools late Harnesses carry quite a few tools now. If every definition goes into the prompt up front, you spend context on tools the task will never use, and the model gets worse at picking the right one. Newer harnesses have added a feature for tool search to alleviate this, where the tool can be loaded and used by the agent itself after searching for it. Let’s say you have a personal assistant as an agent which has this capability. If you ask the agent to export the events you've starred to a calendar, and it searches for "calendar," loads the save_calendar definition, and calls it. For the cache, the question is where that definition goes. The obvious approach is to add the definition to the tool list. That works, but the tool list sits near the top of the prompt, before the conversation. So if the prefix changes everything after it gets processed again. On a long session, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens. The better approach is to put the definition at the end, where new content goes anyway. Except not every model supports that. Some chat templates don't expect a tool definition halfway through a conversation, and the call errors out. So whether a harness can load tools late without paying for it depends on the model. Users shouldn't have to know this, but anyone building a harness does. Things at the top that change The easiest way to wreck the cache is to put something in the system prompt that changes from turn to turn, like a current timestamp, the git status, or a working directory the agent keeps moving through. If the harness re-renders the system prompt with fresh values on every turn, every turn is a full re-read. Things that are fixed for a session but differ between sessions, like the user's name or the date the session started, don't hurt that session. They do stop new sessions from reusing a setup that's already cached, which we'll get to on the engine side. Either way, the fix is the same: put that information in the task message, once, and keep the system prompt identical everywhere. Reasoning effort We hit this one on the Ollama side. In GLM-5.3-Flash, reasoning effort isn't a separate setting the engine handles on the side. The chat template writes it into the very first system block, ahead of the tools and the conversation. Let’s say you're deep into a long task and it isn't going well. You raise effort from low to high.

title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
abstract: Earlier this year, we started seeing more and more devs using coding agents to build with Together AI. It’s not hard to see why: It might take days or even weeks for a developer to wire up an app for production inference by hand, especially if they’re new to the platform. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory. In practice, we had no idea whether the agents pointed at our platform were able to work with Together efficiently, or if they were hitting obstacles, going down rabbit holes or failing outright, and wasting tokens in the process. As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows. GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). This is thanks to GitHub’s phenomenal API, CLI, and docs, all of which make it exceptionally easy for agents to use. (This writer was not even aware GitHub had a CLI until agents started using it for him, and now he probably uses it 1000+ times a day). To improve our AX at Together AI, we needed a way to measure how agent-ready our platform actually was. In this post, we’ll walk through how we run agent evals, two problems they uncovered and how we fixed them, and what we’ve learned. How we run agent evals at Together Building the task list Before we could start evaluating, we needed to know what agents were actually being asked to do … so we could, y’know, figure out if they could do those things. We started building a list of common tasks that developers tackle on Together, like running a batch inference job, building a voice agent, or managing autoscaling for an inference endpoint. By task, we really just mean a prompt, something you’d tell an agent to do—for example: List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. To pass the eval, the agent has to: Find the latest pricing info. Call the regions API endpoint to list the available regions. Combine the two to find the cheapest option. Produce a valid CLI command for creating the cluster. The prompt asks for both availability and pricing, without mentioning that these details live in two different places. This is realistic, as the average user probably doesn’t know up front where each piece of information lives, which could easily trip up both humans and agents. Three configurations After building our list of tasks, we run each one of them three ways: Baseline: The agent receives just the prompt, with no special configuration, mirroring the average developer's workflow. It can use all its default tools, like fetching docs from the web, but we don't give it any specific MCP connectors or skills. MCP: The agent gets direct access to our documentation through our MCP server, so it knows exactly where to search when it hits a roadblock. Skills: We give the agent the Together skill package , which contains instructions and examples for using our services, written specifically for agents. The run matrix Each full evaluation runs every task against each agent configuration using three models, with two attempts at each task—so six attempts per task for each config, as shown here for our run on September 30th: gents passed 192 of 215 scored runs. The GPU cluster task failed every baseline run and passed every skills run. Automating the runs When we started building our evals, we ran everything by hand: open a new terminal, paste a prompt into Claude Code, let the agent do its thing (or fail to do its thing), and repeat for each configuration. It was manual and tedious, so once we figured out the shape of the system we wanted, we started automating it. Now we run each agent in a Together sandbox so they don’t interfere with our local environment or each other. GitHub Actions handles setup, starts the agent, cleans up afterward, and saves the results, while a proxy handles the agent's requests to the Together API and records the activity, so we can see which endpoints the agent calls and what comes back. Scoring a run After a run finishes, an LLM judge reviews the task prompt and the recorded session, then assigns one of three verdicts: Pass: Every task requirement was met. Incomplete: The agent attempted the task, but some required steps were unfinished or unverified. Fail: The agent gave up early, broke an explicit constraint, or produced an incorrect result (RIP). Failed and incomplete verdicts don’t necessarily tell us whether the problem was with the agent, the API, or missing evidence. They just tell us where to start looking. We investigate passing runs too. An agent can often work around confusing responses and still finish, and those recoveries show us what to fix to improve token efficiency. To make that review practical, we built a results viewer that compares how different models and configs performed. For each run, it shows the prompt, the tools the agent used, the responses it got back, and any API activity: Our results viewer comparing setups on the GPU cluster task. Both guided setups passed, and the skills runs used the fewest tool calls and cost the least. Case study 1: GPU cluster pricing Remember the GPU cluster task from earlier? List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. Seems pretty simple, but when we ran our evals early last summer, Sonnet 4.6 passed only 4 of 15 attempts at this task, even with skills enabled. Our post-mortem revealed the same pattern in the failed runs: Sonnet treated the sample output in our CLI reference, which listed a single region and two GPU types, as if it were the live inventory. It also skipped the regions lookup and named what it thought was the cheapest option without ever checking the pricing page. The problems were on our end. First, the sample output wasn’t properly labeled, so nothing told the agent to run the command to retrieve the relevant data. Second, our skill file linked to the GPU clusters marketing page rather than the pricing table, so Sonnet opened the marketing page, didn’t see any real prices, and just made a best-effort guess at the cheapest GPU available. More capable models were able to work around the issue. In that same period, Opus 4.8 passed 13 of 14 attempts using the same config. According to the transcript, it noticed that the list_regions response didn't include prices, so it kept searching until it found them in our docs. This is why it’s crucial to test your product with less capable models; if we had only tested with Opus, it would have taken us much longer to find the gap. Isolating the failure To fix it, we isolated the failure by pulling the GPU clusters skill out of the full skill package, and wrote a narrower prompt that reproduced only this issue. It failed every time when tested against the old skill file, so we had reliable repro steps (use the old skill), and an easy way to test each new version (update the skill). We went through several iterations until we landed on a small change: two new sentences in the skill that point the agent to the pricing table, and explain how to use it with the live regions API: Query GET <https://api.together.ai/v1/compute/regions > or run tg clusters list-regions --json for the live region inventory, supported instance types, and compatible CUDA/driver pairs. Open the GPU Cluster pricing table for current on-demand and reserved rates.

title: Clean data was never enough: How IFS Copperleaf taught AI its business with Databricks Genie One
abstract: IFS Copperleaf is a leading global provider of Asset Investment Planning (AIP) software, helping asset-intensive organizations make better investment decisions, balance risk and value and maximize the impact of their capital investments. With more than 25 years of experience, IFS Copperleaf pioneered the AIP software category and is now part of IFS, a global leader in enterprise cloud and Industrial AI software. Most data teams never get time to ask that question. In the fall of 2025, Misagh Jebeli, IFS Copperleaf’s Enterprise Data Architect, and Lisa Richter, Director of Technology and AI at IFS Copperleaf, made the time. Developers were already shipping AI-written code, while data teams were still building every pipeline by hand, and they were sure that gap would close. “I watched AI change how our developers work almost overnight, and I kept asking why data teams were still hand-building every model before anyone could ask a question. It was inevitable that data engineering would change, too. It’s exciting, and a little scary, to question everything a 20-year career taught you,” Misagh says. Their bet: by 2027, people would stop looking for reports. The tools they already use every day would understand the business, answer in plain language and act on their behalf. Building for that future meant facing today's reality. Like most enterprises, IFS Copperleaf runs on many systems, from CRM and marketing platforms to support, contract and finance tools, each owned by a different part of the business. A cross-functional answer meant manual exports into a spreadsheet versioning abyss, reconciliation and, often, a meeting about whose number was right. Lisa has seen the same problem at every company she has worked for. "Even at the most simplistic level, how many customers do we have? This is a fundamental question, but when you have siloed SaaS systems owned by different parts of the business and inconsistent definitions of what a customer is, it's hard to answer. AI on top of that inconsistent data just puts it on full display with flashing neon lights." They knew what they didn't want: another custom build that goes stale once the people who built it move on. They wanted a foundation that was standardized, governed and usable by business teams without having to wait in a queue. They held it to three outcomes: faster decisions, grounded in trusted data, and no longer dependent on a specialist. With that, they went looking for the platform to build on. IFS Copperleaf's journey with IONA began with an ambitious vision: rethink how employees interact with business data and make advanced analytics accessible to everyone, not just technical specialists. Rather than simply introducing another AI or BI tool, the team set out to create a new way for employees to access information, explore insights and make more informed decisions. When the IFS Copperleaf team started designing IONA, they began exploring the Databricks Platform, specifically the Genie product family. Genie provided not only the AI cowork and conversational analytics features their team needed to drive org-wide adoption, but also invested in building a unified context layer that was critical to IONA’s vision. They naturally became a voice of how advanced customers were looking to build on and deploy Genie, working closely with the engineers and product managers building Genie. The IFS Copperleaf team shared prototypes, brought real business requirements and sent feedback that helped inform the future of several features across Genie One , Genie Agents and Genie Ontology . "We would have moved on to build our own thing," Misagh says. "But we made this partnership happen because we both had the same vision." The textbook approach to enterprise analytics says every table must be cleaned and modeled before anyone can query it. With nearly 30 source systems and tens of thousands of tables, that queue would never empty. So the team flipped it. Finance and the marketing-to-sales funnel, where the stakes are highest, are fully modeled. For everything else, IONA answers directly on the raw data. Data became useful months sooner, and modeling effort went where accuracy matters most. "Every playbook had us start with modeling the data. And we did, at first. But based on industry trends, we intentionally did a 180. We let AI work on the raw data, and have the business teach it what the data means. It was a huge gamble, but it's what made it work," Misagh says. As the IFS Copperleaf team started unifying business data access through Databricks and testing IONA with their teams, business users were immediately relieved and excited to have democratized access to data that had previously been limited to formal analysis or technical practitioners. But once people started asking IONA more complex questions, a signal emerged that Lisa and Misagh had not anticipated: Unlike generic AI tools that may either provide confident but false answers or simply leave users stranded when they lack the context needed to answer a question, IONA, built on Genie and grounded in Genie Ontology, was designed to self-improve and prompt for additional information when needed. As IONA users began understanding the power of a unified context layer for AI and relying on IONA for more of their daily tasks, Lisa and Misagh saw new trends emerge: As employees began working with IONA to refine its understanding of their business, IFS Copperleaf brought that real-world feedback to the Databricks team to help shape the future of Genie. Getting from a tool people liked to one the whole company could rely on meant giving up something most technology teams never do. "Five years ago, I'd have shut this down myself. Business users writing logic that changes the number the whole company sees, with no ticket, no sprint and no release cycle? It challenged every change-control instinct and rule I'd spent my career enforcing. But a small team was never going to know what every number means across the business. The people who own the definitions do. So we didn't put a gate in front of it. We put guardrails around it. The real risk evolved from never letting the business write the rules into making them wait on us," Lisa says. With these policies in place, the team was ready to open up IONA to data from nearly 30 systems across the business such as Salesforce, HubSpot, Confluence, Jira, Freshdesk, G2, M365 and more, so they could give every team one place to ask questions and take action with AI. Skills sit atop the Genie Ontology, the shared business context layer in Databricks. Ontology connects the business's definitions to the metrics, tables, dashboards and agents that use them, so IONA knows that a renewal in Salesforce, a contract in the contract system and a forecast in Finance are about the same customer. It draws on two kinds of knowledge: what the business has manually modeled and what it picks up from everyday use. Another important part of IFS Copperleaf’s philosophy in building IONA was to give users the ability to access AI and governed business context from anywhere they were already working. In addition to giving users direct access to IONA via Genie One, the team ensured that insights could be delivered directly within existing workflows, which drove them to be one of the earliest adopters of the Genie mobile app, Copilot and Teams apps and the Claude MCP plugin. "AI is changing so fast. We want to enable our users to safely experiment in the tool du jour, knowing that six months from now it'll probably be something different. So interoperability isn’t optional. The knowledge must follow the person, with the same definitions and the same rules about who sees what, regardless of whether the interface is Teams, Claude or Genie," Lisa explains. With a 70% activation rate for IFS Copperleaf since its launch in July, there’s no shortage of use cases employees have found to put it to work.

title: Talk to your clinical data: unlocking AWS HealthLake with OpenSharing and Genie One
abstract: Many healthcare and life sciences organizations have standardized on AWS HealthLake to manage clinical data, but extending that data to other platforms for analytics and AI has traditionally required more effort. For companies seeking to use data living in HealthLake with external analytics tooling, this process has required building export pipelines, duplicating data, and managing governance separately in each location. This has limited the interoperability of HealthLake-managed FHIR data across other tools and platforms. In this blog, we present a new solution leveraging OpenSharing (A Linux Foundation AI & Data Project) to enable a first-of-its-kind integration between HealthLake and Databricks. This architecture allows users to query HealthLake data live from Databricks, bringing Databricks governance, analytics, and AI capabilities to clinical datasets. By integrating with HealthLake, Databricks can enable organizations to unlock deeper insights from FHIR data and open the door to a broader set of analytics and AI use cases. Furthermore, that same clinical data can now be explored through natural language with Genie One, allowing users to surface insights without specialized technical workflows or data duplication. The Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standard is a data format which is used to exchange health information across different applications and care settings. AWS HealthLake is a managed healthcare data service for storing and working with data in FHIR format. Healthcare organizations often use HealthLake to normalize this FHIR data, as well as for its standards-compliant API for resources such as patient records, observations, and encounters. HealthLake stores its analytics tables as Apache Iceberg tables in an Amazon S3 bucket owned by the HealthLake service. Customer IAM roles can’t read that bucket directly, so external tools such as Unity Catalog have no direct path to the underlying data. As a result, accessing this data for analytics on external platforms has previously required export pipelines that copy FHIR data out of HealthLake before it can be queried. While many organizations rely on HealthLake’s purpose-built FHIR data store, extending it with governance, analytics, and natural language exploration has been less straightforward. This new integration with Databricks unlocks valuable new insights from this clinical data. Our new integration, shown in the architecture below, uses OpenSharing to securely expose data in HealthLake without requiring any export pipelines or data duplication. This allows HealthLake data to be read directly by Databricks and governed by Unity Catalog as a shared catalog. Today, the only way HealthLake provides direct access to its underlying Iceberg tables is through temporary credentials generated by Lake Formation, and Unity Catalog cannot request these credentials itself. This solution fills that gap with a custom OpenSharing server that runs as a Databricks App, a fully managed serverless deployment. On every table request, the server uses Lake Formation credentials, resolves the table’s current Iceberg snapshot, pre-signs the data files, and returns them in a standard OpenSharing response. Databricks compute then reads the files directly from S3, so no data passes through the server. AWS trusts the app’s own Databricks identity through OIDC federation, protecting sensitive healthcare data. Databricks mounts the share in Unity Catalog like any other share, making the data available for governed analytics, notebooks, dashboards, AI, and natural language exploration with Genie One. With HealthLake data now readable in Databricks, organizations can bring their clinical data directly under Unity Catalog governance. Unity Catalog becomes the entry point for access, with grants, fine-grained access controls (FGAC), attribute-based access controls (ABAC), and role-based access controls (RBAC) on the shared catalog specifying who is permitted to see and query each table. Access and usage can also be audited like any other data asset in Unity Catalog, making clinical data easier to govern and secure. That same shared data can now back Genie One in Databricks, broadening analysis of HealthLake data to less-technical users. This means that clinical analysts, operational teams, or strategy leaders can now explore HealthLake data directly, without filing a ticket with the data team or waiting for a custom report. Organizations can create and curate Genie Agents over the shared catalog by defining core clinical tables, adding plain-language descriptions, and teaching them how to define and interpret clinical concepts like A1C. A user can then ask a question like “How is average A1C trending by month?” and Genie One understands the context, finds the curated Genie Agent, generates the SQL, and returns the summarized answer with a table and chart, all while respecting Unity Catalog permissions. Questions that previously required SQL skills or custom dashboard creation can now be answered in seconds, and the insights living in HealthLake-managed FHIR data become accessible to a broader set of clinical, operational, and business users. This integration extends HealthLake beyond the analytics paths that have traditionally been available. Organizations no longer need to copy and export data to external analytics tools, or rely solely on Athena or Redshift for analytics. Instead, users now have the option to work with HealthLake data directly in Databricks for governed analytics, notebooks, dashboards, and AI, unlocking new value and insights from clinical data.
