title: Tabular foundation models on Databricks AI Runtime
abstract: Many of the most valuable predictive machine learning applications rely on tabular data. From credit risk and customer churn to demand forecasting and predictive maintenance, these use cases have traditionally required teams to develop, train and maintain models for each prediction task. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer another approach: pretrained models that can make predictions on new datasets without task-specific training. Productionizing ML systems at scale remains a challenge for many enterprises for the following reasons: Recently, agentic solutions have helped accelerate these expensive operations, but they still rely on a bespoke-trained model for each ML task or dataset. To remove this dependency, pioneering research labs have applied the transformer architecture to tabular data at scale, creating a new category of models called Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs). Because TFMs come pretrained, they require no training on your dataset, meaning bespoke training and retraining pipelines largely disappear. Despite the impressive accuracy these models demonstrate on public benchmarks, they have not yet cracked into the mainstream of enterprise AI. This is partially due to the nascent nature of the field, as not many practitioners know about them yet, but also due to compute infrastructure requirements. In this article, we'll examine how TFMs work, compare recent models and explain the trade-offs involved in adopting them for enterprise ML. We'll then demonstrate how Databricks AI Runtime supports TFM experimentation and fine-tuning with managed GPU infrastructure, integrated development tools and model governance. TFMs largely eliminate the need for training and the overhead of maintaining bespoke models. They are pretrained on millions of diverse synthetic datasets so that they can infer relationships between variables in an unseen dataset. At prediction time, the labeled rows are passed as context alongside the rows to predict. Attention, the core of the transformer architecture, then relates each new row to those examples. Predictions are produced by a single forward pass, a process called in-context learning (ICL). While this zero-shot approach provides a powerful baseline out of the box, TFMs can also be fine-tuned. By updating the model's pretrained weights on a specific dataset, ML teams can push predictive accuracy even higher for their most critical use cases. The main complexity for transformers in TFMs is handling various input types. Unlike words in text or pixels in an image, a table mixes numerical, categorical, and boolean features, each with its own scale and meaning. Efficiently embedding these inputs into a common latent space has been a major challenge. The community solved this by developing specialized tokenizers that map both categorical and numerical features into a single, shared representation. Once an efficient tokenization for every cell had been achieved, the problem was how to effectively learn the relationship between rows and columns. TabPFNv2 was the first to make this work at foundation-model scale. As shown in Figure 1, it involved applying attention mechanisms sequentially within rows and then within columns, capturing the complex interactions between features and the underlying relationships across different data samples. Despite its success, this approach faces severe scalability limits. By performing dense attention across rows and then columns, the computational cost grows rapidly, making it prohibitively expensive as the number of samples and features increases. As a solution, TabICLv1 uses a row-compression approach, in which specialized encoders represent each row with just four tokens, making attention across samples much cheaper while maintaining competitive predictive performance. This architecture is shown in Figure 2, but it has since been adopted and extended by models like TabPFNv3 , TabFM , and KumoTabular , which are among the top-ranked models in benchmarks like TabArena today. Apart from the architecture, another distinctive feature of TFMs is how they are built: model creators primarily use synthetic data during the pretraining phase. The determining factor in a TFM's out-of-the-box success is whether these researchers can generate synthetic data that accurately represents the distributions and relationships of real-world datasets. To build a robust foundation model, creators must simulate large-scale, diverse data that captures common enterprise quality issues like missingness, outliers, and unobserved features. While Structural Causal Models provide a standardized framework for sampling these pretraining datasets, the exact pipeline configuration depends heavily on the specific TFM. As the TFM landscape rapidly evolves with frequent new releases, evaluating options for enterprise deployment requires careful scrutiny. The following table highlights leading models through the lens of two practical deployment factors: scale and licensing. BSD 3-Clause : Commercially permissive TabFM Non-Commercial License v1.0 * Not commercially permissive TABPFN-3.5 License v1.0 * Not commercially permissive Apache-2.0 : Commercially permissive OpenMDW-1.1 : Commercially permissive *Commercially permissive upon agreement with the model creators. For an exhaustive list of the current state of the art, check benchmarks like TabArena or TALENT . Given the unique trade-offs of each TFM, we recommend evaluating these models directly against your organization's data, as proprietary enterprise workloads often differ drastically from synthetic data or standard benchmarks. Beyond just measuring predictive accuracy, teams must also evaluate the operational cost. While TFMs save massive amounts of engineering time by eliminating bespoke training pipelines, running a foundation model on GPUs inherently costs more per prediction than executing a traditional XGBoost model on a CPU. For any given use case, evaluating a TFM means weighing that accelerated time-to-market and performance lift against the ongoing cost of GPU inference. Inference with TFMs is optimized on GPUs. The models themselves are small enough to fit on a single GPU, but with in-context learning, the entire training set is passed to the model with every prediction. As a result, GPU memory usage grows with the number of rows and features, and can quickly be exhausted at the dataset sizes typical of enterprise ML. The need for a performant GPU leads to three problems: Databricks unifies data and AI in a single open platform. AI Runtime, a fully managed serverless GPU infrastructure, offers this unified experience for enterprise GPU workloads. Experimentation and productionization have never been easier using AI Runtime, which includes features such as: With Databricks AI Runtime, you can run your TFM workloads right where your data lives, using Unity Catalog to govern and manage the lifecycle of your GPU workflows without creating any silos. Clone this repository to see how to run zero-shot inference with various TFMs using Databricks AI Runtime, alongside complete fine-tuning examples for classification and regression with KumoTabular. These examples showcase how AI Runtime helps you easily manage the lifecycle and integration of advanced TFM fine-tuning workflows. Video 2 walks through the fine-tuning notebook with an H100, showing how GPU usage observability is embedded right into the notebook as well as the MLflow experiment used for metric tracking. Additionally, the workflow covers centralized governance and registration through Unity Catalog, facilitating robust version control and structured model lifecycle management. Tabular foundation models promise to reduce the time to market of ML initiatives from months to days, and with Databricks AI Runtime, GPU workloads are no longer an obstacle.

title: Teach Genie One your workflows: The ultimate guide for skills in Genie One
abstract: Every team has “recipes” that govern how they work. The way finance puts together the month-end pack, the checks sales operations runs before a forecast call, the format leadership expects when performing a retrospective. These templates live in people's heads, in old emails and in "here's how I do it" documents that nobody can find. Genie One already understands a lot about your business. Through Genie Ontology , it not only learns your business definitions, but also how your teams use their data. Skills add an extra layer of control: how you like things done. A skill is a workflow recipe that Genie One can follow on demand ensuring a consistent format and output each time. For example, with a skill, users can prompt Genie One to "Put together our trading report for last month", and know that it will return the report the way your team would have prepared it, with the same checks, the same structure and the same level of detail. Genie One leverages skills when they are either called directly by the user, or when it decides that it's relevant to what you've requested. That means you can keep adding skills, each with as much detail as its task needs, and their guidance stays with that task rather than spilling into your other work. Skills are durable, reusable assets. A skill is a written record of how your team works, in plain language and in the open Agent Skills format, so it's yours to keep, review and build upon. Publish it through Unity Gateway and the same recipe can be used by any agent that supports MCP, including the coding agents your teams already use. And once it works, share it across your organisation, so one person's best way of working becomes everyone's. It’s easy to get started with skills. You can build a skill directly in Genie One through one conversation, simply by explaining your workflow in detail once. You should consider a skill when you find yourself explaining the same thing to Genie One more than once. Good signs include: Skills sit alongside the other ways Genie One learns your organisation. A skill holds the method: the steps, checks and format for a piece of work. Genie Ontology tells Genie One what things mean, and a skill tells it a specific way to get something done. Skills also work hand in hand with Genie Agents . A Genie Agent is the domain expert for one area of your organisation. It knows the metric definitions, tables, joins and business rules for one scoped domain, such as sales, finance or HR. A skill is the recipe for a specific task: the steps, the checklist and the output format. For example, a sales pipeline Genie Agent knows the pipeline tables, joins and stage definitions. A "weekly forecast risk memo" skill tells Genie One to compare this week's pipeline with last week's, flag deals that slipped and produce a one-page memo. The Genie Agent supplies the domain knowledge and the skill supplies Genie One with the workflow. The quality of a skill comes from how well you describe the work. Before you start, walk through the task end to end and answer a few questions: Then hand it to Genie One. Describe the workflow in your own words and ask it to interview you before it writes anything. Genie One draws on what it already knows through Genie Ontology, so its questions focus on how you work rather than what your data means. A commercial finance team writes a trading brief for leadership every month. The workflow is simple to describe: pull last month's numbers, check each channel against a few rules, dig into anything unusual, look for emails from the team that explain it, then write a short brief. Described in a couple of sentences, that was enough for Genie One to get started. It found the relevant Genie Agent and governed metric view through Genie Ontology on its own, then asked about the method: which measures matter every month, which breakdowns to show, what counts as unusual, what the write-up should look like and whether to pause for review. Answering in plain language was enough for Genie One to write the skill. Judgement is what makes a skill more than a scheduled report. A dashboard or a fixed job does the same thing every time. Genie One can use a skill to make decisions, like choosing the three changes most worth leadership's attention, following an unusual result until it makes sense and explaining it in plain language, the same way you would trust an experienced colleague to. That doesn’t mean everything should be left open. Some parts need to come out exactly the same every time, whereas others are better left to Genie One's judgement. Be deliberate about which is which. Strict rules suit anything someone else relies on: numbers that are compared over time, a format another team or system expects, the thresholds that decide what gets a closer look and the disclaimers or sign-offs that must always be there. Conditions are worth spelling out too: what must always appear, and what should happen when something is missing. For example, the trading brief always includes a watch list, even when it only says nothing breached a threshold, because a missing section looks like a missed step. Because Genie One only reads the skills it needs, it can be advantageous to keep them specific and focused. A skill that does one job well is easier to test, easier to fix and easier to reuse than one that tries to do everything. The real payoff is that small skills can be chained together. A useful way to think about it: For example, from updating the style guidelines skill once, every other skill that uses it picks up the change. Start with one skill, then split it when the instructions start covering two different jobs, or when you notice the same rules being copied into a second skill. Genie One with a new skill is like a capable new starter: smart and quick to learn, but you check their first few pieces of work to make sure they're delivering what you're looking for. Test the skill the way people will really use it. Ask in your own words rather than by name, and check the result against what you know. A few habits make testing quicker: Let's say a monthly trading brief skill has been built. Genie One pulls last month's numbers, flags anything unusual (such as a product line growing much faster than the rest), checks the team's inbox for context and writes up a short brief. On its first run, two things needed fixing. It reported on September while the month's data was still incomplete, and it flagged product lines so small that their movements didn't matter. Both were fixed in one message. Genie One was told to only report on a month once its data is complete, and to ignore anything under $50,000 in sales. It updated the skill and reran the brief for August, showing every change in the document. After, Genie One was then retested in a fresh chat. "Put together our trading report for last month" loaded the skill without naming it. This time Genie One reported on August, the latest complete month, and only flagged the two items big enough to matter: a jump in online marketplace returns and a spike in business sales. It searched the team's Trading Notes label in Gmail and found an email explaining each one: a retailer's free returns event and a one-off hotel order. A skill should be managed like any other trusted asset. Unity Gateway Skills (Beta) give your organisation one central place to publish, discover and govern skills. When you publish a skill from Genie One, it becomes a Unity Catalog object, protected by the same permissions, tags and audit as your other data assets. You decide who can use it and who can edit it, there are no copies to keep in sync, and teams can find what already exists rather than rebuilding it. Skills start out as your own. When one would be valuable for others in your organisation, publish it through Unity Gateway and share it with the individuals or groups who need it. They can switch it on in Genie One straight away.

title: Introducing the Databricks AI Index: The state of enterprise AI tokenomics
abstract: Developers have more AI models and coding agents to choose from than ever before. Since May 2026, a new flagship proprietary or open-weight model has launched roughly every week, or every 3.7 days when regional labs are included. With so many options, knowing which models perform best, what they cost, and when to switch is becoming harder. At Databricks, we have a unique perspective on this rapidly changing landscape. Thousands of enterprises use Unity Gateway to access and govern AI models, providing us with insights into real-world model adoption and spending. Databricks also heavily leverages AI internally across our 12,000+ employees, and we've invested substantial research in evaluating the quality and cost of new frontier models on enterprise tasks. Today, we're launching the Databricks AI Index , a public resource that brings these insights together. Customers have repeatedly asked us how new models compare and what we're seeing across enterprise AI adoption to help inform their own investments. Now, for the first time, we're making our internal evaluation suite permanently public, with weekly updates as we evaluate new proprietary and open-weight model releases. The Index combines two complementary sources of data: Enterprise AI usage and spending. Aggregated, anonymized data from 10,000+ companies using Unity Gateway , spanning digital natives, Fortune 500, and Global 2000 enterprises, including traffic to external providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI. The Index tracks model adoption through token and spend shares across proprietary and open-weight models, as well as weekly AI spending patterns for individual users. Continuously updated coding-agent evaluations. Building on the coding-agent benchmark we published in July , our latest evaluations draw on real coding-agent workflows from Databricks engineers, captured through Unity Gateway. These workflows span creating and reviewing pull requests, investigating issues, and tackling complex development tasks. Using tasks from our private codebase and withheld tests helps reduce the risk of benchmark contamination while enabling consistent comparisons of model-harness combinations and terms of task success rates and cost per completed task. Together, these data sources show which models enterprises are adopting, how well different combinations of models and harnesses perform, and what they cost. Here are some highlights: Enterprises are increasingly shifting workloads between model versions and providers. At mid-year, most organizations relied on a handful of Anthropic models for the majority of their work. Today, adoption is far more fragmented across model versions and providers alike. OpenAI's share of enterprise token traffic grew meaningfully over this period, driven largely by its 6 series Sol and Astra models. However, model quality continues to strongly influence provider market share; when Claude Opus 5.5 launched, momentum shifted back to Anthropic. In just six weeks, Opus 5.5 surged from 7.2% to 37.9% of proprietary-model tokens, lifting Anthropic's overall share from 57.6% to 68.8%. The pattern of shifting workloads between models and providers aggressively matches our own AI strategy at Databricks, where we quickly evaluate and roll out new models. Two months ago, we introduced an internal Day 1 model rollout process which lets us evaluate new releases within days. This process has helped us manage cost while increasing the quality of internal AI efforts. For example, we found Opus 5.5 delivered improved quality at 29% lower cost per session than its predecessor, helping inform our decision to make it the default model for Claude Code. Enterprises are increasingly moving beyond a single AI provider. As recent as July, approximately 64% of enterprises using Unity Gateway relied on just one model provider. By November 2, that had fallen to 28% as more organizations adopted models from more 2 or more providers. Open-weight models are gaining ground alongside this shift. Their share of enterprise token traffic grew from 7.3% in July to 30.9% in November, more than quadrupling in less than four months. Open-weight models are also becoming increasingly competitive with proprietary alternatives. In our coding quality benchmark, three open-weight models rank among the top 10, including DeepSeek V4.1 and GLM 5.3, which both rank third with a 93.1% pass rate. In our research on open-weight models, we find that their growing capabilities, cost efficiency, and flexibility are making them an increasingly attractive option for enterprises. Choosing the right coding agent means evaluating both the model and the harness running it. Our latest coding-agent benchmark evaluates models across nine AI labs using Claude Code and Codex. Five models from four labs (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Meta, and Anthropic) sit on the cost-quality frontier, delivering the best trade-offs between task success rates and cost. The results show why model rankings alone don't tell the full story. Enterprises need to evaluate model and harness combinations against their own workloads, using real usage data and traces to understand the trade-offs between performance and cost. We use this approach internally at Databricks. When evaluating whether to upgrade from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, we analyzed the cost-quality Pareto frontier and replayed traces from our own workloads. The results showed the upgrade wasn't worth the additional cost for our use cases, so we decided to stay on 4.8. Two models can deliver nearly the same benchmark performance at dramatically different costs. In our coding benchmark, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5 both achieved an 89.1% task success rate. However, Luna averaged just $0.05 per task compared with $1.62 for Opus 5.5, a roughly 32x difference. Cost per task depends on both token prices and the amount of work a model must do to reach an answer. Extra turns, long outputs and failed attempts all increase cost. Gemini 3.8 Flash has a low token price, yet it averaged 140 turns per task and finished as one of the most expensive models in the benchmark at $11.97 per task. For coding agents, lower token prices don't guarantee lower costs when models require more work to complete a task. Higher benchmark performance often comes at a steep price, and even small improvements in quality can carry high costs. Claude Fable 5.1 tops our benchmark with a 96.0% task success rate at $7.47 per task, while Muse Wonder scores 94.9% at just $1.53. That additional 1.1 percentage points of performance comes at nearly five times the cost. Enterprises appear to agree, and we saw Fable 5.1's share of proprietary tokens fall from 5.5% to 0.6% over 6 weeks since its launch. The question for enterprises is how much additional quality a task actually requires. Premium models can be worth the cost for complex, high-stakes work, but less expensive alternatives may be sufficient for routine tasks. Intelligent model routing, such as Smart Routing in Unity Gateway, can help match tasks to appropriate models based on quality and cost. AI spending varies dramatically across enterprise users. A developer running coding agents throughout the day has very different consumption patterns from those of an employee who asks an AI assistant a few questions a day. Our data highlights the stark difference: the median user spent just $2.49 on AI, while the 99th-percentile user spent $699.74, roughly 281x more. Median weekly spending more than doubled from $1.10 over six weeks, while spending at the 90th and 99th percentile remained relatively flat. This suggests that AI consumption is growing among typical users, but a small group still accounts for most of the AI bill. For enterprises, the trend makes visibility into the distribution of spending especially important. Understanding those differences helps organizations set more targeted budgets and spend controls without unnecessarily restricting usage.

title: SC26: IBM shows progress in bringing quantum & HPC together
abstract:
At SC26, IBM accelerates progress in bringing quantum & HPC together At SC26 in Chicago, IBM and partners show how quantum computers are integrating into workflows and tools that the supercomputing workforce already runs. Date 16 Nov 2026 Authors Rafi Letzter Topics Error Correction & Mitigation Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key Takeaways: IBM and NVIDIA are integrating the open-source Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) with Slurm’s Hierarchical Resources (HRES) feature to give Slurm, the high-performance computing (HPC) workload manager NVIDIA develops, more visibility into quantum resources and workloads. IBM, RIKEN, and NVIDIA researchers used ROQUO, RIKEN's new GPU supercomputer, to bring an SQD calculation of an iron–sulfur cluster within 4.3 millihartree of DMRG, a classical method known for its high accuracy, 79× closer than earlier SQD work. IBM and NVIDIA, together with Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab), will launch a modular quantum computing co-design platform to explore computationally demanding problems in high-energy and nuclear physics. IBM and AMD announced Pelagos, an open-source framework that tests quantum error correction decoders against billions of simulated error patterns on GPUs. Managed workflows help researchers deploy, reuse, and run quantum-classical workflows on managed, high-performance classical infrastructure. Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM are finalists for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize for simulating protein-ligand complexes of up to 12,635 atoms with quantum and classical computers working together. IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 runs up to 100,000 samples per second, a 25× throughput gain over IBM Quantum Heron. Researchers can start on IBM quantum computers today with the free IBM Quantum Open Plan. This year, IBM and partners demonstrated quantum advantage . The next job is making quantum computers practical tools for science. We are on that path, which runs through high-performance computing (HPC) centers. In an HPC-plus-quantum paradigm , quantum processors, CPUs, and GPUs work together, with each compute tool managing the part of a problem it handles best. But maturing these integrations requires software that fits into existing HPC workflows, integrating highly performant quantum hardware with classical HPC, and access for the researchers who will use them. IBM and partners are bringing new progress on each of these fronts to SC26 , the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage, and Analysis, November 15–20 in Chicago. In particular, we are unveiling new open-source tools that support QPU-GPU integrations across classical hardware vendors, and working with AMD and NVIDIA on software and platforms that bring together advanced classical and quantum hardware for quantum error correction. Integrating quantum computing and HPC Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM are finalists for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize for outstanding achievement in supercomputing. They earned the spot by simulating protein-ligand complexes of up to 12,635 atoms , the largest molecules known to be simulated with quantum computers. This work is an example of quantum-HPC integration. Classical computers broke each complex into clusters and solved the simpler, less entangled ones. To solve the more complex and entangled clusters, the workflow used IBM Quantum Heron processors at Cleveland Clinic and RIKEN alongside classical HPC as part of a method called sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). The team has since automated the workflow using ROQUO, RIKEN’s new supercomputer built on NVIDIA GB200 NVL4 systems. ROQUO also powers new research from IBM, RIKEN, and NVIDIA. The team used SQD to study Fe₄S₄, an iron–sulfur cluster found inside the proteins of living cells. Its strongly interacting electrons make it hard to simulate.
The researchers started SQD from a broken-symmetry reference state, a starting approximation that better captures the magnetic interactions between the cluster's iron atoms. The results came within 4.3 millihartree of the accuracy achieved with the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG), a classical simulation method known for its high accuracy. That's 79× closer than the team's earlier closed-loop SQD result on the same cluster. In Illinois, a team from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (U of I.), the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA), and IBM connected NCSA's DeltaAI supercomputer to an IBM quantum computer. Within six months of expanding their collaboration in April , they used the combined system to model Cu₃C₆O₆, a strongly correlated kagome-lattice metal. Its structure forms a pattern of corner-sharing triangles, and its electrons interact too strongly for standard approximations to describe. The team will present the results at SC26. Platforms for error correction research Error correction research needs the same mix of quantum and classical hardware. Error-correcting codes spread information across many qubits and check them over and over for signs of trouble. A decoder reads each round of checks, works out which errors occurred, and has to keep pace with the quantum processor. That's why ORNL, IBM, and AMD put its classical hardware right next to the qubits in the co-design platform for quantum error correction they launched on November 5. IBM hosts the platform at its site in Poughkeepsie, New York. It pairs IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processors with Umbra, the HPC system of the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Quantum Science Center at ORNL, built on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ CPUs. Researchers use it to develop and test decoders and error correction workflows on real quantum hardware without building that infrastructure themselves. Researchers also test decoders using simulators. That lets them study how a decoder would perform on future quantum computers, or how its performance would change alongside properties like physical error rates. They simulate billions of possible error patterns, feed them into the decoder, and observe how well it corrects them. This takes a lot of classical compute time. IBM and AMD built a new tool called Pelagos to speed them up. The open-source tool runs these tests using GPUs. We wrote Pelagos using the Triton framework, so it runs on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs. Pelagos allowed decoder tests to run up to 97× faster than they would on a single CPU core. Pelagos also enables researchers to distribute decoder simulation workloads across multiple GPUs. While more GPUs can mean more simulation power, orchestrating complex workloads across multiple GPUs can be challenging. Pelagos does this well. The team found that it ran the GPU decoding portion of the workload 7.5× faster across eight AMD Instinct™ MI300X and MI355X accelerators than it did with a single GPU. The team also ran Pelagos on Lux, an AMD-powered system at ORNL. An accompanying survey paper reviews decoding methods using CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and specialized accelerators. Soon IBM and NVIDIA, together with Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab), will launch a modular quantum computing co-design platform to explore computationally demanding problems in high-energy and nuclear physics. This work aligns with the DOE's Quantum Genesis initiative, which aims to deploy the world's first fault-tolerant, scientifically relevant quantum computing capability by 2028. Putting quantum to work through the tools HPC workers already use HPC centers run on schedulers. Slurm, the open-source workload manager that many centers use to queue jobs, decides which job gets which CPUs and GPUs, and when. A quantum processor that sits outside that system leaves researchers to stitch their hybrid jobs together by hand. QRMI is a thin layer of open-source middleware that lets the scheduler treat a quantum processing unit (QPU) as another resource alongside CPUs and GPUs.

title: IBM, AMD advance quantum error correction decoding at scale
abstract: IBM, AMD advance quantum error correction decoding at scale New open-source tool from IBM and AMD helps researchers evaluate quantum error-correction decoders at scale for future fault-tolerant quantum systems. Date 16 Nov 2026 Authors Blake Johnson Robert Davis Topics Software Research Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: IBM and AMD released Pelagos, a new open-source framework for evaluating quantum error-correction decoders at scale. Pelagos uses GPU acceleration to help researchers run large decoder-evaluation campaigns more efficiently across modern computing infrastructure. New research demonstrates efficient multi-GPU scaling for Pelagos on AMD Instinct™ accelerators and ORNL HPC systems. An accompanying survey paper examines the growing role of decoding systems, classical infrastructure, and hardware-software co-design in fault-tolerant quantum computing. Together, these efforts support the IBM-AMD vision for quantum-centric supercomputing and the recently launched quantum error-correction co-design platform. Earlier this month, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and AMD announced a new quantum error-correction co-design platform that brings together IBM quantum processors and AMD-powered HPC infrastructure. At SC26, the collaboration is taking another step toward that vision with the open-source release of Pelagos , a GPU-accelerated framework designed to help researchers evaluate quantum error-correction decoders at scale. Dealing with quantum computers means dealing with quantum errors. To make quantum computing useful at scale, we must detect and correct those errors continuously—and much of the computational work surrounding that process happens on classical computers. As quantum error correction advances, proving that a decoder works becomes increasingly computationally demanding. Researchers often need to evaluate billions of sampled error patterns to understand how a decoder performs under realistic conditions. Those studies can require large simulation campaigns and substantial classical computing resources. Pelagos was built to make that work faster, more scalable, and more accessible to the broader research community. Alongside the Pelagos release, IBM and AMD are publishing new research demonstrating how the framework scales efficiently across multiple GPUs, including deployments on AMD-powered HPC systems. An accompanying survey paper places these developments in a broader context, highlighting the growing importance of classical infrastructure, decoding systems, and hardware-software co-design in the future of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Its central message is that fault-tolerant quantum computing will require advances not just in quantum hardware, but also in the classical systems responsible for decoding, orchestration, and data movement. The path to fault-tolerant quantum computing is an enormous classical-computing challenge, requiring CPUs, GPUs and sophisticated software to process, evaluate and ultimately help correct errors at tremendous scale. That's where IBM and AMD see an opportunity to bring together leadership quantum technology and high-performance classical computing. Accelerating decoder research with Pelagos Quantum computers are inherently susceptible to errors, making quantum error correction a foundational requirement for useful large-scale quantum computing. Error-correcting codes protect quantum information by continuously checking for signs that an error has occurred. Those checks generate data known as syndromes, which identify where an error may have happened without revealing the underlying quantum information itself. A decoder analyzes those syndromes and determines the most likely correction. As codes grow larger and researchers push toward lower logical error rates, evaluating decoder performance requires increasingly large simulation campaigns and substantial classical computing resources. Pelagos, named after the Greek word for “open sea,” is designed to help researchers navigate the challenge of decoder evaluation. Developing better decoders is essential for reliable quantum computing, but evaluating them can be extraordinarily expensive. Pelagos accelerates this workflow by combining GPU acceleration with a developer-friendly software architecture. Built using the Triton programming framework , it supports both AMD and NVIDIA GPU environments while providing a common platform for large-scale decoder evaluation. Built as an open-source framework, Pelagos gives researchers an approachable, reusable foundation for developing and evaluating new decoder algorithms. The result is a tool designed for quantum error-correction researchers, decoder developers, and HPC practitioners alike. Earlier studies showed Pelagos delivering up to 97× higher throughput than a single CPU core and performance comparable to hundreds of CPU cores for decoder-evaluation workloads. By making the framework open source, IBM and AMD aim to lower barriers to experimentation and encourage broader collaboration across the community. The release is accompanied by new research focused on scaling Pelagos across modern multi-GPU systems. While Pelagos already enabled large distributed studies, the new work improves how individual compute nodes coordinate and utilize multiple GPUs. The approach uses process-level orchestration, parallel host-side operations, and shared-memory techniques to maximize throughput while minimizing coordination overhead. Tests on AMD Instinct™ MI300X and MI355X accelerators demonstrated strong scaling across eight GPUs, with the GPU decoding stage achieving speedups of up to roughly 7.5× relative to a single-GPU configuration. Researchers also deployed the framework on Lux, an AMD-powered system at ORNL, illustrating how Pelagos can take advantage of production-class HPC infrastructure. Scaling quantum error correction for the HPC era For the HPC community, these results show how modern GPU infrastructure can accelerate decoder-evaluation studies as quantum error-correction codes and decoders become more sophisticated. As researchers investigate larger codes, more sophisticated decoders, and lower target error rates, the classical resources required to evaluate those systems continue to grow. Efficient use of GPUs and large-scale compute environments will play an increasingly important role in advancing the field. That broader trend is explored in the accompanying survey paper on hierarchical decoding for quantum error correction. The paper reviews the rapidly expanding landscape of decoding algorithms, execution strategies, and hardware platforms, from CPUs and GPUs to FPGAs and specialized accelerators. Viewed in that context, Pelagos becomes more than a software release. It is a practical example of the kind of infrastructure the field increasingly needs. The survey paper provides a framework for understanding the growing demands of decoding systems, while Pelagos gives researchers a concrete tool they can use today to explore solutions. The project also reflects the broader direction of IBM and AMD's collaboration. The recently launched ORNL-IBM-AMD quantum error-correction co-design platform combines IBM quantum hardware with AMD CPUs and GPUs in a shared environment optimized for low-latency quantum-classical workflows. Pelagos complements that effort by helping researchers develop and validate the decoding techniques that future error-corrected systems will depend upon. Building the infrastructure for fault-tolerant quantum computing As the quantum industry moves toward larger logical systems and increasingly sophisticated error-correction strategies, collaboration between quantum and classical computing communities will become even more important. Pelagos is designed to help bridge those worlds by bringing modern HPC techniques to one of the most important challenges in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
abstract: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC . The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons. The company has demonstrated a humanoid robot named the Phantom MK-1 and is touting an upcoming robot called the Phantom MK-2. Foundation has touted its humanoid robots for roles in warehouses and other workplaces—but has courted media coverage by claiming it is developing humanoid robots for battlefield use. Now CNBC’s reporting based on “people with direct knowledge of the matter” indicates that insiders worry the startup could soon collapse without additional funding. Foundation’s business claims Eric Trump holds an equity stake in Foundation and was announced as its chief strategy advisor in March 2026, according to the Financial Times . Investment funds linked to both Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are involved with multiple military technology companies that have received Pentagon loans and contracts worth more than $3.2 billion as of July 2026, according to The Washington Post .

title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
abstract: On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop "more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”

title: Jensen Huang allies build a "war room" to get him back at Nvidia
abstract: Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the company’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate. Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip company this week. One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they said. The efforts had Huang’s support, they added. A public campaign to reinstate Huang has gathered steam over the weekend. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among executives backing a public letter demanding that its board “Bring Jensen Back.” Huang continues to command fierce loyalty from some employees, several of whom have gone public in calling for his return in the days since he resigned and have signed the open letter.

title: Fable 5.2 is the New Bazooka
abstract: You do not always want a bazooka. Sometimes, though, you absolutely want a bazooka. That’s what Claude Fable 5.2 is for. This is your bazooka. For most purposes, for a thousand household uses, Claude Fable 5.2 will not be appreciably better than Claude Opus 5.5. You might or might not prefer its style, or prefer it for any given task. If you are staying within your quota either way then both are good choices for a daily driver. When you have a difficult task, or a very complex task, or a long task? The kind of task where prior to this you would have considered reaching for Astra? The kind of task that raises your ambitions? It’s time. Get the bazooka. Ethan Mollick calls Fable 5.2 ‘almost’ AGI, or ‘jagged AGI .’ He asked it to do the most impressive thing it could, then to hack some hardware, start a profitable business, reconstruct history’s hardest humanities class and do (actually interesting and useful) original academic research , The Official Pitch Fable 5.2 is considerably cheaper than Fable 5.1. They’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.1 was slow. Fable 5.2 is substantially faster. Try Claude : They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1. You can make it even faster, by a factor of 2.5, if you are willing to double the price to $16/$80. That is a remarkably good deal. And it communicates more clearly. ​ Try Claude : Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. The first wave of testimonials talk about how Mythos 5.2 solves problems and finds issues that other models do not, and how it understands your intent. It is Anthropic’s most capable public model for cybersecurity engineering. Later waves of testimonials talk about providing exceptional performance. The statements are still AI-written, but they feel scarier and more substantial these days. Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics, one working largely anonymously : The spinless modular bootstrap at central charge and the Hawking-Page transition at weak coupling . They claim major progress in robotics and hardware engineering. Claude : Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots, even on tasks it has never explicitly been trained to do. On RoboDojo, a benchmark with a simulated two-arm robot, it outperformed other models and most AI systems built to control robots. Alex Albert (Anthropic, Claude Relations): btw robotics will fall to the bitter lesson too Anthropic : Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world , showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots. … Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots. The system prompt is here as per our friend Pliny, clocking in at 950k characters . Time to run the ‘read this entire project and fix everything’ prompts again . Choose Your Fighter Anthropic recommends that you default most tasks to Opus 5.5 at medium effort . For well-scoped everyday work you can move down to Sonnet 5.5, or to Haiku 5.5 for the simplest high-volume work like classification, routing and extraction. Move up to Fable 5.2 for the hardest technical projects in coding, finance and the sciences. Or in some cases you can move to high effort, but if you’re considering max you probably want to move to a bigger model instead. Or, if you don’t want to leave a person hanging, go fast: Addy Osmani (claude.dev Blog): A faster setup finishes sooner and can miss more. Think through how long a person can wait before you pick your model and effort level. For replies a person waits on, start Sonnet 5.5 at low or medium . Often next generation models are faster than their predecessors. Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1. Sonnet 5.5 runs 30% faster than Sonnet 5. This all seems like reasonable advice if you are scaling what you are doing, and thus will be using a lot of tokens. If things are not going to scale, I find it is more important to not have to think hard about which models and effort levels to be using. As in, my decision tree is by default to continue to use Opus 5.5 for most things. For editing I use Opus 5.5 on Max, unless I am in a hurry, much to Fable 5.2’s chagrin, because Opus 5.5 is actively better there and there’s no reason not to max out. Fable 5.2 is there for when I need it for other task types. Official Benchmarks Some benchmarks show minimal gains over Opus 5.5 whereas others show large gains. Opus 5.5 still has the edge in a few places, GDPval-AA and AA-Briefcase Elo, where a judge evaluates the deliverable rather than the evaluation being fully objective. Remote Labor Index (RLI) stands out as a large and important gain. This alone establishes that Fable 5.2 can importantly handle previously impossible tasks. Here are their chosen charts from the model card and the official announcement: There are several other evals listed that did not make the chart, many of which did not show substantial improvement. Here are most of them, slash lines are [without/with tools], some of which had additional compute scaling charts. When unstated the comparison is to the best past Claude model score: DeepSWE v1.1 of 74.3%. Terminal-Bench 4.0 67.6% versus 66.4% for Opus 5.5 or 55.8% for Fable 5.1, and a public leaderboard of GPT-6.1 Sol at 58.2%. Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 of 74.6% versus 58.7% for Opus 5.5 and 68% for Astra. CursorBench 4.0 of 60% versus 58% for Opus 5.5. STEM professor bench of 61.8% versus 53.7% for Opus 5.5. ProgramBench of 85.6% versus 87.6% for Fable 5.1 and 91.2% for Opus 5.5. DRACO got to 87.7% still slightly short of Opus 5.5 at 88.3%. WANDR improved from 72.3% to 82.1%. Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean improved from 21% to 35% for max team size. A team of 1,000 agents then fully formalized the proof in 30 hours. Chartography on Opus 5.5 from 64/89 to 73/92. BenchCAD 2.1 improved from 49/65 to 75/83. OSWorld 2.1 improved from 87 to 89 for partial, 53 to 55 for strict. OfficeQA improved from 80% to 83%, or 69% to 73% for Pro. Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) improved from 6.4% to 7.2%. Astra scores 8.6%. AutomationBench improved from 42.5% to 51.4%, essentially via spending more. Carbon has the lead there at 53.9%. Real-World Finance v2 improved its Elo from 1571 to 1637. ARC-AGI-3 verified at 79% standard harness or 97.7% with provider harness. That is a new high for standard harness, but below Astra’s 98.6% for provider harness. HealthBench struggled, down from 62% to 60% length-adjusted. HealthBench Professional looks better, up from 63% to 67% length-adjusted. PhysicianBench also struggled, down from 68% to 64%. Card called this noise. GMMLU is up from 94% to 96%. MLU is up from 93% to 94%. Various life sciences numbers were up a little bit (see 8.18). Two were up a lot. CVE rediscovery improved from 81% to 90%. If you limit the number of reports, the leads go down. Other People’s Benchmarks Come get your benchmarks. Here is the updated ‘standard benchmarks’ chart: Fable 5.2 is the clear leader on the Artificial Analysis intelligence index. It gets a 62 on high, a 65 on max.

title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
abstract: This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right. BFL explains what a still image, a moving camera and a soundtrack each contribute during training. FLUX 3 launch and research overview Watch and listen to the results of generating video and sound together. FLUX 3 Video demos See how the lab teaches a model to make a requested change while preserving the rest of an image. FLUX Kontext examples Andreas Blattmann co-created Stable Diffusion and co-invented the latent diffusion method behind it. Guest bio · Original research Dustin Podell led FLUX Kontext and was the lead author of SDXL. Dustin’s project credits · FLUX Kontext · SDXL The first Latent Space essay grew out of the Stable Diffusion release.
