title: MosaicKV: SLO-Aware KV-Cache Virtualization for Multi-Tenant LLM Serving in the Cloud
abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving has become a first-class cloud workload. The dominant cost driver is no longer compute alone. The key-value (KV) cache consumes tens of gigabytes per replica. It forces providers to either over-provision GPU memory or reject long-context requests. Existing high-throughput engines largely optimize within a single server. They assume KV stays resident in GPU HBM. Under multi-tenancy, HBM is routinely oversubscribed. Naive offloading (e.g., CUDA Unified Memory paging) then creates severe p99 TTFT spikes. These spikes break service-level objectives (SLOs). This paper presents MosaicKV, a KV-cache virtualization layer for multi-tenant LLM inference on shared GPU servers. MosaicKV exposes KV as a schedulable and migratable resource. It jointly optimizes GPU-memory partitioning across tenants. It decides which KV pages stay on HBM versus spill to host DRAM. It also times prefetch and micro-batching to hide PCIe DMA transfer latency. The key insight is that decoding has a predictable layer-by-layer access pattern. By co-designing page layout with a slack-aware scheduler, MosaicKV turns KV offload from reactive paging into a planned pipeline. On an 8-GPU server (8 × H100 SXM 80 GB) serving Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-32B, and Mixtral-8x7B under a 64-tenant mixed workload, MosaicKV improves goodput-under-SLO by 1.93–2.31 × under the same SLO contract (p99 TTFT ≤ 400 ms for interactive tenants; p99 completion ≤ 2 s for best-effort tenants) while reducing peak HBM KV footprint by 38%. Under flash-crowd bursts, MosaicKV keeps interactive-tenant p99 TTFT at 378–386 ms (within SLO). Unified Memory spikes to 1,055 ms (∼ 2.6 × SLO). MosaicKV achieves these gains without model changes. Runtime overhead remains modest (2.9–6.2%). This enables operators to safely run long-context and bursty tenants on shared GPU fleets.

title: Evaluating Agentic Systems Across the Lifecycle: A Taxonomy of Drifts and Success Criteria
abstract: Benchmarks like SWE-bench evaluate agents by checking whether a code patch passes a test suite. But what do you do when there is no test suite—when a “correct” investigation can take dozens of valid paths through 108 tools, and the only judge is an experienced engineer? This is the reality for enterprise agentic systems deployed in domains like site reliability engineering, where the unique combination of agent, model, tools, and business context makes general-purpose benchmarks inapplicable. We present a framework for evaluating such systems across their full lifecycle. We propose three complementary evaluation methods: a static validator that checks deterministic rules against agent traces (zero LLM cost, 34% pass rate on our corpus), a sub-agent auditor that uses an LLM to judge a structured summary (4.4K tokens/eval, 89% pass rate), and an observer agent that analyzes the full execution trace (8.2K tokens/eval, 74% pass rate). Majority-vote consensus across the three yields a 74% pass rate with zero cases of complete disagreement. We systematize six categories of drift that cause validated agents to degrade in production—model, prompt, tool availability, scope of access, third-party systems, and success criteria—and define detection and response strategies for each. We validate on a production SRE agent swarm with 108 tools across seven operational domains (Kubernetes, MongoDB, ArgoCD, Grafana, Temporal, JFrog, YugabyteDB), processing 53 alerts spanning 9 categories.

title: Memory-Decoupled Layer-Wise Fine-Tuning for Efficient On-Device LLM Adaptation
abstract: Federated Fine-Tuning (FFT) is essential for customizing Large Language Models (LLMs) at the edge while preserving data privacy. However, its scalability is severely constrained by the memory bottleneck. Our analysis reveals that the massive static memory footprint of LLM parameters exceeds the physical capacity of edge devices, rendering standard end-to-end training infeasible. In this paper, we propose EdgeLLM, a Cloud-Edge memory management system that democratizes efficient edge LLM adaptation via progressive layer training. Specifically, EdgeLLM re-architects the training process into a sequential pipeline: it dynamically manages the device memory hierarchy by maintaining only a minimal granular subset of layers on-chip while aggressively offloading inactive ones. To maximize system efficiency and convergence stability, EdgeLLM integrates four key components: (1) Resource Scheduler, which continuously probes device runtime memory availability to maximize resource utilization via dynamic workload mapping; (2) Training Coordinator, which bridges the semantic gap caused by offloading via virtualized context synthesis, ensuring coherent feature learning without full-graph residence; (3) Execution Planner, which optimizes the computation path by intelligently pruning redundancy and prioritizing task-critical layers for targeted adaptation; and (4) I/O Manager, which neutralizes the layer-swapping overhead through asynchronous prefetching and eviction. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that EdgeLLM effectively breaks the memory wall, unlocking participation for resource-constrained devices previously excluded from the training cohort. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, EdgeLLM delivers up to 11.86% performance improvement, accelerates model convergence by 2.08 × , and reduces communication overhead by 1.78 ×.

title: Familiar-Other Framing: Can Framing Project Pre-Existing Relationships with Familiar Others onto Dialogue Systems?
abstract: With recent advancements in large language models, the development of dialogue systems that imitate specific individuals has progressed, allowing users to project their impressions of the target person onto the system designed to imitate someone with whom they have a relationship, referred to as a familiar other. However, the impact of framing alone—informing users that the system is imitating a familiar other—on user impressions of the system remains unclear. To investigate this, we conducted an evaluation using a course support dialogue system. The results revealed that among students who rated their relationship with the course instructor highly, framing enhanced the perception of the system as a familiar other, even in a system that did not incorporate utterance imitation.

title: “I Can Talk to AI, but the Making Is Mine” Professional Artists’ Use of Generative Agents for Creative Work
abstract: Survey research finds that professional visual artists overwhelmingly dislike generative AI, yet many encounter it in their working lives. We interviewed five professional visual artists working across physical and digital media about where in the creative process they use a generative agent, how they use it, and why they use it in some phases and not others. We mapped the interviews onto the four phases of Mace and Ward’s model of the creative process. Participants used the agent only for gathering information within artwork conception and for developing ideas, and they kept idea conception, making, and finishing to themselves, citing authorship, craft, and the fear of feeding the model. We offer this account as a record of how professional artists place a generative agent while capabilities and norms are still taking shape.

title: A Concept of a Dialogue System Using a Stereotypical Mental Model of Others
abstract: In order for Large Language Models to communicate smoothly with humans, it is necessary to read “unstated intentions”—intentions that are not explicitly expressed in the interlocutor’s utterances. Previous studies proposed dialogue systems that respond while inferring the interlocutor’s unstated intentions; however, the beliefs and desires that form the basis of these intentions were fixed regardless of the interlocutor. In this study, we propose a dialogue system that sets predefined stereotypical Mental Models of Others for each assumed interlocutor type and generates responses by switching to the appropriate model based on the interlocutor’s utterances.

title: Shared View, Different Readings: Human–AI Alignment in Place Interpretation for XR Agents
abstract: AI agents in smart glasses and XR devices may share users’ views yet interpret places differently. In this study, we compared interpretations from 12 participants and Gemini 3.1 Pro across twelve places using matched field-of-view recordings. Compared with disagreement among humans, human–AI gaps were larger for place meaning and important cues; no additional gap was detected for place function or activity contexts. AI ratings tracked human patterns across scenes but varied less and showed little correspondence with individual differences within the same scene. These findings position functional judgments as tentative defaults but call for greater care with place meanings, cues, and individual impressions.

title: Registers Have Rhythms: Crossing Speech Style with Reply Timing in an LLM Journaling Agent
abstract: An agent that answers instantly and is never away keeps the rhythm of a service desk, seating its user as a customer. A register is indexed across several channels, so a peer relationship may require congruence between speech and timing. We demonstrate a local-LLM journaling agent implementing ma, the meaningful interval between turns, through a stochastic delay, a deferred read receipt, per-sentence message bursts, and push notifications. Prior work studies a user waiting at the screen; withholding the receipt lets them leave. In a within-subject pilot (N = 5), Likert ratings tracked phase order, not condition; the condition difference appears in what participants said. Three of five raised the read receipt unprompted, in the vocabulary of interpersonal obligation, and two said the agent’s speech style constrained their writing. At the booth, visitors cross speech style with timing, including the incongruent pairings we could not run.

title: The Delegation Boundary: Willingness to Delegate to AI Agents Depends on Retained Override More Than on Domain
abstract: What people hand over to an AI agent has a boundary: a point at which advice becomes action taken on their behalf. We examine that distinction across six agent scenarios rated by 296 U.S. adults, analyzed as 3 (domain) × 2 (advisory versus substitutive). Advisory scenarios received higher ratings in each domain, with a larger partial η2 for scenario category than for domain (.465 versus.053). The contrast was positive in every subgroup examined, but domain-specific differences showed low internal consistency (α =.08), giving limited support for a single cross-domain tendency. Objective AI knowledge and awareness of model limitations were associated with overall willingness in opposite directions. These vignette contrasts do not isolate a causal effect of retained override.

title: The AI engagement paradox: algorithmic congruence and its inverted-U effect on tourist experience quality
abstract:
Despite widespread adoption of AI agents in restaurant and gastronomic tourism settings across Asia, practitioners consistently observe a counterintuitive pattern: increasing AI service involvement initially enhances but subsequently undermines tourist experience quality. This study aims to term this the “AI engagement paradox” and introduce algorithmic hospitality congruence (AHC), a new second-order construct to theorise and empirically confirm the inverted-U relationship between AI congruence and gastronomic tourist experience quality (GTEQ).
 
 
 
 A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was used across three Asian markets (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok). Phase 1 comprised 24 semi-structured interviews using the critical incident technique to develop AHC construct items. Phase 2 involved a quantitative survey (N = 412). AHC was grounded in cognitive load theory (CLT). Polynomial regression with response surface methodology confirmed the inverted-U effect; partial least squares structural equation modelling validated the construct. Common-method-bias mitigation and endogeneity-robustness checks used temporal separation, Harman’s single-factor test with a marker variable and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction.
 
 
 
 AHC comprising culinary AI precision (CAP), emotional service resonance and cultural contextual fit (CCF) demonstrated robust construct and discriminant validity. AHC exhibited a significant inverted-U effect on GTEQ. Cultural collectivism steepened the negative slope, while digital literacy shifted the tipping point rightward.
 
 
 
 This study delivers empirically grounded deployment guidance for hospitality operators in AI-integrated gastronomic settings. The validated 15-item AHC scale provides a diagnostic instrument for monitoring AI-experience alignment. Operators are advised to benchmark their AHC composite score against the estimated tipping-point zone (4.18–5.04 on a seven-point scale), differentiate deployment intensity by tourist digital literacy, apply conservative ceiling margins for high-collectivist segments and treat CCF as a foundational design requirement rather than a localisation afterthought. Digital literacy investment is reframed as a direct hospitality revenue strategy.
 
 
 
 This is among the first studies to theorise and empirically confirm an inverted-U effect of AI congruence in gastronomic tourism. AHC is rigorously differentiated from five related constructs and grounded in CLT from the outset. The findings challenge the linear AI benefit assumption dominant in hospitality AI research and provide indicative deployment guidance for practitioners.

title: Pick Your Poison: Effects of Miscalibrated AI Advice and Silent Updates on Reliance
abstract: In AI-assisted decision-making, achieving warranted trust is essential: users should follow accurate advice while rejecting wrong suggestions. But as LLM-based AI agents reshape decision support, such agents often display miscalibrated confidence – ranging from confidently incorrect hallucinations to overly non-committal hedging. To understand how this behavior and unannounced system changes impact user trust, we conducted a two-phase online study (N=90) evaluating advice-seeking and reliance after confidence calibration is silently updated. We found that users’ willingness to seek AI advice is driven overwhelmingly by their pre-existing (positive) attitudes toward AI, not by the system’s prior performance. However, once they actively consult the AI, their reliance is significantly higher if they previously encountered a confidently incorrect or a non-committal system rather than a calibrated baseline. This effect dampens over time, with qualitative insights showing how unannounced background changes can erode perceived quality. These findings demonstrate that safe AI integration requires addressing individual user biases and transparently communicating updates.

title: Human Oversight in Agentic AI: Explainability, Anthropomorphism, and the Boundary of Cognitive Forcing
abstract: Explainability helps users assess evidence behind an AI recommendation, but it may not change decisions when that evidence goes unexamined. The problem is sharper in agentic decision support, where one assistant interprets evidence, explains its assessment, and recommends an action, while anthropomorphic delivery may add social credibility. Cognitive forcing, operationalised here as Human Intervention Checkpoints (HICs), requires users to specify what the assistant should examine before it recommends. We report a randomised 2 × 2 × 2 hiring experiment (N = 211) in which recruiters assessed a candidate whose unmet role-critical requirements were stated in every recommendation. Advancement was not associated with explanatory provenance, anthropomorphic delivery, HIC presence, or opening source documents. Post-task perceived explainability was associated with perceived anthropomorphism and trust, and trust was associated with advancement. In HIC-present conditions, 70 participants directed the assistant to a role-critical requirement and received Hold, yet 46 advanced. The findings identify a boundary of cognitive forcing: influence over what the agent evaluated and recommended did not reliably carry through to the final human decision.

title: Surgical Suppression of LLM Sycophancy via Sparse Autoencoder Feature Intervention
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy: they bend analyses toward a user’s stated preference rather than maintain an objective stance, undermining their value as decision-support agents in human–agent interaction. We propose a fine-grained intervention that suppresses sycophantic behavior without retraining. Using a pre-trained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) on the residual stream of gemma-2-9b-it, we decompose hidden states into sparse interpretable features. Candidate sycophancy features are selected by combining a gradient-based importance score with a sycophancy-specificity log-ratio and removed at inference time via zero-ablation. On the SycophancyEval Feedback benchmark, intervening at layer 31 reduces the sycophancy rate from \(41.0\%\) to \(34.8\%\) (p < 0.001, McNemar), turns \(34.7\%\) of originally sycophantic responses neutral, and improves fluency. The effect transfers to held-out prompts, consistent with a substantial part of sycophancy being mediated by a small set of late-layer features, and suggesting sparse features as a runtime control surface for keeping interactive agents objective.

title: “I check it when it feels wrong” – Computer Science Student Usage and Perspectives on AI Chatbots
abstract: We present a qualitative interview study with 17 Canadian computer science and software engineering undergraduates exploring their self-initiated, unsupervised AI chatbot use. We find that most participants, despite being CS students often assumed to have stronger technical intuitions, lacked an accurate understanding of how generative AI produces output. This miscalibration was associated with plausibility-based fact-checking: participants who described genAI as a retrieval or database system had no reliable trigger for verifying confidently-stated misinformation. We discuss implications for AI literacy education and human-AI interaction design.

title: AutoPrompt: A Real-Time Multimodal Agent for Closed-Loop Interaction through Generative Visuals in Live Performance
abstract: Recent advances in multi-agentic AI enables the interaction of multiple specialised AI agents rather than a single general-purpose AI. However, there has been little exploration of how this can be used within the creative community. We present AutoPrompt, a real-time multimodal agent that perceives a performer’s vocal and visual expression and generates prompts for a generative visual system, forming a closed perception-action loop in live performance. We tested AutoPrompt with two professional dancers during a workshop where their movement, language and emotions influenced live AI-generated visuals. Through this workshop we identified which modalities and mechanisms support creative expression and explored the benefits and limitations of the system, laying the groundwork for future work to examine how multi-agent AI can be better integrated into the creative arts.

title: Predict Me if You Can: Simulating User Responses with Synthetic Data: Evaluating the Fidelity of LLM-Based Synthetic Respondents
abstract: Conditioning language models on persona profiles is standard practice for generating synthetic survey responses, yet the relative contribution of different attributes to the fidelity of synthetic survey responses has not been systematically quantified. To test this, we conditioned four large language models (LLMs) on profiles of 258 employed South Korean adults surveyed on AI-related job replacement risk. We grouped 11 attributes into three blocks (demographics, socioeconomic position & ideology, experience) and evaluated four cumulative levels of persona richness. A leave-one-out ablation identified the most impactful block. Fidelity generally rose with richer personas, and ablation showed that only experience-related attributes contributed meaningfully, while demographic attributes were net-neutral at best. For human-agent interaction (HAI) research with synthetic respondents, fidelity hinges on attribute relevance, not information quantity — neither the largest model nor all attributes maximize it.

title: Gradis:A Human–AI Collaborative Framework for Workforce-Aligned Curriculum Generation and Personalized Learning
abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and evolving workforce requirements have widened the gap between traditional educational curricula and industry needs. Recent developments in large language models (LLMs) and intelligent tutoring systems have improved curriculum generation and personalized learning experiences. However, most existing solutions remain focused on isolated educational tasks and lack a unified framework that integrates workforce intelligence, organizational knowledge, human expertise, and adaptive learning. This paper proposes Gradis, a human–AI collaborative framework for workforce-aligned curriculum generation and personalized learning. Gradis integrates organizational knowledge, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and human expert validation to support the generation and expert-guided refinement of adaptive curricula in response to changing industry needs. Unlike fully automated educational systems, Gradis positions human experts as key decision-makers throughout the curriculum lifecycle while leveraging AI to improve scalability, efficiency, and personalization.

title: Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies
abstract: As social agents, robots, conversational AI systems, and virtual characters become embedded in everyday environments, HAI is shifting from isolated one-human/one-agent interaction toward socially embedded multi-person and multi-agent settings. This workshop explores how trust, blame, and responsibility emerge, become distributed, and are negotiated among users, agents, developers, institutions, bystanders, and broader social contexts. We focus on agents as social participants in complex environments, including group dynamics, psychological safety, agent refusal, moral consideration, and legal or governance questions. The workshop aims to develop a preliminary issue map, research agenda, and interdisciplinary network for socially sustainable human-agent societies.

title: Exploring How Anthropomorphism and Autonomy Affect Users’ Politeness Toward AI Chatbots in Psychological Support Contexts
abstract: The Media Equation Theory, proposed in the last century, suggests that people tend to respond politely to computers mindlessly, as they would to humans. In the generative AI era, however, both the forms of user interaction interfaces and the usage contexts of AI have evolved significantly. This prompts us to revisit the classic theory and conduct more nuanced studies to reexamine it. Specifically, we explore users’ politeness toward AI chatbots in the context of psychological support through two controlled experiments, focusing on two factors marginalized by the Media Equation Theory: anthropomorphism and autonomy. Study 1 examined the effects of anthropomorphism and perceived autonomy on users’ self-reported politeness toward chatbots through a human-chatbot conversation experiment. Study 2 incorporated gender as an additional variable and conducted a follow-up experiment. Results showed that chatbots’ appearance anthropomorphism negatively predicted users’ politeness, whereas perceived autonomy positively predicted users’ politeness. Follow-up interviews further indicated that politeness toward AI chatbots follows a different logic from the mindlessness proposed by the Media Equation Theory, revealing the paradoxical coexistence of users’ conscious awareness of AI’s non-human nature and their expectations for human-like capabilities. Overall, this work seeks to extend the classic theory in human-AI interaction and provide implications for the design of AI chatbots.

title: From Perceived Trust to Delegation in Agentic AI: Reliability, Apparent Bistability, and Delegation Thresholds
abstract: Trust is central to human–agent interaction, but agentic AI raises a stronger question: when does perceived trust translate into delegated action? This poster introduces an agent-based simulation in which agents delegate when trust exceeds a threshold, observe success or failure, and update trust through outcome feedback with tunable failure sensitivity. We vary AI reliability and delegation thresholds while examining social conformity and failure sensitivity. Results show that unreliable systems drive abandonment, while intermediate regimes can produce apparent bistability: identical AI reliability can lead to adoption or rejection depending on initial trust and the delegation threshold. Conformity can sustain delegation by preventing isolated trust collapse. These findings suggest that delegation thresholds act as control parameters for sustained reliance. Future work will validate the model with human participants and heterogeneous agent profiles and tasks.

title: Sincerity or Treasure: Bounded Strategic Communication Gameplay with LLM Agent
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents enable new forms of human-agent interaction by supporting flexible reasoning and natural language communication. However, unrestricted interaction often makes agent behavior difficult to understand and strategically engage with. This work presents Sincerity or Treasure, an AI-native strategy game that investigates how humans influence an LLM agent through bounded strategic communication. In the game, players interact with Jesika, an LLM-driven character, by selectively revealing limited clues and adding natural-language framing. Instead of treating language as simple dialogue, the game makes information selection and linguistic framing strategic actions. A preliminary study with 26 participants shows that players adapted their communication strategies through deception, trust management, and adjustment of expression. These findings suggest that bounded strategic communication can create meaningful gameplay and interaction space where an agent's reasoning process becomes a central component of game system.

title: Simulating Mutual Subjectivity: An Agent-Based Framework with LLM-Generated Dual-Perspective Reports for Tethered Side-by-Side Walking
abstract: Two people walking side by side negotiate direction continuously, with neither fully leading nor following. This paper presents a prototype simulation framework for studying such mutual subjectivity in tethered side-by-side walking. Two agents joined by an ON/OFF tether are each governed by a Self-Fulfillment Drive and a Relatedness Drive, and a large language model (LLM) generates pseudo-subjective reports from both perspectives. In an illustrative run, the agent configured for high relatedness read a slack tether as separation — inverting the semantics the model assigns to that state. Because the error tracks the very parameter the framework exists to vary, we argue it is a structural hazard for any use of LLMs to voice simulated agent state, not merely an underspecified prompt.

title: Autonomy of Boundedly Rational Agents in Dyadic Interactions
abstract: AI agents now work alongside people in domains ranging from autonomous vehicles to conversational systems. A recurring question is when an agent’s behavior counts as self-determined rather than merely reactive to its human partner. This matters for ethical conduct, which is widely argued to require some form of autonomy. Yet, its computational meaning is rarely made precise. In this paper, we study an agent’s autonomy in dyadic interactions, measured by the extent to which the agent’s behavior is explained by its own state rather than by its partner’s signals. This quantity captures information-theoretic self-determination as inferred from interaction traces. We characterize autonomy as a function of how deterministically the agent acts, how strongly it optimizes payoffs, and how much past interaction it retains. Using analytical and numerical results from four distinct games, we find that autonomy peaks at high but sub-maximal determinism and is dissociable from rationality. All four settings achieve the same level of autonomy regardless of the agent’s payoff disposition, so rationality never raises the ceiling. What the payoff structure determines is the direction in which rationality trades against determinism. Payoff-seeking play economizes on determinism in one setting, payoff-avoiding play in another, and neither matters where the agent cannot influence its payoff. Our results suggest design principles for interactive agents that remain consistent and self-determined.

title: A Real-time Multimodal Adaptive Mixed Reality System for Procedural Task Guidance
abstract: Procedural tasks often require users to interpret instructions, monitor task progress, and recover from errors while interacting with physical objects. Mixed reality (MR) can support such tasks by presenting guidance directly within the user’s workspace. However, providing effective assistance remains challenging as user behavior, task progress, and support requirements may vary. We present a real-time multimodal adaptive MR system for procedural task guidance that integrates semantic task tracking, user-state estimation, and adaptive assistance within a unified closed-loop architecture. The system represents procedures as dependency-aware task graphs, continuously tracks task progress , and estimates procedural difficulty from gaze, hand, and head-motion signals. These signals are used to dynamically adapt guidance content, timing, and presentation through an LLM-based assistance module. We implemented the system on Microsoft HoloLens 2 and evaluated it through technical validation and a user study involving 20 participants performing procedural tasks of varying complexity. Results demonstrate robust closed-loop operation, achieving an action-recognition F1 score of 0.97 and 100% step-completion accuracy. User study results indicate that adaptive guidance reduced procedural difficulties and recovery time following task deviations, particularly during more complex procedures.

title: How Does Multi-Agent System Architecture Shape Human-Agent Interaction in Long-Horizon Strategic Tasks?
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly used in tasks requiring coordination, yet existing benchmarks provide limited support for long-horizon studies involving both humans and alternative MAS organizations. We present an agent-agnostic, turn-based strategic simulation for comparing four organizational configurations within a common protocol. The environment combines simultaneous planning, partial observability, territorial competition, and text-based diplomacy. We outline two planned evaluations: AI-only simulations and mixed sessions with two MAS-controlled and four human-controlled players. Outcomes include strategic performance, communication patterns, computational cost, and post-session trust. Because the configurations differ in decision authority, observation scope, communication, and diplomacy, the study compares complete organizational configurations rather than isolated architectural factors. The framework provides a basis for controlled studies of long-term Human-Agent Interaction.

title: Integrating a Multi-Tier Memory Manager into a Educational RAG System
abstract: Large language model agents often perform well within one conversation yet do not persist interaction-derived state, procedures, and user context needed for sustained collaboration when the session ends. This paper presents the integration of a memory-first extension to a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agent, in which memory is treated as an explicit architectural layer rather than an enlarged chat history. The current prototype implements a Memory Core and Memory Manager for persistent conversational, semantic, procedural, and episodic memory. At the same time, the complete memory-aware architecture and its evaluation protocol are presented as ongoing work. Relational tables preserve conversational events, while vector-enabled SQL tables store embedded memory units enriched with timestamps, source, intent, confidence, and lifecycle metadata. Deterministic and agent-triggered operations support read, write, update, and delete operations and context-window segmentation. The proposed interface is designed to expose the memory type and provenance associated with retrieved information. The work reframes agent memory as both an engineering and a human-agent interaction problem: useful persistence requires not only accurate recall, but also transparent, controllable, and correctable remembering.

title: Just an AI: How Do Humans Respond to LLM Disclosure?
abstract: Disclosure of AI limitations, knowledge, and underlying architecture is a transparency mechanism that helps users calibrate expectations and trust-related behavior. However, it is unclear how users respond to such disclosures. We qualitatively analyzed 336 LLM disclosure segments from publicly accessible naturalistic human-LLM conversations. We coded LLM disclosure types, along with their preceding human triggers and subsequent human responses. For human responses, we found that explicit acceptance of LLM disclosure is rare, regardless of the trigger or disclosure type. Instead, users tend to explore further or redirect to a new topic. When users object, they do not object to the disclosure’s informative value but to its repetitive, formulaic delivery. We discuss implications for designing and operationalizing the efficiency of LLM disclosures as transparency mechanisms.
